What are we to think of this? The afferent nerves are images, the brain is an image, the shocks transmitted by the sensory nerves and propagated in the brain are images too. For this image that I call a cerebral shock to engender the external images, it would have to contain them in one way or another, and the representation of the whole material universe would have to be implied in that of this molecular movement. Now, it would suffice to enunciate such a proposition to discover its absurdity. It is the brain that is part of the material world, and not the material world that is part of the brain. Suppress the image which bears the name of material world, and you annihilate at the same time the brain and the cerebral shock which are parts of it. Suppose, on the contrary, that these two images, the brain and the cerebral shock, vanish: by hypothesis you efface only them, that is to say very little, an insignificant detail in an immense picture. The picture as a whole, that is to say the universe, subsists intact. To make the brain the condition of the total image is truly to contradict oneself, since the brain, by hypothesis, is a part of this image. Neither the nerves nor the nerve centres can therefore condition the image of the universe. Let us pause on this last point. Here are the external images, then my body, then finally the modifications brought by my body to the surrounding images. I see well how the external images influence the image that I call my body: they transmit movement to it. And I see also how this body influences the external images: it gives movement back to them. My body is therefore, in the whole of the material world, an image which acts like other images, receiving and giving back movement, with this sole difference, perhaps, that my body appears to choose, within certain limits, the manner of giving back what it receives. But how should my body in general, my nervous system in particular, engender all or part of my representation of the universe? Say that my body is matter or say that it is image, I care little for the word. If it is matter, it is a part of the material world, and the material world, consequently, exists around it and outside it. If it is image, this image can give only what has been put into it, and since it is, by hypothesis, the image of my body only, it would be absurd to wish to draw from it that of the whole universe. My body, an object destined to move objects, is therefore a centre of action; it cannot give birth to a representation. But if my body is an object capable of exercising a real and new action on the objects that surround it, it must occupy in relation to them a privileged situation. In general, any image whatever influences other images in a determinate, even calculable, manner, in conformity with what are called the laws of nature. As it will not have to choose, it has no need either to explore the surrounding region, or to try itself out in advance on several merely possible actions. The necessary action will accomplish itself of its own accord, when its hour has struck. But I have supposed that the rôle of the image that I call my body was to exercise a real influence on other images, and consequently to decide between several materially possible steps. And since these steps are no doubt suggested to it by the greater or lesser advantage it can draw from the surrounding images, these images must needs outline in some manner, on the face they turn towards my body, the use my body could make of them. In fact, I observe that the size, the shape, even the colour of external objects are modified according as my body approaches or recedes from them, that the strength of odours and the intensity of sounds increase and diminish with distance, and finally that this distance itself represents above all the measure in which the surrounding bodies are, in some sort, secured against the immediate action of my body. As my horizon widens, the images that surround me seem to be drawn upon a more uniform ground and to become indifferent to me. The more I narrow this horizon, the more the objects it circumscribes are graded distinctly according to the greater or lesser facility of my body in touching and moving them. They send back to my body, therefore, as a mirror would do, its possible influence; they arrange themselves according to the increasing or decreasing powers of my body. The objects which surround my body reflect its possible action upon them. I will now, without touching the other images, modify slightly the one I call my body. In this image I sever in thought all the afferent nerves of the cerebro-spinal system. What is going to happen? A few strokes of the scalpel will have cut through a few bundles of fibres: the rest of the universe, and even the rest of my body, will remain what they were. The change effected is therefore insignificant. In fact, "my perception" as a whole vanishes. Let us then examine more closely what has just taken place. Here are the images which make up the universe in general, then those which surround my body, and then, finally, my body itself. In this last image, the habitual rôle of the centripetal nerves is to transmit movements to the brain and the spinal cord; the centrifugal nerves send this movement back to the periphery. The severing of the centripetal nerves can therefore produce only one really intelligible effect, which is to interrupt the current that runs from the periphery to the periphery by way of the centre; it is, consequently, to put my body in the impossibility of drawing, from amid the things that surround it, the quality and quantity of movement necessary to act upon them. That concerns action, and action only. Yet it is my perception that vanishes. What does this mean, if not that my perception traces out precisely, in the ensemble of images, after the manner of a shadow or a reflection, the virtual or possible actions of my body? Now, the system of images in which the scalpel has effected only an insignificant change is what is generally called the material world; and, on the other hand, what has just vanished is "my perception" of matter. Hence, provisionally, these two definitions: I call matter the ensemble of images, and perception of matter these same images referred to the possible action of one certain determinate image, my body. Let us go more deeply into this last relation. I consider my body with its centripetal and centrifugal nerves, with its nerve centres. I know that external objects impress upon the afferent nerves disturbances which are propagated to the centres, that the centres are the scene of very varied molecular movements, and that these movements depend on the nature and position of the objects. Change the objects, modify their relation to my body, and everything is changed in the interior movements of my perceptive centres. But everything is also changed in "my perception". My perception is therefore a function of these molecular movements; it depends on them. But how does it depend on them? You will perhaps say that it translates them, and that, in the last analysis, I represent to myself nothing other than the molecular movements of the cerebral substance. But how could this proposition have the slightest meaning, since the image of the nervous system and of its interior movements is, by hypothesis, merely that of a certain material object, whereas I represent to myself the material universe in its totality? It is true that an attempt is made here to turn the difficulty. We are shown a brain analogous, in its essence, to the rest of the material universe, and consequently an image, if the universe is image. Then, since it is wished that the interior movements of this brain should create or determine the representation of the whole material world, an image which infinitely overflows that of the cerebral vibrations, a pretence is made of no longer seeing in these molecular movements, nor in movement in general, images like the others, but something which would be more or less than an image, in any case of a nature other than the image, and from which representation would issue by a veritable miracle. Matter thus becomes something radically different from representation, and of which we consequently have no image; over against it a consciousness void of images is posited, of which we can form no idea; finally, to fill consciousness, an incomprehensible action of this formless matter upon this matterless thought is invented. But the truth is that the movements of matter are very clear as images, and that there is no occasion to look in movement for anything other than what is seen in it. The only difficulty would be to make the infinite variety of representations arise from these very particular images; but why should anyone think of this, when, by everyone's admission, the cerebral vibrations form part of the material world, and when these images, consequently, occupy only a very small corner of representation? — What, then, are these movements in the end, and what rôle do these particular images play in the representation of the whole? — I cannot doubt it: they are, within my body, movements intended to prepare, by beginning it, the reaction of my body to the action of external objects. Images themselves, they cannot create images; but they mark at every moment, as a compass that is moved about would do, the position of one certain determinate image, my body, in relation to the surrounding images. In the ensemble of representation they are very little; but they have a capital importance for that part of representation which I call my body, for they sketch out at every moment its virtual movements. There can therefore be only a difference of degree, and not a difference of nature, between the so-called perceptive faculty of the brain and the reflex functions of the spinal cord. The cord transforms the excitations received into movements executed; the brain prolongs them into merely nascent reactions; but, in the one case as in the other, the rôle of nervous matter is to conduct, to compound with one another, or to inhibit movements. Whence comes it, then, that "my perception of the universe" appears to depend on the internal movements of the cerebral substance, to change when they vary and to vanish when they are abolished? The difficulty of this problem lies chiefly in our representing the grey matter and its modifications as things that would be sufficient to themselves and could be isolated from the rest of the universe. Materialists and dualists agree on this point, at bottom. They consider apart certain molecular movements of the cerebral matter: then some see in our conscious perception a phosphorescence which follows these movements and lights up their trail; the others unroll our perceptions in a consciousness which unceasingly expresses in its own way the molecular disturbances of the cortical substance: in the one case as in the other, it is states of our nervous system that perception is supposed to trace out or translate. But can the nervous system be conceived as living without the organism which nourishes it, without the atmosphere in which the organism breathes, without the earth which this atmosphere bathes, without the sun round which the earth revolves? More generally, does not the fiction of an isolated material object imply a kind of absurdity, since this object borrows its physical properties from the relations which it maintains with all the others, and owes each of its determinations, and consequently its very existence, to the place which it occupies in the ensemble of the universe? Let us not say, therefore, that our perceptions depend simply on the molecular movements of the cerebral mass. Let us say that they vary with them, but that these movements themselves remain inseparably bound up with the rest of the material world. It is then no longer merely a question of knowing how our perceptions are attached to the modifications of the grey matter. The problem widens, and is also posed in much clearer terms. Here is a system of images which I call my perception of the universe, and which is utterly overturned by slight variations of one certain privileged image, my body. This image occupies the centre; by it all the others are regulated; at each of its movements everything changes, as if one had turned a kaleidoscope. Here, on the other hand, are the same images, but each referred to itself; influencing one another no doubt, but in such a way that the effect always remains proportioned to the cause: this is what I call the universe. How are we to explain that these two systems coexist, and that the same images should be relatively invariable in the universe, infinitely variable in perception? The problem pending between realism and idealism, perhaps even between materialism and spiritualism, is therefore posed, in our view, in the following terms: How is it that the same images can enter at once into two different systems, the one in which each image varies for itself and in the well-defined measure in which it undergoes the real action of the surrounding images, the other in which all vary for a single one, and in the variable measure in which they reflect the possible action of this privileged image? Every image is internal to certain images and external to others; but of the ensemble of images we cannot say that it is internal or external to us, since interiority and exteriority are only relations between images. To ask whether the universe exists in our thought only or outside of it is therefore to state the problem in insoluble terms, supposing them to be intelligible; it is to condemn oneself to a sterile discussion, in which the terms thought, existence, universe, will necessarily be taken on either side in entirely different senses. To settle the dispute, a common ground must first be found on which the struggle may be joined, and since, for the one party and the other, we grasp things only in the form of images, it is in terms of images, and of images only, that we must pose the problem. Now, no philosophical doctrine denies that the same images can enter at once into two distinct systems, the one which belongs to science, and in which each image, being referred only to itself, keeps an absolute value, the other which is the world of consciousness, and in which all the images are regulated upon a central image, our body, whose variations they follow. The question posed between realism and idealism then becomes very clear: what are the relations which these two systems of images sustain with each other? And it is easy to see that subjective idealism consists in deriving the first system from the second, materialist realism in drawing the second from the first. The realist, in fact, starts from the universe, that is to say from an ensemble of images governed in their mutual relations by immutable laws, in which the effects remain proportioned to their causes, and whose character is to have no centre, all the images unfolding on one and the same plane which extends indefinitely. But he is quite obliged to observe that, besides this system, there are perceptions, that is to say systems in which these same images are referred to a single one among them, are arranged in tiers around it on different planes, and are transfigured as a whole by slight modifications of this central image. It is from this perception that the idealist starts, and in the system of images which he gives himself there is a privileged image, his body, upon which the other images are regulated. But as soon as he wishes to connect the present with the past and to foresee the future, he is quite obliged to abandon this central position, to replace all the images on the same plane, to suppose that they no longer vary for him but for themselves, and to treat them as if they formed part of a system in which each change gives the exact measure of its cause. On this condition alone does the science of the universe become possible; and since this science exists, since it succeeds in foreseeing the future, the hypothesis that founds it is not an arbitrary hypothesis. The first system alone is given to present experience; but we believe in the second by the very fact that we affirm the continuity of past, present and future. Thus, in idealism as in realism, one of the two systems is posited, and an attempt is made to deduce the other from it. But in this deduction neither realism nor idealism can succeed, because neither of the two systems of images is implied in the other, and each of them is sufficient to itself. If you give yourself the system of images which has no centre, and in which each element possesses its absolute magnitude and value, I do not see why this system should adjoin to itself a second, in which each image takes on an indeterminate value, subject to all the vicissitudes of a central image. It will therefore be necessary, in order to engender perception, to summon up some deus ex machina such as the materialist hypothesis of consciousness as epiphenomenon. Among all the images with absolute changes which have first been posited, the one we call our brain will be chosen, and the interior states of this image will be conferred the singular privilege of being doubled, no one knows how, by the reproduction, this time relative and variable, of all the others. It is true that it will afterwards be pretended to attach no importance to this representation, to see in it a phosphorescence left behind by the cerebral vibrations: as if the cerebral substance and the cerebral vibrations, embedded in the images which compose this representation, could be of a different nature from them! Every realism will thus make of perception an accident, and consequently a mystery. But conversely, if you give yourself a system of unstable images arranged around a privileged centre and profoundly modified by imperceptible displacements of this centre, you exclude at the outset the order of nature, that order which is indifferent to the point where one places oneself and to the term from which one begins. You will be able to restore this order only by summoning up, in your turn, a deus ex machina, by supposing, by an arbitrary hypothesis, some pre-established harmony or other between things and mind, or at least, to speak like Kant, between sensibility and understanding. It is then science that will become an accident, and its success a mystery. — You cannot, therefore, deduce either the first system of images from the second, or the second from the first, and these two opposed doctrines, realism and idealism, when they are at last replaced on the same ground, come, in contrary directions, to stumble against the same obstacle. By digging now beneath the two doctrines, you would discover in them a common postulate, which we shall formulate thus: perception has an interest that is wholly speculative; it is pure knowledge. The whole discussion bears on the rank that must be assigned to this knowledge in relation to scientific knowledge. Some give themselves the order demanded by science, and see in perception only a confused and provisional science. Others posit perception first, set it up as an absolute, and hold science to be a symbolic expression of the real. But for the one party and the other, to perceive means above all to know. Now, it is this postulate that we contest. It is belied by the examination, even the most superficial, of the structure of the nervous system in the animal series. And it cannot be accepted without profoundly obscuring the threefold problem of matter, of consciousness and of their relation. If, in fact, we follow step by step the progress of external perception from the moneron up to the higher vertebrates, what do we find? We find that, in the state of a simple protoplasmic mass, living matter is already irritable and contractile, that it undergoes the influence of external stimuli, and that it responds to them by mechanical, physical and chemical reactions. As we rise in the series of organisms, we see the physiological work divide. Nerve cells appear, become diversified, and tend to group themselves into a system. At the same time, the animal reacts to external excitation by more varied movements. But even when the disturbance received is not at once prolonged into a completed movement, it seems merely to await the occasion for it, and the same impression which transmits to the organism the modifications of its surroundings determines or prepares it to adapt itself to them. In the higher vertebrates, the distinction becomes, no doubt, radical between pure automatism, which has its seat chiefly in the spinal cord, and voluntary activity, which requires the intervention of the brain. One might imagine that the impression received, instead of blossoming forth into movements again, is spiritualised into knowledge. But it suffices to compare the structure of the brain with that of the cord to be convinced that there is only a difference of complication, and not a difference of nature, between the functions of the brain and the reflex activity of the medullary system. What happens, in fact, in reflex action? The centripetal movement communicated by the excitation is reflected at once, by means of the nerve cells of the cord, into a centrifugal movement determining a muscular contraction. In what, on the other hand, does the function of the cerebral system consist? The peripheral disturbance, instead of being propagated directly to the motor cell of the cord and imparting to the muscle a necessary contraction, ascends first to the encephalon, then descends again to the same motor cells of the cord which intervened in the reflex movement. What has it gained, then, by this detour, and what has it gone to seek in the so-called sensory cells of the cerebral cortex? I do not understand, I shall never understand, that it draws there the miraculous power of transforming itself into a representation of things, and I hold this hypothesis, moreover, to be useless, as will be seen presently. But what I see very well is that these cells of the various so-called sensory regions of the cortex, cells interposed between the terminal arborisations of the centripetal fibres and the motor cells of the Rolandic zone, allow the disturbance received to reach at will this or that motor mechanism of the spinal cord and thus to choose its effect. The more these interposed cells multiply, the more amoeboid prolongations they put forth, capable no doubt of drawing together in various ways, the more numerous and the more varied also will be the paths capable of opening before one and the same disturbance coming from the periphery, and the more, consequently, will there be systems of movements among which one and the same excitation leaves the choice. The brain, in our view, must therefore be nothing other than a kind of central telephone exchange: its rôle is to "give the connection", or to make it wait. It adds nothing to what it receives; but as all the perceptive organs send into it their last prolongations, and as all the motor mechanisms of the cord and the bulb have their appointed representatives in it, it really does constitute a centre, in which the peripheral excitation comes into relation with this or that motor mechanism, chosen and no longer imposed. On the other hand, since an enormous multitude of motor paths can open in this substance, all together, to one and the same disturbance coming from the periphery, this disturbance has the faculty of dividing infinitely there, and consequently of losing itself in innumerable motor reactions, merely nascent. Thus the rôle of the brain is sometimes to conduct the movement gathered to a chosen organ of reaction, sometimes to open to this movement the totality of the motor paths so that it may sketch out there all the possible reactions with which it is pregnant, and so that it may analyse itself by dispersing. In other words, the brain appears to us to be an instrument of analysis in respect of the movement gathered and an instrument of selection in respect of the movement executed. But in the one case as in the other, its rôle is limited to transmitting and dividing movement. And no more in the higher centres of the cortex than in the cord do the nervous elements work with a view to knowledge: they do no more than sketch out all at once a plurality of possible actions, or organise one of them. That is to say that the nervous system has nothing of an apparatus which would serve to fabricate or even to prepare representations. Its function is to receive excitations, to set up motor apparatuses, and to present the greatest possible number of these apparatuses to a given excitation. The more it develops, the more numerous and the more distant become the points of space which it puts in relation with ever more complex motor mechanisms: thus grows the latitude it leaves to our action, and in this precisely consists its increasing perfection. But if the nervous system is constructed, from one end of the animal series to the other, with a view to an action less and less necessary, must we not think that perception, whose progress is regulated by its own, is also wholly oriented towards action, not towards pure knowledge? And from that point, must not the increasing richness of this perception itself simply symbolise the increasing share of indetermination left to the choice of the living being in its conduct towards things? Let us then start from this indetermination as from the true principle. Let us seek, once this indetermination is posited, whether we could not deduce from it the possibility and even the necessity of conscious perception. In other words, let us give ourselves that system of solidary and well-linked images which is called the material world, and let us imagine here and there, in this system, centres of real action represented by living matter: I say that around each of these centres there must be arranged images subordinated to its position and variable with it; I say, consequently, that conscious perception must occur, and that, moreover, it is possible to understand how this perception arises. Let us remark first that a rigorous law connects the extension of conscious perception with the intensity of action which the living being has at its disposal. If our hypothesis is well founded, this perception appears at the precise moment when a disturbance received by matter is not prolonged into necessary reaction. In the case of a rudimentary organism, it is true, an immediate contact with the object of interest will be required for the disturbance to occur, and then the reaction can scarcely be made to wait. Thus, in the lower species, touch is at once passive and active; it serves to recognise a prey and to seize it, to feel danger and to make an effort to avoid it. The various prolongations of the protozoa, the ambulacra of the echinoderms, are organs of movement as well as of tactile perception; the stinging apparatus of the coelenterates is an instrument of perception at the same time as a means of defence. In a word, the more immediate the reaction must be, the more perception must resemble a simple contact, and the complete process of perception and reaction is then scarcely distinguishable from a mechanical impulsion followed by a necessary movement. But as the reaction becomes more uncertain, as it leaves more room for hesitation, so there increases the distance at which the action of the object of interest makes itself felt upon the animal. By sight, by hearing, it puts itself in relation with an ever greater number of things, it undergoes more and more distant influences; and whether these objects promise it an advantage or threaten it with a danger, promises and threats put back their date of maturity. The share of independence which a living being has at its disposal, or, as we shall say, the zone of indetermination which surrounds its activity, thus makes it possible to evaluate a priori the number and the remoteness of the things with which it is in relation. Whatever this relation may be, whatever therefore the intimate nature of perception, we may affirm that the amplitude of perception exactly measures the indetermination of the consequent action, and consequently state this law: perception has at its disposal space in the exact proportion in which action has at its disposal time. But why does this relation of the organism to more or less distant objects take the particular form of a conscious perception? We have examined what takes place in the organised body; we have seen movements transmitted or inhibited, metamorphosed into accomplished actions or scattered into nascent actions. These movements appeared to us to concern action, and action only; they remain absolutely foreign to the process of representation. We then considered action itself and the indetermination which surrounds it, an indetermination which is implied in the structure of the nervous system, and with a view to which this system appears to have been constructed far rather than with a view to representation. From this indetermination, accepted as a fact, we were able to conclude to the necessity of a perception, that is to say of a variable relation between the living being and the more or less distant influences of the objects which interest it. Whence comes it that this perception is consciousness, and why does everything happen as if this consciousness were born of the interior movements of the cerebral substance? To answer this question, we shall begin by greatly simplifying the conditions in which conscious perception is accomplished. In fact, there is no perception that is not impregnated with recollections. With the immediate and present data of our senses we mingle thousands upon thousands of details of our past experience. Most often these recollections displace our real perceptions, of which we then retain only a few indications, mere "signs" intended to recall to us former images. The convenience and rapidity of perception are bought at this price; but from it too arise illusions of every kind. Nothing prevents us from substituting for this perception, wholly permeated with our past, the perception that would belong to a consciousness adult and fully formed, but shut up in the present, and absorbed, to the exclusion of all other work, in the task of moulding itself on the external object. Will it be said that we are making an arbitrary hypothesis, and that this ideal perception, obtained by eliminating individual accidents, no longer answers at all to reality? But we hope precisely to show that individual accidents are grafted on this impersonal perception, that this perception lies at the very base of our knowledge of things, and that it is through having misunderstood it, through not having distinguished it from what memory adds to it or takes away from it, that perception as a whole has been made into a kind of inner and subjective vision, which would differ from recollection only by its greater intensity. Such, then, will be our first hypothesis. But it naturally entails another. However short a perception is supposed to be, it always occupies a certain duration, and consequently demands an effort of memory, which prolongs a plurality of moments into one another. Even, as we shall try to show, the "subjectivity" of sensible qualities consists above all in a kind of contraction of the real, effected by our memory. In short, memory in these two forms, inasmuch as it covers a ground of immediate perception with a layer of recollections and inasmuch also as it contracts a multiplicity of moments, constitutes the principal contribution of individual consciousness to perception, the subjective side of our knowledge of things; and in neglecting this contribution in order to make our idea clearer, we shall advance much further than is fitting along the path on which we have set out. We shall be quits by retracing our steps afterwards, and by correcting, above all through the reinstatement of memory, whatever our conclusions may have of the excessive. What follows, then, should be regarded only as a schematic exposition, and we shall ask that by perception there be understood provisionally not my concrete and complex perception, the one that my recollections swell and that always offers a certain thickness of duration, but pure perception, a perception that exists by right rather than in fact, the perception that a being placed where I am, living as I live, but absorbed in the present, and capable, by the elimination of memory in all its forms, of obtaining from matter a vision at once immediate and instantaneous, would have. Let us place ourselves, then, in this hypothesis, and ask how conscious perception is to be explained. To deduce consciousness would be a very bold undertaking, but it is really not necessary here, because in positing the material world we have given ourselves a set of images, and because it is, moreover, impossible to give ourselves anything else. No theory of matter escapes this necessity. Reduce matter to atoms in motion: these atoms, even stripped of physical qualities, are nevertheless determined only in relation to a possible vision and a possible contact, the former without illumination and the latter without materiality. Condense the atom into centres of force, dissolve it into vortices evolving in a continuous fluid: this fluid, these movements, these centres are themselves determined only in relation to an impotent touch, an ineffectual impulse, a discoloured light; they are images still. It is true that an image may be without being perceived; it may be present without being represented; and the distance between these two terms, presence and representation, seems precisely to measure the interval between matter itself and the conscious perception we have of it. But let us examine these things more closely and see in what exactly this difference consists. If there were more in the second term than in the first, if, in order to pass from presence to representation, something had to be added, the distance would be impassable, and the passage from matter to perception would remain wrapped in an impenetrable mystery. It would not be so if one could pass from the first term to the second by way of diminution, and if the representation of an image were less than its mere presence; for then it would suffice that the present images were forced to abandon something of themselves for their simple presence to convert them into representations. Now, here is the image that I call a material object; I have the representation of it. Whence comes it that it does not seem to be in itself what it is for me? It is that, being bound up with the totality of the other images, it continues into those that follow it just as it prolonged those that precede it. To transform its pure and simple existence into representation, it would suffice to suppress all at once what follows it, what precedes it, and also what fills it, retaining of it only the outer crust, the superficial film. What distinguishes it, as a present image, as an objective reality, from a represented image, is the necessity under which it lies of acting through each of its points upon all the points of the other images, of transmitting the whole of what it receives, of opposing to every action an equal and contrary reaction, of being, in short, merely a road along which the modifications propagated throughout the immensity of the universe pass in every direction. I should convert it into representation if I could isolate it, if above all I could isolate its envelope. The representation is indeed there, but always virtual, neutralised, at the moment when it would pass into act, by the obligation to continue itself and lose itself in something else. What is needed to obtain this conversion is not to illuminate the object, but on the contrary to obscure certain of its sides, to diminish it by the greater part of itself, so that the residue, instead of remaining embedded in its surroundings like a thing, detaches itself from them like a picture. Now, if living beings constitute in the universe "centres of indetermination," and if the degree of this indetermination is measured by the number and elevation of their functions, one can conceive that their mere presence may be equivalent to the suppression of all those parts of objects in which their functions are not interested. They will let themselves be traversed, in a way, by those of the external actions that are indifferent to them; the others, isolated, will become "perceptions" by their very isolation. Everything will then happen for us as if we reflected upon surfaces the light which emanates from them, light which, always propagating itself, would never have been revealed. The images that surround us will appear to turn towards our body, but illuminated this time, the face that interests it; they will detach from their substance what we shall have arrested in passing, what we are capable of influencing. Indifferent to one another by reason of the radical mechanism that binds them, they present to one another reciprocally all their faces at once, which is to say that they act and react among themselves through all their elementary parts, and that none of them, consequently, is perceived or consciously perceives. If, on the contrary, they strike somewhere against a certain spontaneity of reaction, their action is diminished to that extent, and this diminution of their action is precisely the representation we have of them. Our representation of things would thus arise, in sum, from their being reflected against our freedom. When a ray of light passes from one medium into another, it generally traverses it while changing direction. But the respective densities of the two media may be such that, for a certain angle of incidence, refraction is no longer possible. Then total reflection occurs. A virtual image of the luminous point is formed, which symbolises, in a way, the impossibility for the rays of light to pursue their course. Perception is a phenomenon of the same kind. What is given is the totality of the images of the material world together with the totality of their internal elements. But if you suppose centres of genuine, that is to say spontaneous, activity, the rays which reach them and which would interest this activity, instead of passing through them, will appear to turn back to trace the contours of the object that sends them. There will be nothing positive there, nothing added to the image, nothing new. Objects will merely abandon something of their real action in order thus to figure their virtual action, that is to say, at bottom, the possible influence of the living being upon them. Perception thus resembles those phenomena of reflection which come from a refraction that has been prevented; it is like an effect of mirage. This amounts to saying that for images there is a simple difference of degree, and not of kind, between being and being consciously perceived. The reality of matter consists in the totality of its elements and of their actions of every kind. Our representation of matter is the measure of our possible action upon bodies; it results from the elimination of what does not interest our needs and, more generally, our functions. In a sense one might say that the perception of any unconscious material point whatever, in its instantaneity, is infinitely vaster and more complete than ours, since this point gathers and transmits the actions of all the points of the material world, whereas our consciousness reaches only certain parts of them by certain sides. Consciousness, in the case of external perception, consists precisely in this choice. But there is, in this necessary poverty of our conscious perception, something positive which already announces mind: it is, in the etymological sense of the word, discernment. The whole difficulty of the problem that occupies us comes from picturing perception as a photographic view of things, taken from a determinate point with a special apparatus, such as the organ of perception, and then developed in the cerebral substance by I know not what process of chemical and psychical elaboration. But how can we fail to see that the photograph, if photograph there be, is already taken, already printed, within the very interior of things and for all the points of space? No metaphysics, not even any physics can evade this conclusion. Compose the universe out of atoms: in each of them are felt, in a quality and a quantity varying with the distance, the actions exercised by all the atoms of matter. Out of centres of force? The lines of force emitted in every direction by all the centres direct upon each centre the influences of the entire material world. Out of monads, finally? Each monad, as Leibniz wished, is the mirror of the universe. Everyone is thus in agreement on this point. Only, if we consider any place whatever in the universe, we may say that the action of the whole of matter passes through it without resistance and without loss, and that the photograph of the whole is translucent there: what is lacking, behind the plate, is a black screen on which the image would stand out. Our "zones of indetermination" would play, in a way, the part of the screen. They add nothing to what is; they merely make the real action pass and the virtual action remain. This is not an hypothesis. We confine ourselves to formulating the data without which no theory of perception can do. No psychologist, indeed, will approach the study of external perception without positing at least the possibility of a material world, that is to say, at bottom, the virtual perception of all things. In this merely possible material mass he will isolate the particular object that I call my body, and in this body the perceptive centres: he will show me the disturbance arriving from any point of space whatever, propagating itself along the nerves, reaching the centres. But here a coup de théâtre takes place. This material world which surrounded the body, this body which shelters the brain, this brain in which centres were distinguished, are abruptly dismissed; and as if by a magic wand, there is made to spring up, in the manner of something absolutely new, the representation of what had been posited at first. This representation is pushed out of space, so that it may have nothing more in common with the matter from which one started: as to matter itself, one would like to do without it, and yet one cannot, because its phenomena present among themselves an order so rigorous, so indifferent to the point chosen as origin, that this regularity and this indifference truly constitute an independent existence. One will then have to resign oneself to retaining of matter its phantom. At least it will be stripped of all the qualities that give life. In an amorphous space one will cut out figures that move; or again (which comes to nearly the same thing), one will imagine relations of magnitude that would compose with one another, functions that would evolve by developing their content: henceforth the representation, laden with the spoils of matter, will unfold freely in an unextended consciousness. But it is not enough to cut; one must sew. These qualities which you have detached from their material support, you will now have to explain how they are to rejoin it. Each attribute of which you diminish matter widens the interval between the representation and its object. If you make this matter unextended, how will it receive extension? If you reduce it to homogeneous movement, whence then will quality arise? Above all, how can one imagine a relation between the thing and the image, between matter and thought, since each of these two terms possesses, by definition, only what is lacking to the other? Thus difficulties will spring up under your feet, and every effort you make to dispel one of them can only resolve it into many others. What do we ask of you, then? Simply to renounce your stroke of the magic wand, and to continue on the road on which you had first entered. You had shown us the external images reaching the organs of sense, modifying the nerves, propagating their influence in the brain. Go on to the end. The movement will traverse the cerebral substance, not without having lingered there, and will then flower out into voluntary action. That is the whole of the mechanism of perception. As to perception itself, as image, you have not to retrace its genesis, since you posited it at the outset and could not, moreover, fail to posit it: in giving yourself the brain, in giving yourself the least particle of matter, were you not giving yourself the totality of images? What you have to explain, then, is not how perception arises, but how it is limited, since it would be, by right, the image of the whole, and is reduced, in fact, to what interests you. But if it is distinguished from the pure and simple image precisely in that its parts are ordered in relation to a variable centre, its limitation is understood without difficulty: indefinite by right, it is restricted, in fact, to outlining the share of indetermination left to the doings of that special image which you call your body. And consequently, conversely, the indetermination of the movements of the body, as it results from the structure of the grey matter of the brain, gives the exact measure of the extent of your perception. We must not be astonished, then, if everything happens as if your perception resulted from the internal movements of the brain and issued, in a way, from the cortical centres. It cannot come from them, for the brain is an image like the others, enveloped in the mass of the other images, and it would be absurd that the container should issue from the contained. But since the structure of the brain gives the minute plan of the movements among which you have the choice, since, on the other hand, the portion of external images which seems to turn back upon itself to constitute perception outlines precisely all the points of the universe upon which these movements would have a hold, conscious perception and cerebral modification correspond rigorously. The reciprocal dependence of these two terms is thus simply due to their being, both of them, a function of a third, which is the indetermination of will. Take, for example, a luminous point P whose rays act on the different points a, b, c of the retina. At this point P science localises vibrations of a certain amplitude and a certain duration. At this same point P consciousness perceives light. We propose to show, in the course of this study, that they are both right, and that there is no essential difference between this light and these movements, provided that we restore to movement the unity, the indivisibility and the qualitative heterogeneity which an abstract mechanics denies it, provided also that we see in sensible qualities so many contractions effected by our memory: science and consciousness would coincide in the instantaneous. Let us confine ourselves provisionally to saying, without probing too far here into the sense of the words, that the point P sends luminous disturbances to the retina. What is going to happen? If the visual image of the point P were not given, we should have to seek how it is formed, and should very soon find ourselves confronted with an insoluble problem. But however we set about it, we cannot help positing it at the outset: the sole question, then, is to know why and how this image is chosen to form part of my perception, while an infinity of other images remain excluded from it. Now, I see that the disturbances transmitted from the point P to the various retinal corpuscles are conducted to the optic centres, subcortical and cortical, often also to other centres, and that these centres sometimes transmit them to motor mechanisms, sometimes arrest them provisionally. The nervous elements concerned are thus indeed what gives the disturbance received its efficacy; they symbolise the indetermination of will; on their integrity this indetermination depends; and consequently every lesion of these elements, by diminishing our possible action, will diminish perception to the same extent. In other words, if there exist in the material world points where the disturbances gathered are not mechanically transmitted, if there are, as we said, zones of indetermination, these zones must precisely be met with on the path of what is called the sensori-motor process; and thenceforward everything must happen as if the rays Pa, Pb, Pc were perceived along this path and then projected in P. What is more, if this indetermination is something that escapes experiment and calculation, it is not so with the nervous elements on which the impression is gathered and transmitted. It is with these elements, then, that physiologists and psychologists will have to deal; by them the whole detail of external perception will be regulated and through them explained. One may say, if one likes, that the excitation, after travelling along these elements, after reaching the centre, is converted there into a conscious image which is then externalised at the point P. But in expressing oneself thus, one merely bows to the requirements of scientific method; one does not at all describe the real process. In fact, there is not an unextended image which would be formed in consciousness and then projected in P. The truth is that the point P, the rays it emits, the retina and the nervous elements concerned form a solidary whole, that the luminous point P is part of this whole, and that it is indeed in P, and not elsewhere, that the image of P is formed and perceived. In thus representing things to ourselves, we do no more than return to the naive conviction of common sense. All of us began by believing that we entered into the object itself, that we perceived it in itself, and not in ourselves. If the psychologist disdains so simple an idea, one so close to the real, it is because the intracerebral process, that minute part of perception, appears to him the equivalent of the whole of perception. Suppress the perceived object while retaining this internal process; it seems to him that the image of the object remains. And his belief is readily explained: there are numerous states, such as hallucination and dream, in which images arise that imitate external perception in every respect. Since in such cases the object has disappeared while the brain subsists, he concludes that the cerebral phenomenon suffices for the production of the image. But we must not forget that in all psychological states of this kind memory plays the leading part. Now, we shall try to show farther on that, perception once admitted as we understand it, memory must arise, and that this memory, no more than perception itself, has its real and complete condition in a cerebral state. Without yet entering upon the examination of these two points, let us confine ourselves to presenting a very simple observation, which is moreover not new. Many persons born blind have their visual centres intact: yet they live and die without ever having formed a visual image. Such an image can therefore appear only if the external object has played a part at least once: it must consequently, the first time at least, have entered effectively into the representation. Now we ask nothing else for the moment, for it is pure perception that we are treating of here, and not perception complicated by memory. Reject, then, the contribution of memory, consider perception in the raw state, and you are bound to recognise that there is never an image without an object. But as soon as you join to the intracerebral processes the external object which is their cause, I see very well how the image of this object is given with it and in it; I do not at all see how it would arise from the cerebral movement. When a lesion of the nerves or of the centres interrupts the path of the nervous disturbance, perception is diminished to that extent. Need we be astonished at it? The part of the nervous system is to utilise this disturbance, to convert it into practical doings, really or virtually accomplished. If, for one reason or another, the excitation no longer passes, it would be strange if the corresponding perception still took place, since this perception would then put our body in relation with points of space which would no longer directly invite it to make a choice. Cut the optic nerve of an animal; the disturbance starting from the luminous point is no longer transmitted to the brain and thence to the motor nerves; the thread which connected the external object with the motor mechanisms of the animal, passing through the optic nerve, is broken: visual perception has therefore become impotent, and in this impotence unconsciousness precisely consists. That matter might be perceived without the aid of a nervous system, without organs of sense, is not theoretically inconceivable; but it is practically impossible, because a perception of this kind would serve no purpose. It would suit a phantom, not a living being, that is to say, one that acts. The living body is represented as an empire within an empire, the nervous system as a being apart, whose function would be first to elaborate perceptions, then to create movements. The truth is that my nervous system, interposed between the objects which shake my body and those which I could influence, plays the part of a simple conductor, which transmits, distributes or inhibits movement. This conductor is composed of an enormous multitude of threads stretched from the periphery to the centre and from the centre to the periphery. There are as many threads going from the periphery towards the centre as there are points of space capable of soliciting my will and of putting, so to speak, an elementary question to my motor activity: each question put is precisely what is called a perception. Perception is therefore diminished by one of its elements whenever one of the so-called sensory threads is cut, because then some part of the external object becomes impotent to solicit activity, and also whenever a stable habit has been contracted, because this time the ready-made reply makes the question needless. What disappears in the one case as in the other is the apparent reflection of the disturbance upon itself, the return of the light to the image from which it starts, or rather that dissociation, that discernment by which perception detaches itself from the image. We may therefore say that the detail of perception is moulded exactly upon that of the so-called sensory nerves, but that perception, as a whole, has its true raison d'être in the tendency of the body to move. What generally creates an illusion on this point is the apparent indifference of our movements to the excitation that occasions them. It seems that the movement of my body to reach and modify an object remains the same, whether I have been made aware of its existence by hearing, or it has been revealed to me by sight or touch. My motor activity then becomes an entity apart, a kind of reservoir from which movement issues at will, always the same for the same action, whatever the kind of image that has solicited it to be produced. But the truth is that the character of movements that are externally identical is internally modified, according as they answer to a visual, tactile or auditory impression. I perceive a multitude of objects in space; each of them, as a visual form, solicits my activity. I suddenly lose my sight. No doubt I still have at my disposal the same quantity and the same quality of movements in space; but these movements can no longer be coordinated with visual impressions; they will henceforth have to follow tactile impressions, for example, and a new arrangement will no doubt take shape in the brain; the protoplasmic expansions of the motor nervous elements, in the cortex, will be in relation, this time, with a much smaller number of those nervous elements which are called sensory. My activity is therefore really diminished, in the sense that, if I can produce the same movements, objects furnish me with less occasion for them. And consequently the sudden interruption of optical conduction has had as its essential, profound effect the suppression of a whole part of the solicitations of my activity: now this solicitation, as we have seen, is perception itself. We here put our finger on the error of those who make perception arise from the sensory disturbance proper, and not from a kind of question put to our motor activity. They detach this motor activity from the perceptive process, and since it appears to survive the abolition of perception, they conclude that perception is localised in the so-called sensory nervous elements. But the truth is that it is no more in the sensory centres than in the motor centres; it measures the complexity of their relations, and exists where it appears. Psychologists who have studied childhood know well that our representation begins by being impersonal. It is little by little, and by dint of inductions, that it adopts our body as its centre and becomes our representation. The mechanism of this operation is, moreover, easy to understand. As my body moves about in space, all the other images vary; this one, on the contrary, remains invariable. I must therefore make of it a centre, to which I shall refer all the other images. My belief in an external world does not come, cannot come, from my projecting outside myself inextensive sensations: how would these sensations acquire extension, and from where could I draw the notion of externality? But if it is granted, as experience attests, that the whole of images is given first, I see very well how my body comes to occupy in this whole a privileged situation. And I understand also how the notion of the inside and the outside is then born, which at the outset is merely the distinction between my body and other bodies. Start indeed from my body, as is commonly done; you will never make me understand how impressions received on the surface of my body, and which concern only this body, are going to constitute themselves for me into independent objects and form an external world. Give me, on the contrary, images in general; my body will necessarily end by taking shape in the midst of them as a distinct thing, since they change ceaselessly and it remains invariable. The distinction between the inside and the outside will thus come down to that between the part and the whole. There is first the whole of images; there are, within this whole, "centres of action" against which the interesting images seem to be reflected; this is how perceptions are born and actions prepared. My body is what takes shape at the centre of these perceptions; my person is the being to which these actions must be referred. Things grow clear if one proceeds thus from the periphery of representation to the centre, as the child does, as immediate experience and common sense invite us to do. Everything grows obscure, on the contrary, and problems multiply, if one claims to proceed, with the theorists, from the centre to the periphery. Whence then comes this idea of an external world constructed artificially, piece by piece, out of inextensive sensations of which we understand neither how they would come to form an extended surface, nor how they would then be projected outside our body? Why do people want it, against all appearances, that I should go from my conscious self to my body, then from my body to other bodies, whereas in fact I place myself at once in the material world in general, in order progressively to delimit that centre of action which will be called my body and thus to distinguish it from all the others? There are, in this belief in the originally inextensive character of our external perception, so many illusions combined, one would find, in this idea that we project outside ourselves purely internal states, so many misunderstandings, so many halting answers to ill-posed questions, that we cannot claim to shed light on them all at once. We hope that it will come little by little, as we show more clearly, behind these illusions, the metaphysical confusion of undivided extension with homogeneous space, the psychological confusion of "pure perception" with memory. But they are connected, besides, with real facts, which we can already point out in order to rectify their interpretation. The first of these facts is that our senses need education. Neither sight nor touch immediately succeeds in localising its impressions. A series of comparisons and inductions is necessary, by which we gradually coordinate our impressions with one another. From this one leaps to the idea of sensations inextensive by essence, which would constitute extension by being juxtaposed. But who does not see that, in the very hypothesis in which we have placed ourselves, our senses will equally need education, not, no doubt, in order to agree with things, but in order to come to agreement among themselves? Here, in the midst of all the images, is a certain image which I call my body and whose virtual action is translated by an apparent reflection, upon themselves, of the surrounding images. As many kinds of possible action as there are for my body, so many different systems of reflection there will be for other bodies, and each of these systems will correspond to one of my senses. My body therefore behaves like an image which would reflect others while analysing them from the point of view of the various actions to be exercised upon them. And consequently each of the qualities perceived by my different senses in the same object symbolises a certain direction of my activity, a certain need. Now, will all these perceptions of a body by my various senses, on being brought together, give the complete image of this body? No, doubtless, since they have been gathered from the whole. To perceive all the influences from all the points of all bodies would be to descend to the state of a material object. To perceive consciously means to choose, and consciousness consists above all in this practical discernment. The diverse perceptions of the same object that my various senses give will therefore not reconstitute, on being brought together, the complete image of the object; they will remain separated from one another by intervals which measure, in a way, so many voids in my needs: it is to fill these intervals that an education of the senses is necessary. This education has as its end to harmonise my senses with one another, to re-establish between their data a continuity which has been broken by the very discontinuity of the needs of my body, in short to reconstruct approximately the whole of the material object. Thus, in our hypothesis, the necessity of an education of the senses will be explained. Let us compare this explanation with the preceding one. In the first, inextensive sensations of sight will combine with inextensive sensations of touch and of the other senses to give, by their synthesis, the idea of a material object. But, to begin with, one does not see how these sensations will acquire extension, nor above all how, once extension has been acquired by right, the preference of this or that one of them, in fact, for such a point of space will be explained. And then one may ask by what happy agreement, by virtue of what pre-established harmony, these sensations of different kinds are going to coordinate themselves together to form a stable object, henceforth solidified, common to my experience and to that of all men, subject, with regard to other objects, to those inflexible rules which are called the laws of nature. In the second, on the contrary, the "data of our different senses" are qualities of things, perceived first in them rather than in us: is it astonishing that they should join up again, when abstraction alone has separated them? In the first hypothesis, the material object is nothing of all that we perceive: on one side will be placed the conscious principle with the sensible qualities, on the other a matter of which nothing can be said, and which is defined by negations because it has first been stripped of everything that reveals it. In the second, an ever deeper knowledge of matter is possible. Far from cutting off from it anything perceived, we must on the contrary bring together all the sensible qualities, rediscover their kinship, re-establish between them the continuity that our needs have broken. Our perception of matter is then no longer relative nor subjective, at least in principle and setting aside, as we shall see presently, affection and above all memory; it is simply split up by the multiplicity of our needs. In the first hypothesis, mind is as unknowable as matter, for there is attributed to it the indefinable capacity of evoking sensations, one knows not whence, and of projecting them, one knows not why, into a space where they will form bodies. In the second, the rôle of consciousness is clearly defined: consciousness means possible action; and the forms acquired by mind, those which veil its essence from us, will have to be set aside in the light of this second principle. We thus catch a glimpse, in our hypothesis, of the possibility of distinguishing mind from matter more clearly, and of effecting a rapprochement between them. But let us leave this first point aside, and come to the second. The second alleged fact would consist in what has long been called the "specific energy of the nerves". It is known that the excitation of the optic nerve by an external shock or by an electric current will give a visual sensation, and that this same electric current, applied to the acoustic nerve or to the glossopharyngeal, will make one perceive a flavour or hear a sound. From these very particular facts one passes to those two very general laws, that different causes, acting on the same nerve, excite the same sensation, and that the same cause, acting on different nerves, provokes different sensations. And from these laws themselves one infers that our sensations are simply signals, that the rôle of each sense is to translate in its own language homogeneous and mechanical movements taking place in space. Whence, finally, the idea of splitting our perception into two distinct parts, henceforth incapable of rejoining each other: on one side homogeneous movements in space, on the other inextensive sensations in consciousness. It is not for us to enter upon the examination of the physiological problems which the interpretation of the two laws raises: in whatever way these laws are understood, whether specific energy is attributed to the nerves, or transferred to the centres, one runs up against insurmountable difficulties. But it is the laws themselves that appear more and more problematic. Lotze had already suspected their falsity. He waited, before believing in them, "until sound-waves should give the eye the sensation of light, or luminous vibrations make the ear hear a sound1". The truth is that all the alleged facts seem reducible to a single type: the unique stimulus capable of producing different sensations, the multiple stimuli capable of engendering one and the same sensation, are either the electric current or a mechanical cause capable of determining in the organ a modification of the electric equilibrium. Now one may ask whether electric excitation does not comprise diverse components, corresponding objectively to sensations of different kinds, and whether the rôle of each sense is not simply to extract from the whole the component that interests it: it would then indeed be the same excitations that would give the same sensations, and diverse excitations that would provoke different sensations. To speak with more precision, it is difficult to admit that the electrification of the tongue, for example, does not occasion chemical modifications; now it is these modifications that we call, in all cases, flavours. On the other hand, if the physicist has been able to identify light with an electro-magnetic disturbance, one may say conversely that what he here calls an electro-magnetic disturbance is light, so that it would indeed be light that the optic nerve would objectively perceive in electrification. For no sense did the doctrine of specific energy appear more solidly established than for the ear; nowhere has the real existence of the thing perceived become more probable. We shall not insist on these facts, because an exposition and thorough discussion of them will be found in a recent work1. Let us confine ourselves to remarking that the sensations spoken of here are not images perceived by us outside our body, but rather affections localised in our very body. Now it follows from the nature and the destination of our body, as we shall see, that each of its so-called sensitive elements has its own real action, which must be of the same kind as its virtual action upon the external objects that it ordinarily perceives, so that one would thus understand why each of the sensitive nerves appears to vibrate according to a determinate mode of sensation. But, to elucidate this point, it is fitting to probe more deeply into the nature of affection. We are thereby led to the third and last argument which we wished to examine. This third argument is drawn from the fact that one passes, by insensible degrees, from the representative state, which occupies space, to the affective state, which appears unextended. From this one concludes to the natural and necessary inextension of every sensation, extension being added to sensation, and the process of perception consisting in an externalisation of internal states. The psychologist starts indeed from his body, and since the impressions received at the periphery of this body seem to him sufficient for the reconstitution of the entire material universe, it is to his body that he first reduces the universe. But this first position is not tenable; his body has and can have neither more nor less reality than all other bodies. It is therefore necessary to go further, to follow the application of the principle to the end, and, after having narrowed the universe to the surface of the living body, to contract this body itself into a centre which one will end by supposing unextended. Then, from this centre one will set out inextensive sensations which will swell, so to speak, grow larger in extension, and finally give our extended body first, then all the other material objects. But this strange supposition would be impossible if there were not precisely between images and ideas, the latter unextended and the former extended, a series of intermediate states, more or less confusedly localised, which are the affective states. Our understanding, yielding to its habitual illusion, poses this dilemma, that a thing is extended or is not; and as the affective state vaguely participates in extension, is imperfectly localised, it concludes that this state is absolutely inextensive. But then the successive degrees of extension, and extension itself, are going to be explained by I know not what acquired property of inextensive states; the history of perception is going to become that of internal and inextensive states extending themselves and projecting themselves outwards. Would one put this argument in another form? There is hardly a perception which cannot, by an increase in the action of its object upon our body, become affection and more particularly pain. Thus one passes insensibly from the contact of the pin to the prick. Inversely, decreasing pain gradually coincides with the perception of its cause and is externalised, so to speak, into representation. It seems therefore indeed that there is a difference of degree, and not of kind, between affection and perception. Now the former is intimately bound up with my personal existence: what would a pain detached from the subject that feels it be, in fact? It must therefore, it seems, be so with the second also, and external perception must be constituted by the projection, into space, of affection become harmless. Realists and idealists agree in reasoning in this manner. The latter see nothing else, in the material universe, than a synthesis of subjective and inextensive states; the former add that there is, behind this synthesis, an independent reality which corresponds to it; but both conclude, from the gradual passage from affection to representation, that the representation of the material universe is relative, subjective, and, so to speak, that it has issued from us, instead of our having first disengaged ourselves from it. Before criticising this contestable interpretation of an exact fact, let us show that it succeeds in explaining, that it does not even succeed in clarifying, either the nature of pain or that of perception. That affective states essentially bound up with my person, and which would vanish if I disappeared, should come, by the mere effect of a diminution of intensity, to acquire extension, to take a determinate place in space, to constitute a stable experience, always in agreement with itself and with the experience of other men, is what we shall hardly be brought to understand. Whatever one does, one will be led to restore to sensations, in one form or another, first extension, then the independence which it was wished to dispense with. But, on the other hand, affection will be hardly any clearer, on this hypothesis, than representation. For if one does not see how affections, on diminishing in intensity, become representations, one does not understand any better how the same phenomenon, which was first given as perception, becomes affection through an increase of intensity. There is in pain something positive and active, which is ill explained by saying, with certain philosophers, that it consists in a confused representation. But there lies not yet the principal difficulty. That the gradual increase of the stimulus ends by transforming perception into pain is incontestable; it is none the less true that the transformation takes shape from a precise moment: why this moment rather than another? and what is the special reason which makes a phenomenon of which I was at first only the indifferent spectator suddenly acquire for me a vital interest? I therefore grasp, in this hypothesis, neither why, at a determinate moment, a diminution of intensity in the phenomenon confers upon it a right to extension and to an apparent independence, nor how an increase of intensity creates, at one moment rather than another, this new property, source of positive action, which is called pain. Let us now return to our hypothesis, and show how affection must, at a determinate moment, spring from the image. We shall understand also how one passes from a perception, which occupies extension, to an affection which is believed to be inextensive. But some preliminary remarks are indispensable on the real signification of pain. When a foreign body touches one of the prolongations of the amoeba, this prolongation retracts; each part of the protoplasmic mass is therefore equally capable of receiving the excitation and of reacting against it; perception and movement are here merged in a single property which is contractility. But as the organism grows more complex, labour is divided, functions are differentiated, and the anatomical elements thus constituted alienate their independence. In an organism such as ours, the so-called sensitive fibres are exclusively charged with transmitting excitations to a central region from which the disturbance will be propagated to motor elements. It seems therefore that they have renounced individual action in order to concur, in the quality of advanced sentinels, in the evolutions of the whole body. But they remain none the less exposed, in isolation, to the same causes of destruction which threaten the organism as a whole: and whereas this organism has the faculty of moving to escape danger or to repair its losses, the sensitive element retains the relative immobility to which the division of labour condemns it. Thus pain is born, which is nothing other, in our view, than an effort of the injured element to put things back in place, a kind of motor tendency on a sensitive nerve. All pain must therefore consist in an effort, and in an impotent effort. All pain is a local effort, and it is this very isolation of the effort that is the cause of its impotence, because the organism, by reason of the solidarity of its parts, is no longer fit except for effects of the whole. It is also because the effort is local that pain is absolutely disproportionate to the danger run by the living being: the danger may be mortal and the pain slight; the pain may be unbearable (like that of a toothache) and the peril insignificant. There is therefore, there must be, a precise moment at which pain intervenes: it is when the interested portion of the organism, instead of welcoming the excitation, repels it. And it is not merely a difference of degree that separates perception from affection, but a difference of kind. This being laid down, we have considered the living Body as a kind of centre from which there is reflected, upon surrounding objects, the action that these objects exercise upon it: in this reflection external perception consists. But this centre is not a mathematical point: it is a body, exposed, like all the bodies of nature, to the action of external causes which threaten to disintegrate it. We have just seen that it resists the influence of these causes. It does not confine itself to reflecting the action from without; it struggles, and thus absorbs something of this action. There would be the source of affection. One might therefore say, by way of metaphor, that if perception measures the reflecting power of the body, affection measures its absorbing power. But this is only a metaphor. One must look at things more closely, and understand well that the necessity of affection flows from the existence of perception itself. Perception, understood as we understand it, measures our possible action upon things and thereby, inversely, the possible action of things upon us. The greater the power of acting of the body (symbolised by a higher complication of the nervous system), the vaster the field that perception embraces. The distance which separates our body from a perceived object therefore truly measures the greater or lesser imminence of a danger, the nearer or more remote term of a promise. And consequently our perception of an object distinct from our body, separated from our body by an interval, never expresses anything but a virtual action. But the more the distance decreases between this object and our body, the more, in other words, the danger becomes urgent or the promise immediate, the more virtual action tends to be transformed into real action. Pass now to the limit, suppose that the distance becomes nil, that is to say that the object to be perceived coincides with our body, that is to say, finally, that our own body is the object to be perceived. Then it is no longer a virtual action but a real action that this quite special perception will express: affection consists in this very thing. Our sensations are therefore to our perceptions what the real action of our body is to its possible or virtual action. Its virtual action concerns other objects and takes shape in those objects; its real action concerns itself and consequently takes shape in itself.
