By it the intelligent, or rather intellectual, recognition of a perception already experienced would become possible; in it we should take refuge every time that we go back up, in order to seek there a certain image, the slope of our past life. But every perception is prolonged into nascent action; and as the images, once perceived, become fixed and aligned in this memory, the movements which continued them modify the organism, create in the body new dispositions to act. Thus is formed an experience of an altogether different order, which is deposited in the body, a series of ready-made mechanisms, with more and more numerous and varied reactions to external excitations, with ready-made replies to a constantly increasing number of possible solicitations. We become conscious of these mechanisms at the moment they come into play, and this consciousness of a whole past of efforts stored up in the present is still a memory, but a memory profoundly different from the first, always bent upon action, seated in the present and looking only to the future. It has retained of the past only the intelligently co-ordinated movements which represent its accumulated effort; it recovers these past efforts, not in memory-images which recall them, but in the rigorous order and the systematic character with which the actual movements are accomplished. In truth, it no longer represents our past to us, it acts it; and if it still deserves the name of memory, it is no longer because it preserves bygone images, but because it prolongs their useful effect into the present moment. Of these two memories, of which the one imagines and the other repeats, the second can supply the place of the first and even often give the illusion of it. When the dog greets his master with joyous barks and caresses, he recognises him, without any doubt; but does this recognition imply the evocation of a past image and the bringing together of this image with the present perception? Does it not consist rather in the consciousness which the animal takes of a certain special attitude adopted by its body, an attitude which its familiar relations with its master have gradually composed for it, and which the mere perception of the master now provokes in it mechanically? Let us not go too far! in the animal itself, vague images of the past perhaps overflow the present perception; one could even conceive that its whole past should be virtually outlined in its consciousness; but this past does not interest it enough to detach it from the present which fascinates it, and its recognition must be lived rather than thought. In order to evoke the past in the form of an image, we must be able to abstract ourselves from present action, we must know how to attach value to the useless, we must will to dream. Man alone is perhaps capable of an effort of this kind. Even so, the past to which we thus go back is slippery, always on the point of escaping us, as if this regressive memory were thwarted by the other memory, more natural, whose forward movement carries us to act and to live. When psychologists speak of recollection as of a contracted fold, as of an impression which engraves itself more and more deeply by repetition, they forget that the immense majority of our recollections bear on the events and details of our life, whose essence is to have a date and consequently never to be reproduced. The recollections which are acquired voluntarily by repetition are rare, exceptional. On the contrary, the registering, by memory, of facts and images unique of their kind goes on at every moment of duration. But as learnt recollections are the most useful, they are the more noticed. And as the acquisition of these recollections by the repetition of the same effort resembles the already known process of habit, we prefer to push this kind of recollection into the foreground, to set it up as the model recollection, and to see in spontaneous recollection no more than this same phenomenon in its nascent state, the beginning of a lesson learnt by heart. But how can we fail to recognise that the difference is radical between what must be constituted by repetition and what, by essence, cannot be repeated? Spontaneous recollection is perfect at once; time can add nothing to its image without distorting it; it will keep for memory its place and its date. On the contrary, the learnt recollection will issue from time as the lesson comes to be better known; it will become more and more impersonal, more and more foreign to our past life. Repetition has therefore not at all the effect of converting the first into the second; its rôle is simply to utilise more and more the movements by which the first is continued, in order to organise them among themselves, and, by setting up a mechanism, to create a habit of the body. This habit is moreover recollection only because I remember having acquired it; and I remember having acquired it only because I appeal to spontaneous memory, that which dates events and registers them only once. Of the two memories we have just distinguished, the first therefore appears to be indeed memory par excellence. The second, that which psychologists ordinarily study, is habit illumined by memory rather than memory itself. It is true that the example of a lesson learnt by heart is rather artificial. Yet our existence flows on in the midst of a limited number of objects, which pass before us more or less often: each of them, at the same time as it is perceived, provokes on our part movements, at least nascent ones, by which we adapt ourselves to it. These movements, by repeating themselves, create a mechanism for themselves, pass into the state of habit, and determine in us attitudes that automatically follow our perception of things. Our nervous system, we said, is scarcely destined for any other use. The afferent nerves bring to the brain an excitation which, after having intelligently chosen its path, is transmitted to motor mechanisms created by repetition. Thus the appropriate reaction is produced, the equilibrium with the environment, the adaptation, in a word, which is the general end of life. And a living being that was content to live would need nothing else. But at the same time as this process of perception and adaptation is pursued, which ends in the recording of the past in the form of motor habits, consciousness, as we shall see, retains the image of the situations through which it has passed one after another, and aligns them in the order in which they followed one another. What use will these memory-images serve? By being preserved in memory, by reproducing themselves in consciousness, will they not distort the practical character of life, mingling dream with reality? So it would be, no doubt, if our actual consciousness, a consciousness which precisely reflects the exact adaptation of our nervous system to the present situation, did not set aside all those past images that cannot be coordinated with the actual perception and form with it a useful whole. At most certain confused recollections, unrelated to the present situation, overflow the usefully associated images, tracing around them a less illuminated fringe which loses itself in an immense obscure zone. But let an accident come that upsets the equilibrium maintained by the brain between the external excitation and the motor reaction, relax for an instant the tension of the threads that run from the periphery to the periphery by way of the centre, and at once the darkened images will push themselves into the full light: it is this last condition that is no doubt realised in the sleep in which we dream. Of the two memories we have distinguished, the second, which is active or motor, will therefore have constantly to inhibit the first, or at least to accept from it only what can usefully illuminate and complete the present situation: thus the laws of the association of ideas are deduced. - But independently of the services they can render by their association with a present perception, the images stored up by spontaneous memory have yet another use. No doubt they are dream-images; no doubt they ordinarily appear and disappear independently of our will; and that is precisely why we are obliged, in order really to know a thing, to hold it at our disposal, to learn it by heart, that is, to substitute for the spontaneous image a motor mechanism capable of supplying its place. But there is a certain effort sui generis which allows us to hold the image itself, for a limited time, under the gaze of our consciousness; and thanks to this faculty, we have no need to wait upon chance for the accidental repetition of the same situations in order to organise the concomitant movements into habit; we make use of the fleeting image to construct a stable mechanism that replaces it. - Either, then, our distinction of two independent memories is, finally, not well founded, or, if it answers to the facts, we shall have to find an exaltation of spontaneous memory in most of the cases where the sensori-motor equilibrium of the nervous system is disturbed, an inhibition, on the contrary, in the normal state, of all the spontaneous recollections that cannot usefully consolidate the present equilibrium, and finally, in the operation by which the habit-recollection is contracted, the latent intervention of the memory-image. Do the facts confirm the hypothesis? We shall not insist, for the moment, either on the first point or on the second: we hope to bring them out in full light when we study the disturbances of memory and the laws of the association of ideas. Let us confine ourselves to showing, with regard to things learnt, how the two memories go side by side here and lend each other mutual support. That lessons impressed upon the motor memory repeat themselves automatically, daily experience shows; but the observation of pathological cases establishes that automatism here extends much further than we think. Dements have been seen to give intelligent answers to a series of questions that they did not understand: language functioned in them after the manner of a reflex1. Aphasics, incapable of pronouncing a word spontaneously, recall without error the words of a melody when they sing it2. Or again they will recite fluently a prayer, the series of numbers, those of the days of the week and the months of the year3. Thus mechanisms of extreme complication, subtle enough to imitate intelligence, can function of themselves once they are constructed, and consequently ordinarily obey the sole initial impulse of the will. But what happens while we are constructing them? When we exercise ourselves in learning a lesson, for example, would not the visual or auditory image that we seek to recompose by movements already be in our mind, invisible and present? From the first recitation, we recognise by a vague feeling of uneasiness some error we have just committed, as if we received from the obscure depths of consciousness a kind of warning4. Concentrate then on what you experience, and you will feel that the complete image is there, but fugitive, a veritable phantom that vanishes at the precise moment when your motor activity would fix its outline. In recent experiments, undertaken moreover with a quite different aim5, the subjects declared that they experienced precisely an impression of this kind. A series of letters was made to appear before their eyes for a few seconds, which they were asked to retain. But, to prevent them from underlining the letters perceived by appropriate movements of articulation, they were required to repeat constantly a certain syllable while they looked at the image. From this resulted a special psychological state, in which the subjects felt themselves in complete possession of the visual image "without being able, however, to reproduce the least part of it at the required moment: to their great surprise, the line disappeared." According to one of them, "there was at the base of the phenomenon a representation of the whole, a sort of complex idea embracing the whole, and in which the parts had an inexpressibly felt unity6." This spontaneous recollection, which no doubt lies hidden behind the acquired recollection, can reveal itself in sudden flashes: but it slips away at the least movement of voluntary memory. If the subject sees the series of letters of which he thought he had retained the image disappear, it is above all while he is beginning to repeat them: "this effort seems to push the rest of the image out of consciousness1." Analyse now the imaginative procedures of mnemonics, and you will find that this science has precisely for its object to bring to the foreground the spontaneous recollection that conceals itself, and to place it, as an active recollection, at our free disposal: for this one first represses every inclination of the acting or motor memory. The faculty of mental photography, says one author2, belongs rather to the subconscious than to consciousness; it obeys the call of the will with difficulty. To exercise it, one must accustom oneself to retaining, for example, several groupings of points all at once, without even thinking of counting them3: one must, in a way, imitate the instantaneity of this memory in order to arrive at its discipline. Even so it remains capricious in its manifestations, and as the recollections it brings have something of the dream about them, it is rare that its more regular intrusion into the life of the mind does not profoundly disturb the intellectual equilibrium. What this memory is, whence it derives and how it proceeds, our next chapter will show. A schematic conception will suffice provisionally. Let us say, then, to sum up what precedes, that the past does appear to be stored up, as we had foreseen, under these two extreme forms, on one side the motor mechanisms that utilise it, on the other the personal memory-images which depict all its events with their outline, their colour and their place in time. Of these two memories, the first is truly oriented in the direction of nature; the second, left to itself, would rather go in the contrary direction. The first, won by effort, remains dependent on our will; the second, wholly spontaneous, shows as much caprice in reproducing as fidelity in preserving. The only regular and certain service that the second can render to the first is to show it the images of what has preceded or followed situations analogous to the present situation, in order to enlighten its choice: in this consists the association of ideas. There is no other case in which the memory that sees again regularly obeys the memory that repeats. Everywhere else, we prefer to construct a mechanism which allows us, if need be, to draw the image anew, because we feel well that we cannot count on its reappearance. Such are the two extreme forms of memory, each considered in the pure state. Let us say it at once: it is through having kept to the intermediate and, in a way, impure forms that the true nature of recollection has been misunderstood. Instead of first dissociating the two elements, memory-image and movement, and then inquiring by what series of operations they come, by abandoning something of their original purity, to flow into one another, we consider only the mixed phenomenon which results from their coalescence. This phenomenon, being mixed, presents on one side the aspect of a motor habit, on the other that of an image more or less consciously localised. But it is insisted that it be a simple phenomenon. It will therefore have to be supposed that the cerebral, medullary or bulbar mechanism which serves as the basis of the motor habit is at the same time the substrate of the conscious image. Hence the strange hypothesis of recollections stored up in the brain, which would become conscious by a veritable miracle, and bring us back to the past by a mysterious process. Some, it is true, attach themselves more to the conscious aspect of the operation and would wish to see in it something other than an epiphenomenon. But as they have not begun by isolating the memory that retains and aligns the successive repetitions in the form of memory-images, as they confuse it with the habit that exercise perfects, they are led to believe that the effect of repetition bears on one and the same indivisible phenomenon, which would simply be strengthened by repeating itself: and as this phenomenon visibly ends by being no more than a motor habit and by corresponding to a mechanism, cerebral or other, they are brought, willy-nilly, to suppose that a mechanism of this kind was from the beginning at the bottom of the image and that the brain is an organ of representation. We are going to consider these intermediate states, and to make in each of them the part of nascent action, that is, of the brain, and the part of independent memory, that is, that of memory-images. What are these states? Being motor on one side, they must, according to our hypothesis, prolong an actual perception; but on the other hand, as images, they reproduce past perceptions. Now the concrete act by which we recapture the past in the present is recognition. It is therefore recognition that we must study. II. Of recognition in general: memory-images and movements. - There are two habitual ways of explaining the feeling of "already seen". For some, to recognise a present perception would consist in inserting it in thought into an old surrounding. I meet a person for the first time: I simply perceive him. If I find him again, I recognise him, in the sense that the concomitant circumstances of the primitive perception, returning to my mind, trace around the actual image a frame which is not the frame actually perceived. To recognise would therefore be to associate with a present perception the images given formerly in contiguity with it1. But, as has rightly been observed2, a renewed perception can suggest the concomitant circumstances of the primitive perception only if the latter is first evoked by the actual state which resembles it. Let A be the first perception; the concomitant circumstances B, C, D remain associated with it by contiguity. If I call A' the same perception renewed, since it is not to A' but to A that the terms B, C, D are linked, it is necessary, in order to evoke the terms B, C, D, that an association by resemblance should first make A arise. In vain will it be maintained that A' is identical with A. The two terms, though similar, remain numerically distinct, and differ at the very least by this simple fact that A' is a perception whereas A is now no more than a recollection. Of the two interpretations we had announced, the first thus comes to merge into the second, which we are going to examine. It is supposed this time that the present perception always goes to seek, in the depths of memory, the recollection of the earlier perception which resembles it: the feeling of "already seen" would come from a juxtaposition or a fusion between the perception and the recollection. No doubt, as has been profoundly observed1, resemblance is a relation established by the mind between terms that it brings together and which it therefore already possesses, so that the perception of a resemblance is rather an effect of association than its cause. But besides this defined and perceived resemblance, which consists in the community of an element seized and disengaged by the mind, there is a vague and in a way objective resemblance, spread over the surface of the images themselves, and which could act as a physical cause of reciprocal attraction2. Shall we allege that an object is often recognised without succeeding in identifying it with an old image? Refuge will be taken in the convenient hypothesis of cerebral traces that would coincide, of cerebral movements that exercise would facilitate3, or of cells of perception communicating with cells in which the recollections repose4. In truth, it is in physiological hypotheses of this kind that all these theories of recognition come, willy-nilly, to lose themselves. They would have all recognition issue from a bringing together of the perception and the recollection; but on the other hand experience is there, which testifies that, most often, the recollection arises only once the perception is recognised. It is therefore necessary to cast back into the brain, in the form of a combination between movements or a liaison between cells, what had first been announced as an association between representations, and to explain the fact of recognition - very clear in our view - by the hypothesis, in our view very obscure, of a brain that would store up ideas. But in reality the association of a perception with a recollection does not at all suffice to account for the process of recognition. For if recognition were effected in this way, it would be abolished when the old images have disappeared, it would always take place when these images are preserved. Psychic blindness, or inability to recognise the objects perceived, would therefore not go without an inhibition of visual memory, and above all the inhibition of visual memory would invariably have psychic blindness as its effect. Now experience verifies neither of these two consequences. In a case studied by Wilbrand1, the patient could, with her eyes closed, describe the town in which she lived and walk about in it in imagination: once in the street, everything seemed new to her; she recognised nothing and could not find her bearings. Facts of the same kind have been observed by Fr. Müller2 and Lissauer3. The patients know how to evoke the inner vision of an object that is named to them; they describe it very well; they cannot, however, recognise it when it is shown to them. The preservation, even conscious, of a visual recollection therefore does not suffice for the recognition of a similar perception. But conversely, in the case studied by Charcot4 and become classical, of a complete eclipse of visual images, all recognition of perceptions was not abolished. One will be easily convinced of this by reading the account of this case closely. The subject no longer recognised, no doubt, the streets of his native town, in that he could neither name them nor find his bearings in them; he knew nevertheless that they were streets, and that he saw houses. He no longer recognised his wife and children; he could say, however, on seeing them, that it was a woman, that they were children. None of this would have been possible if there had been psychic blindness in the absolute sense of the word. What was abolished was therefore a certain kind of recognition, which we shall have to analyse, but not the general faculty of recognising. Let us conclude that not all recognition always implies the intervention of an old image, and that one may equally well appeal to these images without succeeding in identifying the perceptions with them. What, then, is recognition at last, and how shall we define it? There is first, at the limit, a recognition in the instantaneous, a recognition of which the body alone is capable, without any explicit recollection intervening. It consists in an action, and not in a representation. I walk about in a town, for example, for the first time. At each turning of the street, I hesitate, not knowing where I am going. I am in uncertainty, and by that I mean that alternatives are posed to my body, that my movement is discontinuous as a whole, that there is nothing, in one of the attitudes, that announces and prepares the attitudes to come. Later, after a long stay in the town, I shall move about in it mechanically, without having the distinct perception of the objects before which I pass. Now, between these two extreme conditions, the one in which perception has not yet organised the definite movements that accompany it, the other in which these concomitant movements are so organised as to render my perception useless, there is an intermediate condition, in which the object is perceived, but provokes movements linked together, continuous, and which command one another. I began with a state in which I distinguished only my perception; I end with a state in which I am scarcely conscious any longer of anything but my automatism: in the interval there has taken place a mixed state, a perception underlined by a nascent automatism. Now, if the later perceptions differ from the first perception in that they set the body on the way to an appropriate mechanical reaction, if, on the other hand, these renewed perceptions appear to the mind with that aspect sui generis which characterises familiar or recognised perceptions, must we not presume that the consciousness of a well-regulated motor accompaniment, of an organised motor reaction, is here the ground of the feeling of familiarity? At the base of recognition there would thus indeed be a phenomenon of the motor order. To recognise a usual object consists above all in knowing how to use it. This is so true that the first observers had given the name apraxia to this disease of recognition which we call psychic blindness1. But to know how to use it is already to sketch the movements that adapt themselves to it, it is to take a certain attitude or at least to tend toward it by the effect of what the Germans have called "motor impulses" (Bewegungsantriebe). The habit of using the object has therefore ended by organising movements and perceptions together, and the consciousness of these nascent movements, which would follow the perception after the manner of a reflex, would be, here again, at the bottom of recognition. There is no perception that does not extend itself into movement. Ribot2 and Maudsley3 have long since drawn attention to this point. The education of the senses consists precisely in the ensemble of the connections established between the sensory impression and the movement which utilises it. As the impression is repeated, the connection is consolidated. The mechanism of the operation has, moreover, nothing mysterious about it. Our nervous system is evidently disposed with a view to the construction of motor apparatus, linked, through the intermediary of the centres, to sensible excitations, and the discontinuity of the nervous elements, the multiplicity of their terminal arborisations, capable no doubt of drawing together in various ways, render unlimited the number of possible connections between the impressions and the corresponding movements. But the mechanism in course of construction could not appear to consciousness in the same form as the mechanism constructed. Something profoundly distinguishes, and clearly manifests, the systems of movements consolidated in the organism. It is above all, we believe, the difficulty of modifying their order. It is also this preformation of the following movements in the preceding movements, a preformation which makes the part contain the whole virtually, as happens when each note of a learnt melody, for example, remains leaning over the next to watch over its execution4. If, then, every usual perception has its organised motor accompaniment, the usual feeling of recognition has its root in the consciousness of this organisation. That is to say that we ordinarily play out our recognition before thinking it. Our daily life unfolds among objects whose mere presence invites us to play a part: in this consists their aspect of familiarity. Motor tendencies would therefore already suffice to give us the feeling of recognition. But, let us hasten to say, something else is most often joined to them. For while motor apparatuses are being set up under the influence of perceptions ever better analysed by the body, our earlier psychological life is there: it survives itself, as we shall try to prove, with all the detail of its events localised in time. Ceaselessly inhibited by the practical and useful consciousness of the present moment, that is, by the sensori-motor equilibrium of a nervous system stretched between perception and action, this memory simply waits for a fissure to open between the present impression and the concomitant movement, so as to slip its images through. Ordinarily, in order to travel back up the course of our past and discover the known, localised, personal memory-image which would relate to the present, an effort is necessary, by which we disengage ourselves from the action to which our perception inclines us: the latter would push us towards the future; we must fall back into the past. In this sense, movement would rather keep the image away. Yet in a certain respect it contributes to preparing it. For if the whole of our past images remains present to us, the representation analogous to the present perception must still be chosen from among all possible representations. The movements accomplished or merely nascent prepare this selection, or at the very least delimit the field of images in which we shall go to gather. We are, by the constitution of our nervous system, beings in whom present impressions are prolonged in appropriate movements: if old images likewise find the means of being prolonged in these movements, they take the opportunity to slip into the present perception and to have themselves adopted by it. They then appear, in fact, to our consciousness, whereas they would seem, by right, bound to remain covered over by the present state. One might therefore say that the movements which provoke mechanical recognition hinder recognition by images on one side, and favour it on the other. In principle, the present displaces the past. But on the other hand, precisely because the suppression of the old images is due to their inhibition by the present attitude, those whose form could fit into this attitude will meet with less of an obstacle than the others; and if, accordingly, any one of them can clear the obstacle, it is the image similar to the present perception that will clear it. If our analysis is exact, the diseases of recognition will take two profoundly different forms, and two kinds of psychic blindness will be found. Sometimes, indeed, it is the old images that can no longer be evoked; sometimes it is only the link between the perception and the habitual concomitant movements that will be broken, the perception provoking diffuse movements as if it were new. Do the facts bear out this hypothesis? There can be no dispute about the first point. The apparent abolition of visual recollections in psychic blindness is so common a fact that it was able, for a time, to serve to define this affection. We shall have to ask ourselves to what extent and in what sense recollections can really vanish. What interests us for the moment is that cases occur in which recognition no longer takes place without visual memory being practically abolished. Is it then really, as we claim, a matter of a simple disturbance of the motor habits, or at least of an interruption of the link which unites them to sensible perceptions? No observer having put such a question to himself, we should be hard put to answer it if we had not noted here and there, in their descriptions, certain facts which seem to us significant. The first of these facts is the loss of the sense of orientation. All the authors who have dealt with psychic blindness have been struck by this peculiarity. Lissauer's patient had completely lost the faculty of finding his way about his house.1 Fr. Müller insists on the fact that, whereas blind persons learn very quickly to find their way again, a subject afflicted with psychic blindness cannot, even after months of exercise, orient himself in his own room.2 But is the faculty of orienting oneself anything other than the faculty of coordinating the movements of the body with visual impressions, and of mechanically prolonging perceptions in useful reactions? There is a second fact, more characteristic still. We mean the manner in which these patients draw. Two ways of drawing can be conceived. The first would consist in fixing a certain number of points on the paper, by groping, and joining them together while verifying at every moment whether the image resembles the object. This is what would be called drawing "by points". But the means we habitually use is quite another. We draw "in one continuous stroke", after having looked at the model or thought of it. How are we to explain such a faculty, if not by the habit of immediately disentangling the organisation of the most usual contours, that is, by a motor tendency to figure their schema in a single stroke? But if it is precisely habits or correspondences of this kind that dissolve in certain forms of psychic blindness, the patient may perhaps still be able to trace elements of line, which he will join together after a fashion; he will no longer know how to draw in one continuous stroke, because he will no longer have the movement of the contours in his hand. Now this is precisely what experience bears out. Lissauer's observation is already instructive in this respect.3 His patient had the greatest difficulty in drawing simple objects, and if he wished to draw them from memory, he traced detached portions of them, taken here and there, which he did not manage to connect with one another. But cases of complete psychic blindness are rare. Far more numerous are those of word-blindness, that is, of a loss of visual recognition limited to the characters of the alphabet. Now it is a matter of common observation that, in such a case, the patient is powerless to grasp what might be called the movement of the letters when he tries to copy them. He begins to draw them at any point whatever, verifying at every moment whether he remains in agreement with the model. And this is all the more remarkable in that he has often kept intact the faculty of writing from dictation or spontaneously. What is abolished here is therefore indeed the habit of disentangling the articulations of the object perceived, that is, of completing its visual perception by a motor tendency to draw its schema. From which we may conclude, as we had announced, that here is indeed the primordial condition of recognition. But we must now pass from automatic recognition, which is effected chiefly by movements, to that which requires the regular intervention of memory-images. The first is recognition by distraction: the second, as we shall see, is attentive recognition. It too begins with movements. But whereas, in automatic recognition, our movements prolong our perception in order to draw useful effects from it and thus carry us away from the object perceived, here on the contrary they bring us back to the object in order to underline its contours. Hence the preponderant, and no longer accessory, rôle that memory-images play in it. Suppose, indeed, that the movements renounce their practical end, and that motor activity, instead of continuing the perception by useful reactions, retraces its steps in order to outline its salient features: then the images analogous to the present perception, images whose form these movements will already have cast, will come regularly, and no longer accidentally, to pour themselves into this mould, even if, it is true, they must abandon many of their details in order to ease their entry. III. Gradual passage from recollections to movements. Recognition and attention. We touch here upon the essential point of the debate. In the cases where recognition is attentive, that is, where memory-images regularly join the present perception, is it the perception which mechanically determines the appearance of the recollections, or do the recollections spontaneously go forth to meet the perception? On the answer given to this question depends the nature of the relations that will be established between the brain and memory. In every perception, indeed, there is a disturbance transmitted by the nerves to the perceptive centres. If the propagation of this movement to other cortical centres really had the effect of making images arise there, one could maintain, strictly speaking, that memory is only a function of the brain. But if we established that here, as elsewhere, movement can produce only movement, that the rôle of the perceptive disturbance is simply to impress upon the body a certain attitude into which the recollections come to be inserted, then, the whole effect of the material disturbances being exhausted in this work of motor adaptation, we should have to look elsewhere for the recollection. On the first hypothesis, the disorders of memory occasioned by a cerebral lesion would come from the recollections having occupied the injured region and having been destroyed with it. On the second, on the contrary, these lesions would concern our nascent or possible action, but our action only. Sometimes they would prevent the body from taking up, in the presence of an object, the attitude appropriate to the recall of the image: sometimes they would cut this recollection off from its attachments to present reality, that is, by suppressing the last phase of the realisation of the recollection, by suppressing the phase of action, they would thereby also prevent the recollection from becoming actual. But no more in the one case than in the other would a cerebral lesion truly destroy recollections. This second hypothesis will be ours. But before seeking its verification, let us say briefly how we represent to ourselves the general relations of perception, attention and memory. In order to show how a recollection could, by degrees, come to be inserted into an attitude or a movement, we shall have to anticipate somewhat the conclusions of our next chapter. What is attention? On the one hand, the essential effect of attention is to render perception more intense and to bring out its details: considered in its matter, it would therefore reduce itself to a certain magnification of the intellectual state.1 But, on the other hand, consciousness records an irreducible difference of form between this increase of intensity and that which is due to a higher power of the external excitation: it seems indeed to come from within, and to bear witness to a certain attitude adopted by the intelligence. But here precisely obscurity begins, for the idea of an intellectual attitude is not a clear idea. We shall speak of a "concentration of mind",2 or again of an "apperceptive"3 effort to bring the perception under the gaze of the distinct intelligence. Some, materialising this idea, will suppose a particular tension of cerebral energy4 or even a central expenditure of energy added to the excitation received.5 But either one confines oneself to translating thus the psychologically ascertained fact into a physiological language which seems to us still less clear, or it is always to a metaphor that one returns. By degrees, one will be led to define attention by a general adaptation of the body rather than of the mind, and to see in this attitude of consciousness, above all, the consciousness of an attitude. Such is the position taken by Th. Ribot in the debate,6 and although attacked,7 it seems to have kept all its force, provided however, we believe, that one sees in the movements described by Th. Ribot only the negative condition of the phenomenon. Even supposing, indeed, that the concomitant movements of voluntary attention were chiefly movements of arrest, there would remain to be explained the work of the mind which corresponds to them, that is, the mysterious operation by which the same organ, perceiving in the same surroundings the same object, discovers in it an increasing number of things. But one may go further, and maintain that the phenomena of inhibition are only a preparation for the effective movements of voluntary attention. Suppose, indeed, as we have already given to be foreseen, that attention implies a turning back of the mind, which renounces pursuing the useful effect of the present perception: there will first be an inhibition of movement, an action of arrest. But upon this general attitude there will very soon be grafted subtler movements, some of which have been remarked and described,1 and whose rôle is to pass again over the contours of the object perceived. With these movements begins the positive, and no longer merely negative, work of attention. It is continued by recollections. If external perception, indeed, provokes on our part movements which outline its main lines, our memory directs upon the perception received the old images which resemble it and of which our movements have already traced the sketch. It thus creates the present perception anew, or rather it doubles this perception by sending back to it either its own image, or some memory-image of the same kind. If the image retained or recalled does not manage to cover all the details of the image perceived, an appeal is launched to the deeper and more remote regions of memory, until other known details come to be projected upon those which are not known. And the operation can continue without end, memory strengthening and enriching perception, which, in its turn, ever more developed, draws to itself an increasing number of complementary recollections. Let us therefore no longer think of a mind which would dispose of some fixed quantity of light, now diffusing it all around, now concentrating it on a single point. Image for image, we should prefer to compare the elementary work of attention to that of the telegraphist who, on receiving an important despatch, sends it back word for word to the place of origin in order to check its accuracy. But to send a despatch back, one must know how to handle the apparatus. And likewise, in order to reflect upon a perception the image we have received of it, we must be able to reproduce it, that is, to reconstruct it by an effort of synthesis. It has been said that attention was a faculty of analysis, and rightly; but it has not been sufficiently explained how an analysis of this kind is possible, nor by what process we manage to discover in a perception what did not at first show itself in it. The truth is that this analysis is made by a series of attempts at synthesis, or, what comes to the same, by as many hypotheses: our memory chooses in turn various analogous images which it launches in the direction of the new perception. But this choice is not made at random. What suggests the hypotheses, what presides from afar over the selection, are the movements of imitation by which the perception is continued, and which will serve as a common frame for the perception and the images recalled. But then, the mechanism of distinct perception will have to be represented otherwise than is ordinarily done. Perception does not consist merely in impressions gathered or even elaborated by the mind. At most is this so of those perceptions which are dissipated as soon as received, those which we scatter in useful actions. But every attentive perception truly supposes, in the etymological sense of the word, a reflection, that is, the external projection of an actively created image, identical with or similar to the object, and which comes to mould itself upon its contours. If, after fixing an object, we abruptly turn our gaze away, we obtain an after-image of it: must we not suppose that this image was already being produced when we were looking at it? The recent discovery of centrifugal perceptive fibres would incline us to think that things regularly happen in this way, and that, alongside the afferent process which carries the impression to the centre, there is another, inverse one, which brings the image back to the periphery. It is true that this concerns images photographed upon the object itself, and recollections immediately consecutive to the perception, of which they are only the echo. But behind these images identical with the object there are others, stored up in memory, which have with it merely a resemblance, and others again which have only a more or less distant kinship. They all go to meet the perception, and, nourished on its substance, they acquire enough force and life to be externalised with it. The experiments of Münsterberg,1 of Külpe,2 leave no doubt on this last point: every memory-image capable of interpreting our present perception slips into it so well that we no longer know how to discern what is perception and what is recollection. But nothing is more interesting, in this respect, than the ingenious experiments of Goldscheider and Müller on the mechanism of reading.3 Against Grashey, who had maintained in a celebrated work4 that we read words letter by letter, these experimenters have established that ordinary reading is a veritable work of divination, our mind gathering here and there a few characteristic features and filling the whole interval with memory-images which, projected upon the paper, are substituted for the characters actually printed and give us the illusion of them. Thus we ceaselessly create or reconstruct. Our distinct perception is truly comparable to a closed circle, in which the perception-image directed towards the mind and the memory-image launched into space would run one behind the other. Let us insist on this last point. We readily represent attentive perception to ourselves as a series of processes that would proceed along a single thread, the object exciting sensations, the sensations bringing ideas to arise before them, each idea shaking, step by step, more remote points of the intellectual mass. There would thus be a march in a straight line, by which the mind would move ever further from the object, never to return to it. We maintain on the contrary that reflective perception is a circuit, in which all the elements, the object perceived itself included, hold one another in a state of mutual tension as in an electric circuit, so that no disturbance starting from the object can stop on the way in the depths of the mind: it must always return to the object itself. Let no one see here a mere question of words. It is a matter of two radically different conceptions of intellectual work. According to the first, things happen mechanically, and by an altogether accidental series of successive additions. At each moment of an attentive perception, for example, new elements, emanating from a deeper region of the mind, could be joined to the old elements without creating a general disturbance, without requiring a transformation of the system. In the second, on the contrary, an act of attention implies such a solidarity between the mind and its object, it is a circuit so closed, that one cannot pass to states of higher concentration without creating out of whole cloth as many new circuits which envelop the first, and which have nothing in common with one another but the object perceived. Of these different circles of memory, which we shall study in detail later, the narrowest, A, is the nearest to immediate perception. It contains only the object O itself with the after-image which comes back to cover it. Behind it the circles B, C, D, ever wider, answer to increasing efforts of intellectual expansion. It is the whole of memory, as we shall see, that enters into each of these circuits, since memory is always present; but this memory, which its elasticity allows to dilate indefinitely, reflects upon the object an increasing number of suggested things, now the details of the object itself, now concomitant details able to contribute to elucidating it. Thus, after having reconstituted the object perceived, after the manner of an independent whole, we reconstitute with it the ever more remote conditions with which it forms a system. Let us call B', C', D' these causes of increasing depth, situated behind the object, and virtually given with the object itself. It will be seen that the progress of attention has the effect of creating anew not only the object perceived, but the ever vaster systems to which it may be attached; so that, as the circles B, C, D represent a higher expansion of memory, their reflection reaches in B', C', D' deeper layers of reality. Figure 1 The same psychological life would therefore be repeated an indefinite number of times, on the successive storeys of memory, and the same act of the mind could be played at many different heights. In the effort of attention, the mind always gives itself whole, but simplifies or complicates itself according to the level it chooses for accomplishing its evolutions. It is ordinarily the present perception that determines the orientation of our mind; but according to the degree of tension our mind adopts, according to the height at which it places itself, this perception develops in us a greater or lesser number of memory-images. In other words, finally, personal recollections, exactly localised, and whose series would trace the course of our past existence, constitute, taken together, the last and widest envelope of our memory. Essentially fugitive, they materialise only by chance, whether an accidentally precise determination of our bodily attitude attracts them, or the very indetermination of that attitude leaves the field free to the caprice of their manifestation. But this outermost envelope contracts and repeats itself in inner and concentric circles, which, narrower, support the same recollections diminished, ever further removed from their personal and original form, ever more capable, in their banality, of applying themselves to the present perception and determining it after the manner of a species embracing the individual. A moment arrives when the recollection thus reduced fits so well into the present perception that one could not say where the perception ends and where the recollection begins. At that precise moment, memory, instead of making its representations appear and disappear capriciously, regulates itself on the detail of the bodily movements. But as these recollections draw nearer to movement and thereby to external perception, the operation of memory acquires a higher practical importance. Past images, reproduced as they are with all their details and even their affective colouring, are the images of reverie or of dream; what we call acting is precisely to obtain that this memory contract, or rather sharpen itself more and more, until it presents only the cutting edge of its blade to the experience into which it will penetrate. At bottom, it is through not having disentangled here the motor element of memory that people have at one time misunderstood, at another exaggerated, what is automatic in the evocation of recollections. In our view, an appeal is launched to our activity at the precise moment when our perception has automatically decomposed itself into movements of imitation: a sketch is then furnished to us, whose detail and colour we recreate by projecting into it more or less remote recollections. But this is not how things are ordinarily envisaged. At one time absolute autonomy is conferred on the mind; it is granted the power of working on objects present or absent as it pleases; and one then no longer understands the profound disorders of attention and memory which may follow the slightest disturbance of the sensori-motor equilibrium. At another, on the contrary, the imaginative processes are made so many mechanical effects of the present perception; it is wished that, by a necessary and uniform progress, the object should make sensations arise, and the sensations ideas that attach themselves to them: then, as there is no reason why the phenomenon, mechanical at the start, should change its nature on the way, one ends in the hypothesis of a brain in which intellectual states could be deposited, slumber and awaken. In the one case as in the other, the true function of the body is misunderstood, and as one has not seen in what respect the intervention of a mechanism is necessary, one knows no better, once one has appealed to it, where one should stop it. But the moment has come to leave these generalities. We must inquire whether our hypothesis is borne out or refuted by the known facts of cerebral localisation. The disturbances of imaginative memory that correspond to localised lesions of the cortex are always diseases of recognition, whether of visual or auditory recognition in general (psychic blindness and psychic deafness), or of the recognition of words (word-blindness, word-deafness, and so on). Such, then, are the disturbances we must examine. But if our hypothesis is well founded, these lesions of recognition will not at all come from the fact that the recollections occupied the injured region. They will have to be due to two causes: sometimes to the fact that our body can no longer take up automatically, in the presence of the excitation coming from outside, the precise attitude through whose intermediary a selection among our recollections would be effected, sometimes to the fact that the recollections no longer find in the body a point of application, a means of prolonging themselves into action. In the first case, the lesion will bear upon the mechanisms that continue the received disturbance into an automatically executed movement: attention will no longer be able to be fixed by the object. In the second, the lesion will affect those particular centres of the cortex which prepare voluntary movements by supplying them with the necessary sensory antecedent, and which are called, rightly or wrongly, imaginative centres: attention will no longer be able to be fixed by the subject. But, in the one case as in the other, it is actual movements that will be injured or movements to come that will cease to be prepared: there will have been no destruction of recollections. Now, pathology confirms this expectation. It reveals to us the existence of two absolutely distinct kinds of psychic blindness and psychic deafness, of word-blindness and word-deafness. In the first, the visual or auditory recollections are still evoked, but can no longer be applied to the corresponding perceptions. In the second, the evocation of the recollections is itself prevented. Does the lesion bear, as we said, upon the sensori-motor mechanisms of automatic attention in the first case, and upon the imaginative mechanisms of voluntary attention in the other? To verify our hypothesis, we must confine ourselves to one precise example. We could, certainly, show that the visual recognition of things in general, and of words in particular, implies first a semi-automatic motor process, then an active projection of recollections which insert themselves into the corresponding attitudes. But we prefer to hold to the impressions of hearing, and more especially to the hearing of articulate speech, because this example is the most comprehensive of all. To hear speech, indeed, is first to recognise its sound, then to find its meaning again, and finally to carry its interpretation more or less far: in short, it is to pass through all the degrees of attention and to exercise several successive powers of memory. Moreover, there are no disturbances more frequent or better studied than those of the auditory memory of words. Finally, the abolition of acoustic verbal images does not occur without grave lesion of certain determinate convolutions of the cortex: an undisputed example of localisation will therefore be furnished us, on which we may ask whether the brain is really capable of storing up recollections. We must therefore show in the auditory recognition of words: 1º an automatic sensori-motor process; 2º an active and, so to speak, eccentric projection of memory-images. 1º I listen to two persons conversing in an unknown language. Does that suffice for me to hear them? The vibrations that reach me are the same that strike their ears. Yet I perceive only a confused noise in which all the sounds resemble one another. I distinguish nothing and could repeat nothing. In this same sonorous mass, on the contrary, the two speakers disentangle consonants, vowels and syllables which hardly resemble one another, and finally distinct words. Between them and me, where is the difference? The question is how the knowledge of a language, which is only recollection, can modify the materiality of a present perception, and make some actually hear what others, under the same physical conditions, do not hear. It is supposed, it is true, that the auditory recollections of words, accumulated in memory, respond here to the call of the sound impressions and come to reinforce their effect. But if the conversation I hear is for me only a noise, one may suppose the sound reinforced as much as one likes: the noise, being louder, will be no clearer. For the recollection of the word to let itself be evoked by the word heard, the ear must at least hear the word. How will the sounds perceived speak to memory, how will they choose, in the store of auditory images, those which are to settle upon them, if they have not already been separated, distinguished, perceived at last as syllables and as words? This difficulty does not seem to have sufficiently struck the theorists of sensory aphasia. In word-deafness, indeed, the patient finds himself, with regard to his own language, in the same situation in which we ourselves find ourselves when we hear an unknown language spoken. He has generally kept the sense of hearing intact, but he understands nothing of the words he hears pronounced, and often does not even manage to distinguish them. It is thought that this state has been sufficiently explained by saying that the auditory recollections of words are destroyed in the cortex, or that a lesion, sometimes transcortical, sometimes subcortical, prevents the auditory recollection from evoking the idea, or the perception from reaching the recollection. But, for the latter case at least, the psychological question remains untouched: what is the conscious process that the lesion has abolished, and by what intermediary is the discernment of words and syllables, given at first to the ear as a sonorous continuity, in general effected? The difficulty would be insurmountable if we really had to do only with auditory impressions on one side and auditory recollections on the other. It would not be so if the auditory impressions organised nascent movements, capable of scanning the sentence listened to and of marking its principal articulations. These automatic movements of inner accompaniment, at first confused and ill coordinated, would then disengage themselves better and better by repeating themselves; they would end by tracing a simplified figure, in which the person who listens would find again, in their broad lines and principal directions, the very movements of the person who speaks. Thus there would unfold in our consciousness, in the form of nascent muscular sensations, what we shall call the motor schema of the speech heard. To train one's ear to the elements of a new language would then consist neither in modifying the raw sound nor in adjoining a recollection to it; it would be to coordinate the motor tendencies of the muscles of the voice with the impressions of the ear, it would be to perfect the motor accompaniment. To learn a physical exercise, we begin by imitating the movement as a whole, such as our eyes show it to us from outside, such as we have thought we saw it executed. Our perception of it was confused: confused will be the movement that attempts to repeat it. But whereas our visual perception was that of a continuous whole, the movement by which we seek to reconstitute its image is composed of a multitude of muscular contractions and tensions; and the consciousness we have of it itself comprises manifold sensations, arising from the varied play of the joints. The confused movement which imitates the image is therefore already its virtual decomposition; it carries within it, so to speak, the means of analysing itself. The progress that will arise from repetition and exercise will consist simply in disengaging what was at first enveloped, in giving to each of the elementary movements that autonomy which ensures precision, while preserving for it with the others the solidarity without which it would become useless. It is right to say that habit is acquired by the repetition of effort; but of what use would repeated effort be, if it always reproduced the same thing? The true effect of repetition is to decompose first, to recompose afterwards, and thus to speak to the intelligence of the body. At each new trial it develops enveloped movements; each time it calls the body's attention to a new detail that had passed unnoticed; it makes the body divide and classify; it underlines the essential for it; it finds again, one by one, in the total movement, the lines that mark its inner structure. In this sense a movement is learnt as soon as the body has understood it. Thus it is that a motor accompaniment of the speech heard would break the continuity of this sonorous mass. It remains to be known in what this accompaniment consists. Is it the speech itself, reproduced inwardly? But then the child would be able to repeat all the words that his ear distinguishes; and we ourselves would have only to understand a foreign language in order to pronounce it with the right accent. Things are far from passing so simply. I can grasp a melody, follow its design, even fix it in my memory, and not know how to sing it. I readily disentangle the peculiarities of inflexion and intonation in an Englishman speaking German - I therefore correct him inwardly - ; it does not follow that I would give the right inflexion and intonation to the German sentence if I were speaking. Clinical facts, moreover, here come to confirm daily observation. One can still follow and understand speech when one has become incapable of speaking. Motor aphasia does not entail word-deafness. This is because the schema by means of which we scan the speech heard marks only its salient contours. It is to the speech itself what the sketch is to the finished picture. It is one thing, indeed, to understand a difficult movement, another to be able to execute it. To understand it, it suffices to realise the essential of it, just enough to distinguish it from the other possible movements. But to know how to execute it, one must besides have made one's body understand it. Now, the logic of the body does not admit of things left understood. It demands that all the constituent parts of the movement required be shown one by one, then recomposed together. A complete analysis becomes necessary here, neglecting no detail, and an actual synthesis, in which nothing is abridged. The imaginative schema, composed of a few nascent muscular sensations, was only an outline. The muscular sensations really and completely felt give it colour and life. It remains to be known how an accompaniment of this kind could be produced, and whether it is always produced in reality. We know that the actual pronunciation of a word requires the simultaneous intervention of the tongue and lips for articulation, of the larynx for phonation, and finally of the thoracic muscles for the production of the expiratory current of air. To each syllable pronounced there corresponds therefore the coming into play of a set of mechanisms, all ready-made in the medullary and bulbar centres. These mechanisms are linked to the higher centres of the cortex by the axis-cylinder prolongations of the pyramidal cells of the psycho-motor zone; it is along these paths that the impulse of the will travels. Thus, according as we desire to articulate one sound or another, we transmit the order to act to this or that one of these motor mechanisms. But if the ready-made mechanisms that answer to the various possible movements of articulation and phonation are in relation with the causes, whatever they may be, that set them in action in voluntary speech, there are facts that put beyond doubt the communication of these same mechanisms with the auditory perception of words. Among the numerous varieties of aphasia described by clinicians, two are known first (the 4th and 6th forms of Lichtheim) which seem to imply a relation of this kind. Thus, in a case observed by Lichtheim himself, the subject, following a fall, had lost the memory of the articulation of words and consequently the faculty of speaking spontaneously; he nevertheless repeated with the greatest correctness what was said to him1. On the other hand, in cases where spontaneous speech is intact, but where word-deafness is absolute, the patient no longer understanding anything of what is said to him, the faculty of repeating the speech of another may still be entirely preserved2. Shall it be said, with Bastian, that these phenomena testify simply to a sluggishness of the articulatory or auditory memory of words, the acoustic impressions merely rousing this memory from its torpor3? This hypothesis, to which we shall moreover give a place, does not seem to us to account for the so curious phenomena of echolalia long since pointed out by Romberg4, by Voisin5, by Winslow6, and which Kussmaul has called, with some exaggeration no doubt, acoustic reflexes7. Here the subject repeats mechanically, and perhaps unconsciously, the words heard, as if the auditory sensations converted themselves of their own accord into articulatory movements. Starting from this, some have supposed a special mechanism that would link an acoustic centre of words to an articulatory centre of speech8. The truth appears to lie between these two hypotheses: there is, in these various phenomena, more than absolutely mechanical actions, but less than an appeal to voluntary memory; they testify to a tendency of the auditory verbal impressions to prolong themselves into movements of articulation, a tendency which surely does not escape the habitual control of our will, which perhaps even implies a rudimentary discernment, and which is expressed, in the normal state, by an inner repetition of the salient features of the speech heard. Now, our motor schema is nothing other than this. By going more deeply into this hypothesis, one would perhaps find in it the psychological explanation we asked for a moment ago of certain forms of word-deafness. A few cases are known of word-deafness with complete survival of the acoustic recollections. The patient has kept intact both the auditory recollection of words and the sense of hearing; he nevertheless recognises none of the words he hears pronounced1. A subcortical lesion is supposed here, which would prevent the acoustic impressions from going to find again the auditory verbal images in the centres of the cortex where they would be deposited. But in the first place the question is precisely whether the brain can store up images; and in the second place the very finding of a lesion in the conducting paths of perception would not spare us from seeking the psychological interpretation of the phenomenon. By hypothesis, indeed, the auditory recollections can be recalled to consciousness; by hypothesis, too, the auditory impressions reach consciousness: there must therefore be, in consciousness itself, a gap, a solution of continuity, something in short that opposes the junction of perception and recollection. Now, the fact will be made clear if we remark that the raw auditory perception is truly that of a sonorous continuity, and that the sensori-motor connections established by habit must have as their role, in the normal state, to decompose it: a lesion of these conscious mechanisms, by preventing the decomposition from being effected, would bring to a dead stop the flight of the recollections which tend to settle upon the corresponding perceptions. It is therefore upon the "motor schema" that the lesion might bear. Let the cases, rather rare moreover, of word-deafness with preservation of the acoustic recollections be passed in review: certain characteristic details in this respect will, we believe, be noted. Adler points out as a remarkable fact in word-deafness that the patients no longer react to noises, even intense ones, although hearing has kept in them the greatest fineness2. In other words, the sound no longer finds in them its motor echo. A patient of Charcot's, affected with transient word-deafness, relates that he heard the chime of his clock well, but that he could not have counted the strokes sounded3. He therefore probably did not manage to separate and distinguish them. Another patient will declare that he perceives the words of the conversation, but as a confused noise4. Finally, the subject who has lost the understanding of speech heard recovers it if the word is repeated to him several times and above all if it is pronounced by scanning it, syllable by syllable5. Is not this last fact, established in several absolutely clear cases of word-deafness with preservation of the acoustic recollections, particularly significant? Stricker's error1 was to believe in an integral inner repetition of the speech heard. His thesis would already be refuted by the simple fact that not a single case is known of motor aphasia that has entailed word-deafness. But all the facts concur in demonstrating the existence of a motor tendency to disarticulate sounds, to establish their schema. This automatic tendency does not, moreover, go without a certain rudimentary intellectual work - as we said above: otherwise, how could we identify together, and consequently follow with the same schema, similar words pronounced at different pitches with different timbres of voice? These inner movements of repetition and recognition are like a prelude to voluntary attention. They mark the boundary between will and automatism. By them are prepared and decided, as we foreshadowed, the characteristic phenomena of intellectual recognition. But what is this complete recognition, arrived at full consciousness of itself? 2° We now approach the second part of this study: from movements we pass to recollections. Attentive recognition, we said, is a veritable circuit, in which the external object yields to us ever deeper parts of itself in proportion as our memory, symmetrically placed, adopts a higher tension to project its recollections toward it. In the particular case that occupies us, the object is an interlocutor whose ideas blossom in his consciousness into auditory representations, to materialise themselves afterwards in spoken words. It will therefore be necessary, if we are in the right, for the hearer to place himself at once among the corresponding ideas, and to develop them into auditory representations which will cover over the raw sounds perceived by fitting themselves into the motor schema. To follow a calculation is to redo it on one's own account. To understand the speech of another would likewise consist in reconstituting intelligently, that is to say starting from ideas, the continuity of the sounds the ear perceives. And more generally, to pay attention, to recognise with intelligence, to interpret, would be merged into one and the same operation by which the mind, having fixed its level, having chosen in itself, in relation to the raw perceptions, the point symmetrical to their more or less proximate cause, would let flow toward them the recollections that are going to cover them. Let us hasten to say, this is not how things are ordinarily regarded. Our associationist habits are there, by virtue of which we picture to ourselves sounds that would evoke by contiguity auditory recollections, and the auditory recollections ideas. Then there are the cerebral lesions, which seem to entail the disappearance of recollections: more particularly, in the case that occupies us, one may invoke the characteristic lesions of cortical word-deafness. Thus psychological observation and clinical facts seem to agree. There would be, in the form of physico-chemical modifications of the cells for instance, auditory representations dormant in the cortex: a disturbance coming from outside awakens them, and by an intra-cerebral process, perhaps by transcortical movements that go in search of the complementary representations, they evoke ideas. Let us reflect, nevertheless, on the strange consequences of a hypothesis of this kind. The auditory image of a word is not an object with definitively fixed contours, for the same word, pronounced by different voices or by the same voice at different pitches, gives different sounds. There will therefore be as many auditory recollections of a word as there are pitches of sound and timbres of voice. Will all these images pile up in the brain, or, if the brain chooses, which will it prefer? Let us admit nevertheless that it has its reasons for choosing one: how will this same word, pronounced by a new person, go to join a recollection from which it differs? Let us note, in fact, that this recollection is, by hypothesis, an inert and passive thing, incapable consequently of seizing an inner similarity beneath outward differences. We are told of the auditory image of the word as if it were an entity or a genus: this genus exists, no doubt, for an active memory which schematises the resemblance of complex sounds; but for a brain that registers, and can register, only the materiality of the sounds perceived, there will be of the same word thousands upon thousands of distinct images. Pronounced by a new voice, it will constitute a new image which will be added purely and simply to the others. But here is something no less embarrassing. A word has individuality for us only from the day when our teachers taught us to abstract it. It is not words that we first learn to pronounce, but sentences. A word always anastomoses with those that accompany it, and according to the pace and movement of the sentence of which it forms an integral part, it takes on different aspects: just so, each note of a melodic theme vaguely reflects the whole theme. Let us admit, then, that there are model auditory recollections, figured by certain intra-cerebral arrangements, and awaiting the sonorous impressions as they pass: these impressions will pass without being recognised. Where, in fact, is the common measure, where is the point of contact between the dry, inert, isolated image and the living reality of the word which organises itself with the sentence? I understand very well that beginning of automatic recognition which would consist, as we saw above, in underlining the principal articulations of this sentence, in thus adopting its movement. But unless we suppose all men to have identical voices pronouncing the same stereotyped sentences in the same tone, I do not see how the words heard would go to join their images in the cerebral cortex. Now, if there are truly recollections deposited in the cells of the cortex, we shall find, in sensory aphasia for example, the irreparable loss of certain determinate words, the complete preservation of the others. In fact, this is not how things happen. Sometimes it is the totality of recollections that disappears, the faculty of mental hearing being purely and simply abolished, sometimes there is a general weakening of this function; but it is ordinarily the function that is diminished, and not the number of recollections. It seems that the patient no longer has the strength to recapture his acoustic recollections, that he circles around the verbal image without managing to settle upon it. Often, to make him find a word again, it suffices to put him on the track, to indicate to him the first syllable1, or simply to encourage him1. An emotion may produce the same effect2. Nevertheless cases occur in which it does seem that it is groups of determinate representations that have been effaced from memory. We have passed in review a great number of these facts, and it has seemed to us that they could be distributed into two absolutely sharp categories. In the first, the loss of recollections is generally sudden; in the second it is progressive. In the first, the recollections detached from memory are of any sort, arbitrarily and even capriciously chosen: they may be certain words, certain figures, or even, often, all the words of a language learnt. In the second, the words follow, in disappearing, a methodical and grammatical order, the very one indicated by Ribot's law: proper names are eclipsed first, then common nouns, finally verbs3. These are the external differences. Here now, it seems to us, is the internal difference. In the amnesias of the first kind, which are almost all consequent upon a violent shock, we should incline to believe that the recollections apparently abolished are really present, and not only present, but active. To take an example often borrowed from Winslow4, that of the subject who had forgotten the letter F, and the letter F only, we ask ourselves whether one can abstract from a determinate letter everywhere it is met with, detach it consequently from the spoken or written words with which it forms a body, if one has not first implicitly recognised it. In another case cited by the same author5, the subject had forgotten languages he had learnt and also poems he had written. Having set about composing again, he made over almost the same verses. One often witnesses, moreover, in such cases, a complete restoration of the vanished recollections. Without wishing to pronounce too categorically on a question of this kind, we cannot help finding an analogy between these phenomena and the splittings of personality that M. Pierre Janet has described6: one of them resembles astonishingly those "negative hallucinations" and "suggestions with a point of reference" which hypnotisers induce7. - Quite otherwise are the aphasias of the second kind, the true aphasias. They are due, as we shall try to show presently, to the progressive diminution of a well-localised function, the faculty of actualising the recollections of words. How is it to be explained that the amnesia here follows a methodical course, beginning with proper names and ending with verbs? One would hardly see the means, if the verbal images were truly deposited in the cells of the cortex: would it not be strange, in fact, for the disease always to attack these cells in the same order1? But the fact will be made clear if one admits with us that recollections, in order to be actualised, need a motor adjuvant, and that they require, in order to be recalled, a kind of mental attitude itself inserted in a bodily attitude. Then verbs, whose essence is to express imitable actions, are precisely the words that a bodily effort will enable us to recapture when the function of language is on the point of escaping us: proper names, on the contrary, being, of all words, the furthest removed from those impersonal actions which our body can sketch, are those which a weakening of the function would reach first. Let us note this singular fact, that an aphasic who has become regularly incapable of ever finding again the noun he is seeking will replace it by an appropriate periphrasis in which other nouns will enter2, and sometimes the rebellious noun itself: unable to think the right word, he has thought the corresponding action, and this attitude has determined the general direction of a movement from which the sentence has come forth. Thus it happens to us, having retained the initial of a forgotten name, to find the name again by dint of pronouncing the initial3. - Thus, in the facts of the second kind it is the function that is affected as a whole, and in those of the first kind the forgetting, sharper in appearance, must never in reality be final. No more in the one case than in the other do we find recollections localised in determinate cells of the cerebral substance, and which a destruction of these cells would abolish.
