Mais la vérité est que l'idée générale nous échappe dès que nous prétendons la figer à l'une ou l'autre de ces deux extrémités. Elle consiste dans le double courant qui va de l'une à l'autre, - toujours prête, soit à se cristalliser en mots prononcés, soit à s'évaporer en souvenirs. Cela revient à dire qu'entre les mécanismes sensori-moteurs figurés par le point S et la totalité des souvenirs disposés en AB il y a place, comme nous le faisions pressentir dans le chapitre précédent, pour mille et mille répétitions de notre vie psychologique, figurées par autant de sections A'B', AB', etc., du même cône. Nous tendons à nous éparpiller en AB à mesure que nous nous détachons davantage de notre état sensoriel et moteur pour vivre de la vie du rêve nous tendons à nous concentrer en S à mesure que nous nous attachons plus fermement à la réalité présente, répondant par des réactions motrices à des excitations sensorielles. En fait, le moi normal ne se fixe jamais à l'une de ces positions extrêmes ; il se meut entre elles, adopte tour à tour les positions représentées par les sections intermédiaires, ou, en d'autres termes, donne à ses représentations juste assez de l'image et juste assez de l'idée pour qu'elles puissent concourir utilement à l'action présente. De cette conception de la vie mentale inférieure peuvent se déduire les lois de l'association des idées. Mais avant d'approfondir ce point, montrons l'insuffisance des théories courantes de l'association. Que toute idée surgissant dans l'esprit ait un rapport de ressemblance ou de contiguïté avec l'état mental antérieur, c'est incontestable ; mais une affirmation de ce genre ne nous renseigne pas sur le mécanisme de l'association, et même, à vrai dire, ne nous apprend absolument rien. On chercherait vainement, en effet, deux idées qui n'aient pas entre elles quelque trait de ressemblance ou ne se touchent pas par quelque côté. S'agit-il de ressemblance ? Si profondes que soient les différences qui séparent deux images, on trouvera toujours, en remontant assez haut, un genre commun auquel elles appartiennent, et par conséquent une ressemblance qui leur serve de trait d'union. Considère-t-on la contiguïté ? Une perception A, comme nous le disions plus haut, n'évoque par « contiguïté » une ancienne image B que si elle nous rappelle d'abord une image A' qui lui ressemble, car c'est un souvenir A', et non pas la perception A, qui touche réellement B dans la mémoire. Si éloignés qu'on suppose donc les deux termes A et B l'un de l'autre, il pourra toujours s'établir entre eux un rapport de contiguïté si le terme intercalaire A' entretient avec A une ressemblance suffisamment lointaine. Cela revient à dire qu'entre deux idées quelconques, choisies au hasard, il y a toujours ressemblance et toujours, si l'on veut, contiguïté, de sorte qu'en découvrant un rapport de contiguïté ou de ressemblance entre deux représentations qui se succèdent, on n'explique pas du tout pourquoi l'une évoque l'autre. La véritable question est de savoir comment s'opère la sélection entre une infinité de souvenirs qui tous ressemblent par quelque côté à la perception présente, et pourquoi un seul d'entre eux, - celui-ci plutôt que celui-là, - émerge à la lumière de la conscience. Mais à cette question l'associationnisme ne peut répondre, parce qu'il a érigé les idées et les images en entités indépendantes, flottant, à la manière des atomes d'Épicure, dans un espace intérieur, se rapprochant, s'accrochant entre elles quand le hasard les amène dans la sphère d'attraction les unes des autres. Et en approfondissant la doctrine sur ce point, on verrait que son tort a été d'intellectualiser trop les idées, de leur attribuer un rôle tout spéculatif, d'avoir cru qu'elles existent pour elles et non pour nous, d'avoir méconnu le rapport qu'elles ont à l'activité du vouloir. Si les souvenirs errent, indifférents, dans une conscience inerte et amorphe, il n'y a aucune raison pour que la perception présente attire de préférence l'un d'eux : je ne pourrai donc que constater la rencontre, une fois produite, et parler de ressemblance ou de contiguïté, - ce qui revient, au fond, à reconnaître vaguement que les états de conscience ont des affinités les uns pour les autres. Mais cette affinité même, qui prend la double forme de la contiguïté et de la ressemblance, l'associationnisme n'en peut fournir aucune explication. La tendance générale à s'associer demeure aussi obscure, dans cette doctrine, que les formes particulières de l'association. Ayant érigé les souvenirs-images individuels en choses toutes faites, données telles quelles au cours de notre vie mentale, l'associationnisme est réduit à supposer entre ces objets des attractions mystérieuses, dont on ne saurait même pas dire à l'avance, comme de l'attraction physique, par quels phénomènes elles se manifesteront. Pourquoi une image qui, par hypothèse, se suffit à elle-même, viserait-elle en effet à s'en agréger d'autres, ou semblables, ou données en contiguïté avec elle ? Mais la vérité est que cette image indépendante est un produit artificiel et tardif de l'esprit. En fait, nous percevons les ressemblances avant les individus qui se ressemblent, et, dans un agrégat de parties contiguës, le tout avant les parties. Nous allons de la ressemblance aux objets ressemblants, en brodant sur la ressemblance, ce canevas commun, la variété des différences individuelles. Et nous allons aussi du tout aux parties, par un travail de décomposition dont on verra plus loin la loi, et qui consiste à morceler, pour la plus grande commodité de la vie pratique, la continuité du réel. L'association n'est donc pas le fait primitif; c'est par une dissociation que nous débutons, et la tendance de tout souvenir à s'en agréger d'autres s'explique par un retour naturel de l'esprit à l'unité indivisée de la perception. Mais nous découvrons ici le vice radical de l'associationnisme. Étant donnée une perception présente qui forme tour à tour, avec des souvenirs divers, plusieurs associations successives, il y a deux manières, disions-nous, de concevoir le mécanisme de cette association. On peut supposer que la perception reste identique à elle-même, véritable atome psychologique qui s'en agrège d'autres au fur et à mesure que ces derniers passent à côté de lui. Tel est le point de vue de l'associationnisme. Mais il y en a un second, et c'est celui-là précisément que nous avons indiqué dans notre théorie de la reconnaissance. Nous avons supposé que notre personnalité tout entière, avec la totalité de nos souvenirs, entrait, indivisée, dans notre perception présente. Alors, si cette perception évoque tour à tour des souvenirs différents, ce n'est pas par une adjonction mécanique d'éléments de plus en plus nombreux qu'elle attirerait, immobile, autour d'elle ; c'est par une dilatation de notre conscience tout entière, qui, s'étalant alors sur une plus vaste surface, peut pousser plus loin l'inventaire détaillé de sa richesse. Tel, un amas nébuleux, vu dans des télescopes de plus en plus puissants, se résout en un nombre croissant d'étoiles. Dans la première hypothèse (qui n'a guère pour elle que son apparente simplicité et son analogie avec un atomisme mal compris), chaque souvenir constitue un être indépendant et figé, dont on ne peut dire ni pourquoi il vise à s'en agréger d'autres, ni comment il choisit, pour se les associer en vertu d'une contiguïté ou d'une ressemblance, entre mille souvenirs qui auraient des droits égaux. Il faut supposer que les idées s'entre-choquent au hasard, ou qu'il s'exerce entre elles des forces mystérieuses, et l'on a encore contre soi le témoignage de la conscience, qui ne nous montre jamais des faits psychologiques flottant à l'état indépendant. Dans la seconde, on se borne à constater la solidarité des faits psychologiques, toujours donnés ensemble à la conscience immédiate comme un tout indivisé que la réflexion seule morcelle en fragments distincts. Ce qu'il faut expliquer alors, ce n'est plus la cohésion des états internes, mais le double mouvement de contraction et d'expansion par lequel la conscience resserre ou élargit le développement de son contenu. Mais ce mouvement se déduit, comme nous allons voir, des nécessités fondamentales de la vie ; et il est aisé de voir aussi pourquoi les « associations » que nous paraissons former le long de ce mouvement épuisent tous les degrés successifs de la contiguïté et de la ressemblance. Supposons en effet, un instant, que notre vie psychologique se réduise aux seules fonctions sensori-motrices. En d'autres termes, plaçons-nous, dans la figure schématique que nous avons tracée (page 181), à ce point S qui correspondrait à la plus grande simplification possible de notre vie mentale. Dans cet état, toute perception se prolonge d'elle-même en réactions appropriées, car les perceptions analogues antérieures ont monté des appareils moteurs plus ou moins complexes qui n'attendent, pour entrer en jeu, que la répétition du même appel. Or il y a, dans ce mécanisme, une association par ressemblance, puisque la perception présente agit en vertu de sa similitude avec les perceptions passées, et il y a là aussi une association par contiguïté, puisque les mouvements consécutifs à ces perceptions anciennes se reproduisent, et peuvent même entraîner à leur suite un nombre indéfini d'actions coordonnées à la première. Nous saisissons donc ici, à leur source même et presque confondues ensemble, - non point pensées, sans doute, mais jouées et vécues, - l'association par ressemblance et l'association par contiguïté. Ce ne sont pas là des formes contingentes de notre vie psychologique. Elles représentent les deux aspects complémentaires d'une seule et même tendance fondamentale, la tendance de tout organisme à extraire d'une situation donnée ce qu'elle a d'utile, et à emmagasiner la réaction éventuelle, sous forme d'habitude motrice, pour la faire servir à des situations du même genre. Transportons-nous maintenant, d'un seul bond, à l'autre extrémité de notre vie mentale. Passons, selon notre méthode, de l'existence psychologique simplement « jouée » à celle qui serait exclusivement « rêvée ». Plaçons-nous, en d'autres termes, sur cette base AB de la mémoire (page 181) où se dessinent dans leurs moindres détails tous les événements de notre vie écoulée. Une conscience qui, détachée de l'action, tiendrait ainsi sous son regard la totalité de son passé, n'aurait aucune raison pour se fixer sur une partie de ce passé plutôt que sur une autre. En un sens, tous ses souvenirs différeraient de sa perception actuelle, car, si on les prend avec la multiplicité de leurs détails, deux souvenirs ne sont jamais identiquement la même chose. Mais, en un autre sens, un souvenir quelconque pourrait être rapproché de la situation présente : il suffirait de négliger, dans cette perception et dans ce souvenir, assez de détails pour que la ressemblance seule apparût. D'ailleurs, une fois le souvenir relié à la perception, une multitude d'événements contigus au souvenir se rattacheraient du même coup à la perception, - multitude indéfinie, qui ne se limiterait qu’au point où l'on choisirait de l'arrêter. Les nécessités de la vie ne sont plus là pour régler l'effet de la ressemblance et par conséquent de la contiguïté, et comme, au fond, tout se ressemble, il s'ensuit que tout peut s'associer. Tout à l'heure, la perception actuelle se prolongeait en mouvements déterminés ; maintenant elle se dissout en une infinité de souvenirs également possibles. En AB l'association provoquerait donc un choix arbitraire, comme en S une démarche fatale. Mais ce ne sont là que deux limites extrêmes où le psychologue doit se placer tour à tour pour la commodité de l'étude, et qui, en fait, ne sont jamais atteintes. Il n'y a pas, chez l'homme au moins, d'état purement sensori-moteur, pas plus qu'il n'y a chez lui de vie imaginative sans un substratum d'activité vague. Notre vie psychologique normale oseille, disions-nous, entre ces deux extrémités. D'un côté l'état sensori-moteur S oriente la mémoire, dont il n'est, au fond, que l'extrémité actuelle et active ; et d'autre part cette mémoire elle-même, avec la totalité de notre passé, exerce une poussée en avant pour insérer dans l'action présente la plus grande partie possible d'elle-même. De ce double effort résultent, à tout instant, une multitude indéfinie d'états possibles de la mémoire, états figurés par les coupes A'B', A''B'', etc., de notre schéma. Ce sont là, disions-nous, autant de répétitions de notre vie passée tout entière. Mais chacune de ces coupes est plus ou moins ample, selon qu'elle se rapproche davantage de la base ou du sommet ; et, de plus, chacune de ces représentations complètes de notre passé n'amène à la lumière de la conscience que ce qui peut s'encadrer dans l'état sensori-moteur, ce qui, par conséquent, ressemble à la perception présente au point de vue de l'action à accomplir. En d'autres termes, la mémoire intégrale répond à l'appel d'un état présent par deux mouvements simultanés, l'un de translation, par lequel elle se porte tout entière au-devant de l'expérience et se contracte ainsi plus ou moins, sans se diviser, en vue de l'action, l'autre de rotation sur elle-même, par lequel elle s'oriente vers la situation du moment pour lui présenter la face la plus utile. A ces divers degrés de contraction correspondent les formes variées de l'association par ressemblance. Tout se passe donc comme si nos souvenirs étaient répétés un nombre indéfini de fois dans ces mille et mille réductions possibles de notre vie passée. Ils prennent une forme plus banale quand la mémoire se resserre davantage, plus personnelle quand elle se dilate, et ils entrent ainsi dans une multitude illimitée de « systématisations » différentes. Un mot d'une langue étrangère, prononcé à mon oreille, peut me faire penser à cette langue en général ou à une voix qui le prononçait autrefois d'une certaine manière. Ces deux associations par ressemblance ne sont pas dues à l'arrivée accidentelle de deux représentations différentes que le hasard aurait amenées tour à tour dans la sphère d'attraction de la perception actuelle. Elles répondent à deux dispositions mentales diverses, à deux degrés distincts de tension de la mémoire, ici plus rapprochée de l'image pure, là plus disposée à la réplique immédiate, c'est-à-dire à l'action. Classer ces systèmes, rechercher la loi qui les lie respectivement aux divers « tons » de notre vie mentale, montrer Comment chacun de ces tons est déterminé lui-même par les nécessités du moment et aussi par le degré variable de notre effort personnel, serait une entreprise difficile : toute cette psychologie est encore à faire, et nous ne voulons même pas, pour le moment, nous y essayer. Mais chacun de nous sent bien que ces lois existent, et qu'il y a des rapports stables de ce genre. Nous savons, par exemple, quand nous lisons un roman d'analyse, que certaines associations d'idées qu'on nous dépeint sont vraies, qu'elles ont pu être vécues ; d'autres nous choquent ou ne nous donnent pas l'impression du réel, parce que nous y sentons l'effet d'un rapprochement mécanique entre des étages différents de l'esprit, comme si l'auteur n'avait pas su se tenir sur le plan qu'il avait choisi de la vie mentale. La mémoire a donc bien ses degrés successifs et distincts de tension ou de vitalité, malaisés à définir, sans doute, mais que le peintre de l'âme ne peut pas brouiller entre eux impunément. La pathologie vient d'ailleurs confirmer ici, - sur des exemples grossiers, il est vrai, - une vérité dont nous avons tous l'instinct. Dans les « amnésies systématisées » des hystériques, par exemple, les souvenirs qui paraissent abolis sont réellement présents ; mais ils se rattachent tous, sans doute, à un certain ton déterminé de vitalité intellectuelle, où le sujet ne peut plus se placer. S'il y a ainsi des plans différents, en nombre indéfini, pour l'association par ressemblance, il en est de même de l'association par contiguïté. Dans le plan extrême qui représente la base de la mémoire, il n'y a pas de souvenir qui ne soit lié, par contiguïté, à la totalité des événements qui le précèdent et aussi de ceux qui le suivent. Tandis qu'au point où se concentre notre action dans l'espace, la contiguïté ne ramène, sous forme de mouvement, que la réaction immédiatement consécutive à une perception semblable antérieure. En fait, toute association par contiguïté implique une position de l'esprit intermédiaire entre ces deux limites extrêmes. Si L'on suppose, ici encore, une foule de répétitions possibles de la totalité de nos souvenirs, chacun de ces exemplaires de notre vie écoulée se découpera, à sa manière, en tranches déterminées, et le mode de division ne sera pas le même si l'on passe d'un exemplaire à un autre, parce que chacun d'eux est précisément caractérisé par la nature des souvenirs dominants auxquels les autres souvenirs s'adossent comme à des points d'appui. Plus on se rapproche de l'action, par exemple, plus la contiguïté tend à participer de la ressemblance et à se distinguer ainsi d'un simple rapport de succession chronologique : c'est ainsi qu'on ne saurait dire des mots d'une langue étrangère, quand ils s'évoquent les uns les autres dans la mémoire, s'ils s'associent par ressemblance ou par contiguïté. Au contraire, plus nous nous détachons de l'action réelle ou possible, plus l'association par contiguïté tend à reproduire purement et simplement les images consécutives de notre vie passée. Il est impossible d'entrer ici dans une étude approfondie de ces divers systèmes. Il suffira de faire remarquer que ces systèmes ne sont point formés de souvenirs juxtaposés comme autant d'atomes. Il y a toujours quelques souvenirs dominants, véritables points brillants autour desquels les autres forment une nébulosité vague. Ces points brillants se multiplient à mesure que se dilate notre mémoire. Le processus de localisation d'un souvenir dans le passé, par exemple, ne consiste pas du tout, comme on l'a dit, à plonger dans la masse de nos souvenirs comme dans un sac, pour en retirer des souvenirs de plus en plus rapprochés entre lesquels prendra place le souvenir à localiser. Par quelle heureuse chance mettrions-nous justement la main sur un nombre croissant de souvenirs intercalaires ? Le travail de localisation consiste en réalité dans un effort croissant d'expansion, par lequel la mémoire, toujours présente tout entière à elle-même, étend ses souvenirs sur une surface de plus en plus large et finit par distinguer ainsi, dans un amas jusque-là confus, le souvenir qui ne retrouvait pas sa place. Ici encore, d'ailleurs, la pathologie de la mémoire nous fournirait des renseignements instructifs. Dans l'amnésie rétrograde, les souvenirs qui disparaissent de la conscience sont vraisemblablement conservés sur les plans extrêmes de la mémoire, et le sujet pourra les y retrouver par un effort exceptionnel, comme celui qu'il accomplit dans l'état d'hypnotisme. Mais, sur les plans inférieurs, ces souvenirs attendaient, en quelque sorte, l'image dominante à laquelle ils pussent s'adosser. Tel choc brusque, telle émotion violente, sera l'événement décisif auquel ils s'attacheront : et si cet événement, en raison de son caractère soudain, se détache du reste de notre histoire, ils le suivront dans l'oubli. On conçoit donc que l'oubli consécutif à un choc, physique ou moral, comprenne les événements immédiatement antérieurs, - phénomène bien difficile à expliquer dans toutes les autres conceptions de la mémoire. Remarquons-le en passant : si l'on refuse d'attribuer quelque attente de ce genre aux souvenirs récents, et même relativement éloignés, le travail normal de la mémoire deviendra inintelligible. Car tout événement dont le souvenir s'est imprimé dans la mémoire, si simple qu'on le suppose, a occupé un certain temps. Les perceptions qui ont rempli la première période de cet intervalle, et qui forment maintenant avec les perceptions consécutives un souvenir indivisé, étaient donc véritablement « en l'air » tant que la partie décisive de l'événement n'était pas encore produite. Entre la disparition d'un souvenir avec ses divers détails préliminaires et l'abolition, par l'amnésie rétrograde, d'un nombre plus ou moins grand de souvenirs antérieure, à un événement donné, il y a donc une simple différence de degré, et non pas de nature. De ces diverses considérations sur la vie mentale inférieure découlerait une certaine conception de l'équilibre intellectuel. Cet équilibre ne sera évidemment faussé que par la perturbation des éléments qui lui servent de matière. Il ne saurait être question ici d'aborder les problèmes de pathologie mentale : nous ne pouvons cependant les éluder entièrement, puisque nous cherchons à déterminer la relation exacte du corps à l'esprit. Nous avons supposé que l'esprit parcourait sans cesse l'intervalle compris entre ses deux limites extrêmes, le plan de l'action et le plan du rêve. S'agit-il d'une décision à prendre ? Ramassant, organisant la totalité de son expérience dans ce que nous appelons son caractère, il la fera converger vers des actions où vous trouverez, avec le passé qui leur sert de matière, la forme imprévue que la personnalité leur imprime ; mais l'action ne sera réalisable que si elle vient s'encadrer dans la situation actuelle, c'est-à-dire dans cet ensemble de circonstances qui naît d'une certaine position déterminée du corps dans le temps et dans l'espace. S'agit-il d'un travail intellectuel, d'une conception à former, d'une idée plus ou moins générale à extraire de la multiplicité des souvenirs ? Une grande marge est laissée à la fantaisie d'une part, au discernement logique de l'autre : mais l'idée, pour être viable, devra toucher à la réalité présente par quelque côté, c'est-à-dire pouvoir, de degré en degré et par des diminutions ou contractions progressives d'elle-même, être plus ou moins jouée par le corps en même temps que représentée par l'esprit. Notre corps, avec les sensations qu'il reçoit d'un côté et les mouvements qu'il est capable d'exécuter de l'autre, est donc bien ce qui fixe notre esprit, ce qui lui donne le lest et l'équilibre. L'activité de l'esprit déborde infiniment la masse des souvenirs accumulés, comme cette masse de souvenirs déborde infiniment elle-même les sensations et les mouvements de l'heure présente ; mais ces sensations et ces mouvements conditionnent ce qu'on pourrait appeler l'attention à la vie, et c'est pourquoi tout dépend de leur cohésion dans le travail normal de l'esprit, comme dans une pyramide qui se tiendrait debout sur sa pointe. Qu'on jette d'ailleurs un coup d'œil sur la fine structure du système nerveux, telle que l'ont révélée des découvertes récentes. On croira apercevoir partout des conducteurs, nulle part des centres. Des fils placés bout à bout et dont les extrémités se rapprochent sans doute quand le courant passe, voilà tout ce qu'on voit. Et voilà peut-être tout ce qu'il y a, s'il est vrai que le corps ne soit qu'un lieu de rendez-vous entre les excitations reçues et les mouvements accomplis, ainsi que nous l'avons supposé dans tout le cours de notre travail. Mais ces fils qui reçoivent du milieu extérieur des ébranlements ou des excitations et qui les lui renvoient sous forme de réactions appropriées, ces fils si savamment tendus de la périphérie à la périphérie, assurent justement par la solidité de leurs connexions et la précision de leurs entre-croisements l'équilibre sensori-moteur du corps, c'est-à-dire son adaptation à la situation présente. Relâchez cette tension ou rompez cet équilibre : tout se passera comme si l'attention se détachait de la vie. Le rêve et l'aliénation ne paraissent guère être autre chose. Nous parlions tout à l'heure de la récente hypothèse qui attribue le sommeil à une interruption de la solidarité entre neurones. Même si l'on n'accepte pas cette hypothèse (confirmée pourtant par de curieuses expériences), il faudra bien supposer pendant le sommeil profond une interruption au moins fonctionnelle de la relation établie dans le système nerveux entre l'excitation et la réaction motrice. De sorte que le rêve serait toujours l'état d'un esprit dont l'attention n'est pas fixée par l'équilibre sensori-moteur du corps. Et il paraît de plus en plus probable que cette détente du système nerveux est due à l'intoxication de ses éléments par les produits non éliminés de leur activité normale à l'état de veille. Or, le rêve imite de tout point l'aliénation. Non seulement tous les symptômes psychologiques de la folie se retrouvent dans le rêve, - au point que la comparaison de ces deux états est devenue banale, - mais l'aliénation paraît bien avoir également son origine dans un épuisement cérébral, lequel serait causé, comme la fatigue normale, par l'accumulation de certains poisons spécifiques dans les éléments du système nerveux1. On sait que l'aliénation est souvent Consécutive aux maladies infectieuses, et que d'ailleurs on peut reproduire expérimentalement avec des toxiques tous les phénomènes de la folie2. N'est-il pas vraisemblable, dès lors, que la rupture de l'équilibre mental dans l'aliénation tient tout simplement à une perturbation des relations sensori-motrices établies dans l'organisme ? Cette perturbation suffirait à créer une espèce de vertige psychique, et à faire ainsi que la mémoire et l'attention perdent contact avec la réalité. Qu'on lise les descriptions données par certains fous de leur maladie naissante : on verra qu'ils éprouvent souvent un sentiment d'étrangeté ou, comme ils disent, de « non-réalité », comme si les choses perçues perdaient pour eux de leur relief et de leur solidité1. Si nos analyses sont exactes, le sentiment concret que nous avons de la réalité présente consisterait en effet dans la conscience que nous prenons des mouvements effectifs par lesquels notre organisme répond naturellement aux excitations ; - de sorte que là où les relations se détendent ou se gâtent entre sensations et mouvements, le sens du réel s'affaiblit ou disparaît2. Il y aurait d'ailleurs ici une foule de distinctions à faire, non seulement entre les diverses formes de l'aliénation, mais encore entre l'aliénation proprement dite et ces scissions de la personnalité qu'une psychologie récente en a si curieusement rapprochées3. Dans ces maladies de la personnalité, il semble que des groupes de souvenirs se détachent de la mémoire centrale et renoncent à leur solidarité avec les autres. Mais il est rare qu'on n'observe pas aussi des scissions concomitantes de la sensibilité et de la motricité4. Nous ne pouvons nous empêcher de voir dans ces derniers phénomènes le véritable substrat matériel des premiers. S'il est vrai que notre vie intellectuelle repose tout entière sur sa pointe, c'est-à-dire sur les fonctions sensori-motrices par lesquelles elle s'insère dans la réalité présente, l'équilibre intellectuel sera diversement troublé selon que ces fonctions seront lésées d'une manière ou d'une autre. Or, à côté des lésions qui affectent la vitalité générale des fonctions sensori-motrices, affaiblissant ou abolissant ce que nous avons appelé le sens du réel, il en est d'autres qui se traduisent par une diminution mécanique, et non plus dynamique, de ces fonctions, comme si certaines connexions sensori-motrices se séparaient purement et simplement des autres. Si notre hypothèse est fondée, la mémoire sera très diversement atteinte dans les deux cas. Dans le premier, aucun souvenir ne sera distrait, mais tous les souvenirs seront moins lestés, moins solidement orientés vers le réel, d'où une rupture véritable de l'équilibre mental. Dans le second, l'équilibre ne sera pas rompu, mais il perdra de sa complexité. Les souvenirs conserveront leur aspect normal, mais renonceront en partie à leur solidarité, parce que leur base sensori-motrice, au lieu d'être pour ainsi dire chimiquement altérée, sera mécaniquement diminuée. Pas plus dans un cas que dans l'autre, d'ailleurs, les souvenirs ne seront directement atteints ou lésés. L'idée que le corps conserve des souvenirs sous forme de dispositifs cérébraux, que les pertes et les diminutions de la mémoire consistent dans la destruction plus ou moins complète de ces mécanismes, l'exaltation de la mémoire et l'hallucination au contraire dans une exagération de leur activité, n'est donc confirmée ni par le raisonnement ni par les faits. La vérité est qu'il y a un cas, un seul, où l'observation semblerait d'abord suggérer cette vue : nous voulons parler de l'aphasie, ou plus généralement des troubles de la reconnaissance auditive ou visuelle. C'est le seul cas où l'on puisse assigner à la maladie un siège constant dans une circonvolution déterminée du cerveau ; mais c'est précisément aussi le cas où l'on n'assiste pas à l'arrachement mécanique et tout de suite définitif de tels et tels souvenirs, mais plutôt à l'affaiblissement graduel et fonctionnel de l'ensemble de la mémoire intéressée. Et nous avons expliqué comment la lésion cérébrale pouvait occasionner cet affaiblissement, sans qu'il faille supposer en aucune manière une provision de souvenirs accumulée dans le cerveau. Ce qui est réellement atteint, ce sont les régions sensorielles et motrices correspondant à ce genre de perception, et surtout les annexes qui permettent de les actionner intérieurement, de sorte que le souvenir, ne trouvant plus à quoi se prendre, finit par devenir pratiquement impuissant : or, en psychologie, impuissance signifie inconscience. Dans tous les autres cas, la lésion observée ou supposée, jamais nettement localisée, agit par la perturbation qu'elle apporte à l'ensemble des connexions sensori-motrices, soit qu'elle altère cette masse soit qu'elle la fragmente : d'où une rupture ou une simplification de l'équilibre intellectuel, et, par ricochet, le désordre ou la disjonction des souvenirs. La doctrine qui fait de la mémoire une fonction immédiate du cerveau, doctrine qui soulève des difficultés théoriques insolubles, doctrine dont la complication défie toute imagination et dont les résultats sont incompatibles avec les données de l'observation intérieure, ne peut donc même pas compter sur l'appui de la pathologie cérébrale. Tous les faits et toutes les analogies sont en faveur d'une théorie qui ne verrait dans le cerveau qu'un intermédiaire entre les sensations et les mouvements, qui ferait de cet ensemble de sensations et de mouvements la pointe extrême de la vie mentale, pointe sans cesse insérée dans le tissu des événements, et qui, attribuant ainsi au corps l'unique fonction d'orienter la mémoire vers le réel et de la relier au présent, considérerait cette mémoire même comme absolument indépendante de la matière. En ce sens le cerveau contribue à rappeler le souvenir utile, mais plus encore à écarter provisoirement tous les autres. Nous ne voyons pas comment la mémoire se logerait dans la matière ; mais nous comprenons bien, - selon le mot profond d'un philosophe contemporain, - que « la matérialité mette en nous l'oubli1 ».  ## Chapitre IV. De la délimitation et de la fixation des images. Perception et matière Âme et corps.
e: Let us briefly sum up what precedes. We have distinguished three terms, pure recollection, memory-image and perception, none of which, as it happens, occurs in fact in isolation. Perception is never a simple contact of the mind with the present object; it is wholly impregnated with the memory-images which complete it by interpreting it. The memory-image, in its turn, partakes of the "pure recollection" which it begins to materialise, and of the perception in which it tends to become incarnate: envisaged from this latter point of view, it would be defined as a nascent perception. Finally pure recollection, independent no doubt in right, normally manifests itself only in the coloured and living image which reveals it. If we symbolise these three terms by the consecutive segments AB, BC, CD of one and the same straight line AD, we may say that our thought describes this line in a continuous movement which goes from A to D, and that it is impossible to say with precision where one of the terms ends and the other begins. Besides, this is what consciousness readily observes whenever, in order to analyse memory, it follows the very movement of memory at work. Is it a matter of recovering a recollection, of evoking a period of our history? We are conscious of an act sui generis by which we detach ourselves from the present in order to replace ourselves first in the past in general, then in a certain region of the past: a work of groping, analogous to the focusing of a photographic apparatus. But our recollection still remains in the virtual state; by adopting the appropriate attitude, we merely dispose ourselves to receive it. Little by little it appears like a nebulosity that would condense; from the virtual it passes to the actual state; and as its outlines take shape and its surface takes on colour, it tends to imitate perception. But it remains attached to the past by its deepest roots, and if, once realised, it did not retain something of its original virtuality, if it were not, at the same time as a present state, something that stands out against the present, we should never recognise it as a recollection. The constant error of associationism is to substitute for this continuity of becoming, which is the living reality, a discontinuous multiplicity of inert and juxtaposed elements. Precisely because each of the elements thus constituted contains, by reason of its origin, something of what precedes it and also of what follows it, it ought to take in our eyes the form of a mixed and, as it were, impure state. But on the other hand the principle of associationism requires every psychological state to be a kind of atom, a simple element. Hence the necessity of sacrificing, in each of the phases that have been distinguished, the unstable to the stable, that is to say the beginning to the end. Is it a matter of perception? We shall see in it only the agglomerated sensations that colour it; we shall fail to recognise the recalled images that form its obscure nucleus. Is it a matter, in its turn, of the recalled image? We shall take it ready-made, realised in the state of a faint perception, and we shall close our eyes to the pure recollection which this image has progressively developed. In the competition that associationism thus institutes between the stable and the unstable, perception will therefore always displace the memory-image, and the memory-image the pure recollection. This is why pure recollection disappears altogether. Associationism, cutting the whole of the progress AD in two by a line MO, sees in the portion OD only the sensations that terminate it and that constitute, for associationism, the whole of perception; and on the other hand it reduces the portion AO also to the realised image in which pure recollection, as it blossoms out, culminates. Psychological life is then reduced entirely to these two elements, sensation and image. And as, on the one hand, pure recollection, which made the image an original state, has been drowned in the image, and as, on the other hand, the image has been brought still closer to perception by putting into perception, in advance, something of the image itself, we shall find between these two states nothing more than a difference of degree or of intensity. Hence the distinction between strong states and weak states, the former of which we are supposed to erect into perceptions of the present, the latter, for no one knows what reason, into representations of the past. But the truth is that we shall never reach the past unless we place ourselves in it from the outset. Essentially virtual, the past cannot be grasped by us as past unless we follow and adopt the movement by which it blossoms out into a present image, emerging from darkness into broad daylight. It is in vain that we should seek its trace in something actual and already realised: we might as well look for darkness beneath the light. Therein lies precisely the error of associationism: placed in the actual, it exhausts itself in vain efforts to discover, in a realised and present state, the mark of its past origin, to distinguish recollection from perception, and to erect into a difference of kind what it has condemned in advance to be only a difference of magnitude. To imagine is not to remember. No doubt a recollection, as it becomes actual, tends to live in an image; but the converse is not true, and the image pure and simple will carry me back to the past only if it was indeed in the past that I went to seek it, thus following the continuous progress which has brought it from darkness to light. This is what psychologists too often forget when they conclude, from the fact that a recalled sensation becomes more actual when we dwell on it longer, that the recollection of the sensation was that sensation in its nascent state. The fact they allege is no doubt exact. The more I strive to recall a past pain, the more I tend actually to feel it. But this is readily understood, since the progress of the recollection consists precisely, as we said, in materialising itself. The question is whether the recollection of the pain was truly pain at the outset. Because the hypnotised subject ends by feeling hot when he is insistently told that he is hot, it does not follow that the words of the suggestion are already hot. From the fact that the recollection of a sensation is prolonged into that very sensation, we ought no more to conclude that the recollection was a nascent sensation: for perhaps this recollection plays precisely, in relation to the sensation that is about to be born, the part of the magnetiser who gives the suggestion. The reasoning we are criticising, presented in this form, is therefore already without probative value; it is not yet vicious, because it benefits from the incontestable truth that the recollection is transformed as it becomes actual. But the absurdity breaks out when one reasons by following the inverse course, which ought nevertheless to be equally legitimate on the hypothesis one adopts, that is to say when one makes the intensity of the sensation decrease instead of making the intensity of the pure recollection increase. It ought then to happen, in fact, if the two states differed simply in degree, that at a certain moment the sensation would be metamorphosed into recollection. If the recollection of a great pain, for example, is only a faint pain, then conversely an intense pain which I feel will end, by diminishing, in being a great pain recalled. Now a moment comes, without any doubt, when it is impossible for me to say whether what I feel is a faint sensation that I experience or a faint sensation that I imagine (and this is natural, since the memory-image already partakes of the sensation), but never will this faint state appear to me as the recollection of a strong state. Recollection is therefore something quite different. But the illusion which consists in establishing between recollection and perception only a difference of degree is more than a simple consequence of associationism, more than an accident in the history of philosophy. It has deep roots. It rests, in the last analysis, on a false idea of the nature and object of external perception. One will see in perception only a piece of instruction addressed to a pure mind, and of a wholly speculative interest. Then, since recollection is itself, by essence, knowledge of this kind, because it no longer has an object, one can find between perception and recollection only a difference of degree, perception displacing recollection and thus constituting our present, simply by virtue of the law of the stronger. But there is something quite other between the past and the present than a difference of degree. My present is what interests me, what lives for me, and, to say everything, what provokes me to action, whereas my past is essentially powerless. Let us dwell on this point. By opposing it to present perception, we shall already understand better the nature of what we call "pure recollection." One would in fact seek in vain to characterise the recollection of a past state if one did not begin by defining the concrete mark, accepted by consciousness, of present reality. What is the present moment for me? The property of time is to flow; time already flowed is the past, and we call present the instant in which it flows. But there can be no question here of a mathematical instant. No doubt there is an ideal present, purely conceived, an indivisible limit which would separate the past from the future. But the real, concrete, lived present, the one I speak of when I speak of my present perception, necessarily occupies a duration. Where, then, is this duration situated? Is it on this side or on that of the mathematical point which I determine ideally when I think of the present instant? It is only too evident that it is on this side and on that at once, and that what I call "my present" encroaches at once on my past and on my future. On my past first, for "the moment in which I am speaking is already far from me"; on my future next, for it is toward the future that this moment is inclined, it is toward the future that I tend, and if I could fix this indivisible present, this infinitesimal element of the curve of time, it is the direction of the future that it would show. The psychological state that I call "my present" must therefore be at once a perception of the immediate past and a determination of the immediate future. Now the immediate past, as perceived, is, as we shall see, sensation, since every sensation translates a very long succession of elementary shocks; and the immediate future, as determining itself, is action or movement. My present is therefore at once sensation and movement; and since my present forms an undivided whole, this movement must be bound up with this sensation, must prolong it into action. Whence I conclude that my present consists in a combined system of sensations and movements. My present is, by essence, sensori-motor. This is to say that my present consists in the consciousness I have of my body. Extended in space, my body experiences sensations and at the same time executes movements. Sensations and movements being localised at determinate points of this extension, there can be, at a given moment, only a single system of movements and sensations. This is why my present appears to me to be something absolutely determinate, which stands out against my past. Placed between the matter that influences it and the matter on which it influences, my body is a centre of action, the place where the impressions received choose intelligently their way to be transformed into accomplished movements; it therefore indeed represents the actual state of my becoming, that which, in my duration, is in process of formation. More generally, in this continuity of becoming which is reality itself, the present moment is constituted by the quasi-instantaneous section which our perception makes in the flowing mass, and this section is precisely what we call the material world: our body occupies its centre; it is, of this material world, what we feel directly flowing; in its actual state consists the actuality of our present. Matter, as extended in space, having to be defined, according to us, as a present which is ceaselessly recommencing, conversely our present is the very materiality of our existence, that is to say a whole of sensations and movements, and nothing else. And this whole is determinate, unique for each moment of duration, precisely because sensations and movements occupy places in space and because there cannot be, in the same place, several things at once. How is it that so simple a truth, so evident, and which is, after all, only the idea of common sense, could have been misunderstood? The reason is precisely that one persists in finding only a difference of degree, and not of kind, between actual sensations and pure recollection. The difference, according to us, is radical. My actual sensations are that which occupies determinate portions of the surface of my body; pure recollection, on the contrary, interests no part of my body. No doubt it will engender sensations by materialising itself; but at that precise moment it will cease to be recollection and will pass into the state of a present thing, actually lived; and I shall restore to it its character of recollection only by carrying myself back to the operation by which I evoked it, virtual, from the depths of my past. It is precisely because I shall have made it active that it will have become actual, that is to say a sensation capable of provoking movements. On the contrary, most psychologists see in pure recollection only a weaker perception, a set of nascent sensations. Having thus effaced in advance every difference of kind between sensation and recollection, they are led by the logic of their hypothesis to materialise recollection and to idealise sensation. Is it a matter of recollection? They perceive it only in the form of an image, that is to say already embodied in nascent sensations. Having thus transferred to it the essential of sensation, and not wishing to see in the ideality of this recollection something distinct, which stands out against sensation itself, they are obliged, when they return to pure sensation, to leave to it the ideality which they had thus implicitly conferred on nascent sensation. If the past, in fact, which by hypothesis no longer acts, can subsist in the state of a faint sensation, then there are powerless sensations. If pure recollection, which by hypothesis interests no determinate part of the body, is a nascent sensation, then sensation is not essentially localised at a point of the body. Hence the illusion which consists in seeing in sensation a floating and inextensive state, which would acquire extension and consolidate itself in the body only by accident: an illusion which profoundly vitiates, as we have seen, the theory of external perception, and raises a good number of the questions pending between the various metaphysics of matter. We must make up our minds: sensation is, by essence, extensive and localised; it is a source of movement; pure recollection, being inextensive and powerless, in no way partakes of sensation. What I call my present is my attitude toward the immediate future, it is my imminent action. My present is therefore indeed sensori-motor. Of my past, only that becomes image, and consequently sensation at least nascent, which can collaborate in this action, be inserted into this attitude, in a word make itself useful; but as soon as it becomes image, the past leaves the state of pure recollection and merges with a certain part of my present. The recollection actualised in an image therefore differs profoundly from this pure recollection. The image is a present state, and can partake of the past only through the recollection from which it has issued. Recollection, on the contrary, powerless so long as it remains useless, remains pure of all admixture with sensation, without attachment to the present, and consequently inextensive. This radical powerlessness of pure recollection will help us precisely to understand how it is preserved in the latent state. Without entering yet into the heart of the question, let us confine ourselves to remarking that our repugnance to conceive unconscious psychological states comes chiefly from our holding consciousness to be the essential property of psychological states, so that a psychological state could not cease to be conscious, it seems, without ceasing to exist. But if consciousness is only the characteristic mark of the present, that is to say of the actually lived, that is to say, finally, of the acting, then that which does not act may cease to belong to consciousness without necessarily ceasing to exist in some manner. In other words, in the psychological domain, consciousness would not be synonymous with existence but only with real action or immediate efficacy, and the extension of this term being thus limited, one would have less difficulty in representing to oneself an unconscious psychological state, that is to say, in sum, a powerless one. Whatever idea one may form of consciousness in itself, as it would appear if it were exercised without hindrance, it cannot be denied that, in a being who performs bodily functions, the rôle of consciousness is chiefly to preside over action and to enlighten a choice. It therefore casts its light on the immediate antecedents of the decision and on all those of the past recollections which can usefully be organised with them; the rest remains in shadow. But we find here again, under a new form, the ceaselessly reviving illusion that we have been pursuing since the beginning of this work. One wishes consciousness, even when joined to bodily functions, to be a faculty accidentally practical, essentially turned toward speculation. Then, as one does not see what interest it would have in letting escape the knowledge that it holds, devoted as it would be to pure knowledge, one does not understand that it should renounce illuminating what is not entirely lost to it. Whence it would result that only that belongs to it by right which it possesses in fact, and that, in the domain of consciousness, everything real is actual. But restore to consciousness its true rôle: there will be no more reason to say that the past, once perceived, is effaced, than there is to suppose that material objects cease to exist when I cease to perceive them. Let us insist on this last point, for it is the centre of the difficulties and the source of the equivocations which surround the problem of the unconscious. The idea of an unconscious representation is clear, in spite of a widespread prejudice; one may even say that we make constant use of it and that there is no conception more familiar to common sense. Everyone admits, in fact, that the images actually present to our perception are not the whole of matter. But on the other hand, what can an unperceived material object be, an image not imagined, if not a kind of unconscious mental state? Beyond the walls of your room, which you perceive at this moment, there are the neighbouring rooms, then the rest of the house, finally the street and the town in which you live. It matters little which theory of matter you rally to: realist or idealist, you evidently think, when you speak of the town, of the street, of the other rooms of the house, of so many perceptions absent from your consciousness and yet given outside it. They are not created as your consciousness takes them in; they were therefore already in some manner, and since, by hypothesis, your consciousness did not apprehend them, how could they exist in themselves otherwise than in the unconscious state? Whence comes it, then, that an existence outside consciousness appears to us clear when it is a question of objects, obscure when we speak of the subject? Our perceptions, actual and virtual, extend along two lines, the one horizontal, AB, which contains all the simultaneous objects in space, the other vertical, CI, on which our successive recollections are arranged in stages in time. The point I, the intersection of the two lines, is the only one which is actually given to our consciousness. Whence comes it that we do not hesitate to posit the reality of the whole line AB, although it remains unperceived, and that on the contrary, of the line CI the present I, actually perceived, is the only point that appears to us truly to exist? There are, at the bottom of this radical distinction between the temporal and spatial series, so many confused or ill-sketched ideas, so many hypotheses devoid of any speculative value, that we could not exhaust the analysis of them all at once. To unmask the illusion entirely, one would have to go in search of it at its origin and follow through all its windings the double movement by which we come to posit objective realities without relation to consciousness and states of consciousness without objective reality, space then appearing to preserve indefinitely the things that are juxtaposed in it, whereas time would destroy, as they go, the states that succeed one another in it. Part of this work was done in our first chapter, when we treated of objectivity in general; another part will be done in the last pages of this book, when we speak of the idea of matter. Let us confine ourselves here to pointing out a few essential points. First, the objects arranged in stages along this line AB represent in our eyes what we are going to perceive, whereas the line CI contains only what has already been perceived. Now the past no longer has any interest for us; it has exhausted its possible action, or will recover an influence only by borrowing the vitality of present perception. On the contrary, the immediate future consists in an imminent action, in an energy not yet expended. The unperceived part of the material universe, big with promises and threats, therefore has for us a reality which the periods of our past existence that are actually unperceived neither can nor should have. But this distinction, wholly relative to practical utility and to the material needs of life, takes in our mind the ever more definite form of a metaphysical distinction. We have shown, in fact, that the objects situated around us represent, in different degrees, an action that we can accomplish on things or that we shall have to undergo from them. The term of this possible action is precisely marked by the greater or lesser distance of the corresponding object, so that distance in space measures the proximity of a threat or a promise in time. Space thus furnishes us all at once with the schema of our near future; and as this future must flow on indefinitely, the space which symbolises it has the property of remaining, in its immobility, indefinitely open. Hence it comes that the immediate horizon given to our perception appears to us necessarily surrounded by a wider circle, existing though unperceived, this circle itself implying another which surrounds it, and so on indefinitely. It is therefore of the essence of our actual perception, as extended, to be always only a content in relation to a vaster, and even indefinite, experience which contains it: and this experience, absent from our consciousness since it overflows the perceived horizon, none the less appears to be actually given. But whereas we feel ourselves suspended from these material objects which we thus erect into present realities, on the contrary our recollections, as past, are so many dead weights which we drag along with us and of which we prefer to feign ourselves rid. The same instinct by virtue of which we open space indefinitely before us makes us close up time behind us as it flows. And whereas reality, as extended, appears to us to overflow our perception to infinity, on the contrary, in our inner life, only that seems to us real which begins with the present moment; the rest is practically abolished. Then, when a recollection reappears in consciousness, it makes upon us the effect of a ghost whose mysterious apparition would have to be explained by special causes. In reality, the adherence of this recollection to our present state is quite comparable to that of the unperceived objects to the objects we perceive, and the unconscious plays in the two cases a rôle of the same kind. But we find great difficulty in representing things thus, because we have contracted the habit of underlining the differences, and on the contrary of effacing the resemblances, between the series of objects simultaneously arranged in space and that of the states successively developed in time. In the first, the terms condition one another in a quite determinate manner, so that the appearance of each new term could be foreseen. Thus I know, when I leave my room, which rooms I am going to pass through. On the contrary, my recollections present themselves in an apparently capricious order. The order of the representations is therefore necessary in one case, contingent in the other; and it is this necessity that is, as it were, hypostasised when I speak of the existence of objects outside all consciousness. If I see no inconvenience in supposing given the totality of the objects that I do not perceive, it is because the rigorously determined order of these objects lends them the aspect of a chain, of which my present perception would be no more than one link: this link then communicates its actuality to the rest of the chain. But, looking closely, one would see that our recollections form a chain of the same kind, and that our character, always present to all our decisions, is indeed the actual synthesis of all our past states. In this condensed form, our earlier psychological life exists for us even more than the external world, of which we never perceive more than a very small part, whereas on the contrary we use the totality of our lived experience. It is true that we possess it thus only in abridged form, and that our former perceptions, considered as distinct individualities, make upon us the effect either of having totally disappeared or of reappearing only at the whim of their fancy. But this appearance of complete destruction or of capricious resurrection is due simply to the fact that actual consciousness accepts at each instant the useful and momentarily rejects the superfluous. Ever straining toward action, it can materialise, of our former perceptions, only those which are organised with present perception so as to concur in the final decision. If, in order that my will may manifest itself at a given point of space, my consciousness must cross one by one those intermediaries or obstacles the whole of which constitutes what is called distance in space, on the other hand it is useful to it, in order to enlighten this action, to leap over the interval of time which separates the actual situation from an analogous earlier situation; and as it thus transports itself there at a single bound, the whole intermediate part of the past escapes its grasp. The same reasons which make our perceptions arrange themselves in rigorous continuity in space therefore make our recollections light up in a discontinuous manner in time. We have not to do, as regards unperceived objects in space and unconscious recollections in time, with two radically different forms of existence; but the exigencies of action are inverse, in one case, to what they are in the other. But we touch here upon the capital problem of existence, a problem which we can only graze, on pain of being led, from question to question, to the very heart of metaphysics. Let us say simply that, as regards the things of experience, the only ones that occupy us here, existence seems to imply two conditions together: 1st, presentation to consciousness; 2nd, the logical or causal connexion of what is thus presented with what precedes and what follows. The reality for us of a psychological state or of a material object consists in this double fact, that our consciousness perceives them and that they form part of a series, temporal or spatial, in which the terms determine one another. But these two conditions admit of degrees, and one conceives that, both being necessary, they may be unequally fulfilled. Thus, in the case of actual internal states, the connexion is less close, and the determination of the present by the past, leaving a large place to contingency, has not the character of a mathematical derivation; on the other hand, presentation to consciousness is perfect, an actual psychological state delivering to us the totality of its content in the very act by which we apprehend it. On the contrary, if it is a question of external objects, it is the connexion that is perfect, since these objects obey necessary laws; but then the other condition, presentation to consciousness, is never more than partially fulfilled, for the material object, precisely by reason of the multiplicity of unperceived elements which link it to all other objects, appears to us to contain within it and to hide behind it infinitely more than it lets us see. We ought therefore to say that existence, in the empirical sense of the word, always implies at once, but in different degrees, conscious apprehension and regular connexion. But our understanding, whose function it is to establish sharp distinctions, does not conceive things thus. Rather than admit the presence, in all cases, of the two elements mingled in various proportions, it prefers to dissociate these two elements, and to attribute thus to external objects on the one hand, to internal states on the other, two radically different modes of existence, each characterised by the exclusive presence of the condition which one ought to declare merely preponderant. Then the existence of psychological states will consist entirely in their apprehension by consciousness, and that of external phenomena, likewise entirely, in the rigorous order of their concomitance and succession. Whence the impossibility of leaving to material objects which exist but are not perceived the slightest participation in consciousness, and to unconscious internal states the slightest participation in existence. We showed, at the beginning of this book, the consequences of the first illusion: it ends in falsifying our representation of matter. The second, complementary to the first, vitiates our conception of mind, by spreading over the idea of the unconscious an artificial obscurity. Our past psychological life, the whole of it, conditions our present state, without determining it in a necessary manner; the whole of it also reveals itself in our character, although none of the past states manifests itself explicitly in the character. Together, these two conditions assure to each of the past psychological states a real existence, though an unconscious one. But we are so accustomed to reversing the real order of things, to the greatest advantage of practice, and we are so far under the obsession of images drawn from space, that we cannot help asking where recollection is preserved. We conceive that physico-chemical phenomena take place in the brain, that the brain is in the body, the body in the air that bathes it, and so on; but the past, once accomplished, if it is preserved, where is it? To place it, in the state of a molecular modification, in the cerebral substance seems simple and clear, because we then have a reservoir actually given, which it would suffice to open in order to let the latent images flow into consciousness. But if the brain cannot serve for any such purpose, in what storehouse shall we lodge the accumulated images? We forget that the relation of container to contained borrows its clearness and its apparent universality from the necessity under which we stand of always opening space before us and always closing duration behind us. Because it has been shown that one thing is in another, nothing has thereby been done to throw light on the phenomenon of its preservation. More than this: let us admit for a moment that the past survives itself in the state of a recollection stored up in the brain. Then the brain, in order to preserve the recollection, will have to preserve at least itself. But this brain, as an image extended in space, never occupies anything but the present moment; it constitutes, together with the whole of the rest of the material universe, a ceaselessly renewed section of universal becoming. Either, then, you will have to suppose that this universe perishes and is born again, by a veritable miracle, at every moment of duration, or you will have to transfer to it the continuity of existence that you refuse to consciousness, and make of its past a reality which survives itself and prolongs itself into its present: you will therefore have gained nothing by storing recollection up in matter, and you will find yourself obliged, on the contrary, to extend to the totality of the states of the material world that independent and integral survival of the past which you refused to psychological states. This survival of the past in itself therefore imposes itself in one form or another, and the difficulty we feel in conceiving it comes simply from our attributing to the series of recollections, in time, that necessity of containing and being contained which holds only of the set of bodies instantaneously perceived in space. The fundamental illusion consists in transferring to duration itself, in the course of its flow, the form of the instantaneous sections that we make in it. But how could the past, which by hypothesis has ceased to be, preserve itself by itself? Is there not here a veritable contradiction? We reply that the question is precisely whether the past has ceased to exist, or whether it has simply ceased to be useful. You define the present arbitrarily as that which is, whereas the present is simply that which is being made. Nothing is less than the present moment, if by that you understand the indivisible limit which separates the past from the future. When we think this present as about to be, it is not yet; and when we think it as existing, it is already past. If, on the contrary, you consider the present as concrete and really lived by consciousness, it may be said that this present consists for the most part in the immediate past. In the fraction of a second which makes up the briefest possible perception of light, trillions of vibrations have taken place, of which the first is separated from the last by an enormously divided interval. Your perception, however instantaneous it may be, thus consists in an incalculable multitude of remembered elements, and, to tell the truth, every perception is already memory. Practically, we perceive only the past, the pure present being the ungraspable advance of the past gnawing into the future. Consciousness therefore illumines with its light, at every moment, that immediate part of the past which, leaning over the future, works to realise it and to join it to itself. Solely preoccupied with thus determining an indeterminate future, it may shed a little of its light on those of our states further back in the past which would organise themselves usefully with our present state, that is, with our immediate past; the rest remains obscure. It is in this illumined part of our history that we remain placed, by virtue of the fundamental law of life, which is a law of action: hence the difficulty we feel in conceiving recollections which would be preserved in the shadow. Our repugnance to admitting the integral survival of the past thus arises from the very orientation of our psychological life, a veritable unrolling of states in which we have an interest in looking at what is unrolling, and not at what is entirely unrolled. We thus return, by a long detour, to our point of departure. There are, we said, two profoundly distinct memories: the one, fixed in the organism, is nothing other than the set of intelligently constructed mechanisms which ensure a fitting reply to the various possible interpellations. It makes us adapt ourselves to the present situation, and makes the actions we undergo prolong themselves of their own accord into reactions now accomplished, now merely nascent, but always more or less appropriate. Habit rather than memory, it acts out our past experience but does not evoke its image. The other is true memory. Coextensive with consciousness, it retains and aligns, one after another, all our states as they occur, leaving to each fact its place and consequently marking its date, moving quite really in the definitive past, and not, like the first, in a present which is constantly beginning again. But in distinguishing these two forms of memory so profoundly, we had not shown the link between them. Above the body, with its mechanisms which symbolise the accumulated effort of past actions, the memory that imagines and repeats hovered, suspended in the void. But if we never perceive anything other than our immediate past, if our consciousness of the present is already memory, the two terms which we had at first separated will weld themselves intimately together. Viewed from this new standpoint, indeed, our body is nothing other than the invariably renascent part of our representation, the part ever present, or rather that which has just, at every moment, passed. An image itself, this body cannot store up images, since it is a part of images; and this is why the enterprise is chimerical of seeking to localise past perceptions, or even present ones, in the brain: they are not in it; it is it that is in them. But this quite particular image, which persists in the midst of the others and which I call my body, constitutes at every instant, as we said, a transverse section of universal becoming. It is therefore the place of passage of the movements received and sent back, the link between the things which act on me and the things on which I act, the seat, in a word, of the sensori-motor phenomena. If I represent by a cone SAB the totality of the recollections accumulated in my memory, the base AB, set in the past, remains motionless, while the summit S, which figures at every moment my present, advances ceaselessly, and ceaselessly also touches the moving plane P of my actual representation of the universe. At S is concentrated the image of the body; and, forming part of the plane P, this image confines itself to receiving and giving back the actions emanating from all the images of which the plane is composed. The memory of the body, constituted by the set of sensori-motor systems which habit has organised, is therefore a quasi-instantaneous memory to which the true memory of the past serves as base. Since they do not constitute two separate things, since the first is, we said, merely the moving point inserted by the second in the shifting plane of experience, it is natural that these two functions should lend each other mutual support. On the one hand, indeed, the memory of the past presents to the sensori-motor mechanisms all the recollections capable of guiding them in their task and of directing the motor reaction in the sense suggested by the lessons of experience: in this precisely consist the associations by contiguity and by similarity. But on the other hand the sensori-motor apparatuses furnish to powerless recollections, that is, unconscious ones, the means of taking on a body, of materialising themselves, in short of becoming present. For in order that a recollection should reappear in consciousness, it must descend from the heights of pure memory down to the precise point where action is being accomplished. In other words, it is from the present that the call proceeds to which recollection responds, and it is from the sensori-motor elements of present action that recollection borrows the warmth which gives it life. Is it not by the solidity of this accord, by the precision with which these two complementary memories fit into each other, that we recognise "well-balanced" minds, that is, at bottom, men perfectly adapted to life? What characterises the man of action is the promptness with which he summons to the help of a given situation all the recollections that bear on it; but it is also the insurmountable barrier which useless or indifferent recollections encounter in him as they present themselves at the threshold of consciousness. To live in the pure present, to respond to an excitation by an immediate reaction which prolongs it, is the mark of a lower animal: the man who proceeds thus is an impulsive. But he is hardly better adapted to action who lives in the past for the pleasure of living in it, and in whom recollections emerge into the light of consciousness without profit to the present situation: he is no longer an impulsive, but a dreamer. Between these two extremes lies the happy disposition of a memory docile enough to follow with precision the contours of the present situation, but energetic enough to resist every other call. Good sense, or practical sense, is probably nothing else. The extraordinary development of spontaneous memory in most children is due precisely to the fact that they have not yet made their memory solidary with their conduct. They commonly follow the impression of the moment, and as action does not bend in them to the indications of recollection, so, conversely, their recollections are not limited to the necessities of action. They seem to retain more easily only because they remember with less discernment. The apparent diminution of memory, as the intelligence develops, is thus due to the growing organisation of recollections with acts. Conscious memory thus loses in extent what it gains in penetrating force: it had at first the facility of the memory of dreams, but that is because it was quite really dreaming. This same exaggeration of spontaneous memory is observed, moreover, in men whose intellectual development scarcely exceeds that of childhood. A missionary, after preaching a long sermon to some African savages, saw one of them repeat it verbatim, with the same gestures, from one end to the other1. But if our past remains almost wholly hidden from us because it is inhibited by the necessities of present action, it will recover the force to cross the threshold of consciousness in all the cases in which we detach ourselves from effective action in order to replace ourselves, in some sort, in the life of dream. Sleep, natural or artificial, produces just such a detachment. We have recently been shown in sleep an interruption of contact between the nervous elements, sensory and motor2. Even if we do not stop at this ingenious hypothesis, it is impossible not to see in sleep a relaxation, at least functional, of the tension of the nervous system, which during waking is always ready to prolong the excitation received into an appropriate reaction. Now it is a fact of common observation that memory is "exalted" in certain dreams and in certain somnambulistic states. Recollections which we believed abolished then reappear with striking exactness; we relive in all their details scenes of childhood entirely forgotten; we speak languages which we no longer even remembered having learnt. But nothing is more instructive in this respect than what happens in certain cases of sudden suffocation, in the drowned and the hanged. The subject, brought back to life, declares that he saw pass before him, in a short time, all the forgotten events of his history, with their most minute circumstances and in the very order in which they had occurred3. A human being who dreamed his existence instead of living it would doubtless thus hold under his gaze, at every moment, the infinite multitude of the details of his past history. And he, on the contrary, who repudiated this memory with all that it engenders would constantly play his existence instead of truly representing it to himself: a conscious automaton, he would follow the slope of useful habits which prolong the excitation into an appropriate reaction. The first would never emerge from the particular, and even from the individual. Leaving to each image its date in time and its place in space, he would see wherein it differs from the others and not wherein it resembles them. The other, ever borne along by habit, would on the contrary discern in a situation only the side by which it practically resembles anterior situations. Doubtless incapable of thinking the universal, since the general idea supposes the at least virtual representation of a multitude of remembered images, it is nevertheless in the universal that he would move, habit being to action what generality is to thought. But these two extreme states, the one of an entirely contemplative memory which apprehends only the singular in its vision, the other of an entirely motor memory which stamps the mark of generality upon its action, isolate themselves and manifest themselves fully only in exceptional cases. In normal life they interpenetrate intimately, each thus abandoning something of its original purity. The first expresses itself in the recollection of differences, the second in the perception of resemblances; at the confluence of the two currents the general idea appears. It is not a question here of settling the problem of general ideas as a whole. Among these ideas there are some which do not have perceptions as their sole origin and which relate only very remotely to material objects. We shall leave them aside, in order to consider only the general ideas founded on what we call the perception of resemblances. We wish to follow pure memory, integral memory, in the continuous effort it makes to insert itself into motor habit. In this way we shall make the rôle and nature of this memory better known; but in this way also we shall perhaps clarify, by considering them under a quite particular aspect, the two equally obscure notions of resemblance and generality. By pressing as closely as possible the difficulties of a psychological order raised around the problem of general ideas, we shall come, we believe, to enclose them in this circle: in order to generalise one must first abstract, but in order to abstract usefully one must already know how to generalise. It is around this circle that nominalism and conceptualism gravitate, consciously or unconsciously, each of the two doctrines having in its favour above all the insufficiency of the other. The nominalists, indeed, retaining of the general idea only its extension, see in it simply an open and indefinite series of individual objects. The unity of the idea can therefore consist for them only in the identity of the symbol by which we designate indifferently all these distinct objects. If we are to believe them, we begin by perceiving a thing, then we attach a word to it: this word, reinforced by the faculty or the habit of extending itself to an indefinite number of other things, then sets itself up as a general idea. But in order that the word should thus extend and nevertheless limit itself to the objects it designates, it is still necessary that these objects should present us with resemblances which, by bringing them together, distinguish them from all the objects to which the word does not apply. Generalisation therefore does not go, it would seem, without the abstract consideration of common qualities, and, from step to step, nominalism will be led to define the general idea by its comprehension, and no longer merely by its extension as it wished at first. It is from this comprehension that conceptualism starts. The intelligence, according to it, resolves the superficial unity of the individual into diverse qualities, each of which, isolated from the individual that limited it, becomes, by that very fact, representative of a genus. Instead of considering each genus as comprising in act a multiplicity of objects, it is now wished, on the contrary, that each object should contain in potency, and as so many qualities which it would hold prisoner, a multiplicity of genera. But the question is precisely whether individual qualities, even when isolated by an effort of abstraction, do not remain individual as they were at first, and whether, in order to set them up as genera, a new step of the mind is not necessary, by which it first imposes a name on each quality, then collects under this name a multiplicity of individual objects. The whiteness of a lily is not the whiteness of a sheet of snow; they remain, even when isolated from the snow and the lily, whiteness of lily and whiteness of snow.
