Leibniz, and others after him, have pointed out this contradiction3: it simply arises from Descartes's treating of movement as a physicist after having defined it as a geometer. All movement is relative for the geometer: this means only, in our view, that there is no mathematical symbol capable of expressing that it is the moving body that moves rather than the axes or the points to which it is related. And this is quite natural, since these symbols, always destined for measurements, can express only distances. But that there is a real movement, no one can seriously contest: otherwise nothing would change in the universe, and above all it is not clear what would be the meaning of the consciousness we have of our own movements. In his controversy with Descartes, More alluded humorously to this last point: "When I sit quietly, and another, going away from me a thousand paces, is red with fatigue, it is he who moves and I who rest4." But if there is an absolute movement, can we persist in seeing in movement only a change of place? We shall then have to erect diversity of place into an absolute difference, and to distinguish absolute positions in an absolute space. Newton went as far as that5, followed moreover by Euler6 and by others. But can this be imagined or even conceived? One place would be absolutely distinguished from another place only by its quality, or by its relation to the whole of space: so that space would become, on this hypothesis, either composed of heterogeneous parts or finite. But to a finite space we should give another space as a barrier, and beneath heterogeneous parts of space we should imagine a homogeneous space as a support: in both cases it is to homogeneous and indefinite space that we should necessarily return. We cannot therefore prevent ourselves either from holding every place to be relative or from believing in an absolute movement. Shall it be said, then, that real movement is distinguished from relative movement in that it has a real cause, in that it emanates from a force? But we should have to come to an understanding about the sense of this last word. In the natural sciences force is only a function of mass and velocity; it is measured by acceleration; we know it, we evaluate it only by the movements it is supposed to produce in space. Bound up with these movements, it shares their relativity. Hence the physicists who seek the principle of absolute movement in force so defined are led back, by the logic of their system, to the hypothesis of an absolute space which they wished at first to avoid1. We shall therefore have to fall back on the metaphysical sense of the word, and to support the movement perceived in space upon profound causes, analogous to those which our consciousness believes it grasps in the feeling of effort. But is the feeling of effort really that of a profound cause? And have not decisive analyses shown that there is nothing else in this feeling than the consciousness of movements already carried out or begun at the periphery of the body? It is therefore in vain that we should wish to found the reality of movement upon a cause distinct from it: analysis always brings us back to movement itself. But why look elsewhere? So long as you lean movement against the line it traverses, the same point appears to you in turn, according to the origin to which you relate it, at rest or in movement. It is no longer so if you extract from movement the mobility which is its essence. When my eyes give me the sensation of a movement, this sensation is a reality, and something is effectively happening, whether an object is moving before my eyes or my eyes are moving before the object. All the more am I assured of the reality of movement when I produce it after having willed to produce it, and when the muscular sense brings me the consciousness of it. This is to say that I touch the reality of movement when it appears to me, within myself, as a change of state or of quality. But then, how should it not be the same when I perceive changes of quality in things? Sound differs absolutely from silence, as also one sound from another sound. Between light and darkness, between colours, between shades, the difference is absolute. The passage from one to the other is, likewise, an absolutely real phenomenon. I hold, then, the two ends of the chain, the muscular sensations within me, the sensible qualities of matter outside me, and in neither case do I grasp the movement, if there is movement, as a simple relation: it is an absolute. – Between these two extremities come to be placed the movements of external bodies properly so called. How are we to distinguish here an apparent movement from a real one? Of what object, externally perceived, can it be said that it moves, of what other that it remains motionless? To put such a question is to admit that the discontinuity established by common sense between objects independent of one another, each having its individuality, comparable to a kind of persons, is a well-founded distinction. On the contrary hypothesis, in fact, it would no longer be a question of knowing how changes of position are produced in such and such determinate parts of matter, but how a change of aspect is accomplished in the whole, a change whose nature we should moreover still have to determine. Let us therefore formulate at once our third proposition: III. – Every division of matter into independent bodies with absolutely determinate contours is an artificial division. A body, that is to say an independent material object, presents itself to us at first as a system of qualities, in which resistance and colour – data of sight and touch – occupy the centre and hold suspended, so to speak, all the others. On the other hand, the data of sight and touch are those which extend most manifestly in space, and the essential character of space is continuity. There are intervals of silence between sounds, for hearing is not always occupied; between odours, between flavours we find voids, as if smell and taste functioned only occasionally: on the contrary, as soon as we open our eyes our whole visual field is coloured, and since solids are necessarily contiguous with one another, our touch must follow the surface or the edges of objects without ever meeting a true interruption. How do we break up the continuity originally perceived in material extension into as many bodies, each of which would have its substance and its individuality? Doubtless this continuity changes its aspect from one moment to another: but why do we not simply and purely observe that the whole has changed, as when a kaleidoscope has been turned? Why do we seek, in short, in the mobility of the whole, for tracks followed by moving bodies? A moving continuity is given to us, in which everything changes and remains at once: how is it that we dissociate these two terms, permanence and change, in order to represent permanence by bodies and change by homogeneous movements in space? This is not a datum of immediate intuition; but neither is it a requirement of science, for science, on the contrary, proposes to rediscover the natural articulations of a universe that we have cut up artificially. What is more, in demonstrating better and better the reciprocal action of all material points upon one another, science returns, in spite of appearances, as we shall see, to the idea of universal continuity. Science and consciousness are at bottom in agreement, provided that we envisage consciousness in its most immediate data and science in its most distant aspirations. Whence then comes the irresistible tendency to constitute a discontinuous material universe, with bodies of sharply cut edges, which change place, that is to say their relation to one another? Beside consciousness and science, there is life. Beneath the principles of speculation, so carefully analysed by philosophers, there are those tendencies whose study has been neglected and which are explained simply by the necessity in which we find ourselves of living, that is to say, in reality, of acting. Already the power conferred upon individual consciousnesses of manifesting themselves by acts requires the formation of distinct material zones corresponding respectively to living bodies: in this sense, my own body, and, by analogy with it, the other living bodies, are those which I am best justified in distinguishing in the continuity of the universe. But once this body is constituted and distinguished, the needs it experiences lead it to distinguish and constitute others. In the humblest of living beings, nutrition requires a search, then a contact, finally a series of efforts converging towards a centre: this centre will become precisely the independent object which is to serve as food. Whatever the nature of matter, it may be said that life will already establish in it a first discontinuity, expressing the duality of the need and of that which is to serve to satisfy it. But the need of nourishment is not the only one. Others are organised around it, all having as their object the preservation of the individual or of the species: now, each of them leads us to distinguish, beside our own body, bodies independent of it which we must seek or flee. Our needs are thus so many beams of light which, trained upon the continuity of sensible qualities, outline distinct bodies in it. They can satisfy themselves only on condition of carving out of this continuity a body, then of delimiting in it other bodies with which this one will enter into relation as with persons. To establish these quite particular relations between portions thus cut out of sensible reality is precisely what we call living. But if this first subdivision of the real answers much less to immediate intuition than to the fundamental needs of life, how could we obtain a closer knowledge of things by pushing the division still further? Thereby we prolong the vital movement; we turn our back on true knowledge. That is why the crude operation which consists in decomposing the body into parts of the same nature as itself leads us to an impasse, since we soon feel ourselves unable to conceive either why this division should stop, or how it could be pursued to infinity. It represents, in effect, an ordinary form of useful action, wrongly transported into the domain of pure knowledge. We shall therefore never explain the simple properties of matter by particles, whatever they may be: at most we shall follow as far as corpuscles, artificial like the body itself, the actions and reactions of this body towards all the others. Such is precisely the object of chemistry. It studies bodies rather than matter; one can understand, then, that it should stop at an atom, still endowed with the general properties of matter. But the materiality of the atom is dissolving more and more under the physicist's gaze. We have no reason, for example, to represent the atom to ourselves as solid rather than liquid or gaseous, nor to picture the reciprocal action of atoms as collisions rather than in any other way. Why do we think of a solid atom, and why of collisions? Because solids, being the bodies over which we have the most manifest hold, are those which interest us most in our relations with the external world, and because contact is the only means which we seem to have at our disposal for making our body act upon other bodies. But very simple experiments show that there is never real contact between two bodies which push one another1; and on the other hand solidity is far from being an absolutely clear-cut state of matter2. Solidity and collision thus borrow their apparent clarity from the habits and necessities of practical life; - images of this kind throw no light on the ground of things. If there is, besides, one truth which science has placed beyond all dispute, it is that of a reciprocal action of all the parts of matter upon one another. Between the supposed molecules of bodies attractive and repulsive forces are exerted. The influence of gravitation extends across interplanetary spaces. Something therefore exists between the atoms. It will be said that this is no longer matter, but force. We shall picture to ourselves, stretched between the atoms, threads which we shall make thinner and thinner, until we have rendered them invisible and even, as is believed, immaterial. But what use could this crude image serve? The preservation of life doubtless requires that we should distinguish, in our daily experience, inert things and the actions exerted by these things in space. As it is useful to us to fix the seat of the thing at the precise point where we could touch it, its palpable contours become for us its real limit, and we then see in its action a something, we know not what, which detaches itself from it and differs from it. But since a theory of matter proposes precisely to recover reality beneath these usual images, all relative to our needs, it is from these images that it must first abstract itself. And, in fact, we see force and matter draw near and join one another as the physicist deepens their effects. We see force becoming material, the atom becoming ideal, these two terms converging towards a common limit, the universe thus recovering its continuity. We shall still speak of atoms; the atom will even keep its individuality for our mind which isolates it; but the solidity and inertia of the atom will dissolve either into movements or into lines of force, whose reciprocal solidarity will re-establish universal continuity. To this conclusion, though they started from entirely different points, the two physicists of the nineteenth century who have penetrated furthest into the constitution of matter, Thomson and Faraday, were necessarily bound to come. For Faraday, the atom is a "centre of forces". By this he means that the individuality of the atom consists in the mathematical point where there cross the indefinite lines of force, radiating through space, which really constitute it: each atom thus occupies, to use his expressions, "the whole of space to which gravitation extends", and "all atoms interpenetrate one another1". Thomson, placing himself in an altogether different order of ideas, supposes a perfect fluid, continuous, homogeneous and incompressible, which would fill space: what we call an atom would be a ring of invariable form whirling in this continuity, and owing its properties to its form, its existence and consequently its individuality to its movement2. But in both hypotheses we see vanishing, as we approach the ultimate elements of matter, the discontinuity which our perception established at the surface. Psychological analysis had already revealed to us that this discontinuity is relative to our needs: every philosophy of nature ends by finding it incompatible with the general properties of matter. To tell the truth, vortices and lines of force are never in the physicist's mind more than convenient figures, intended to schematise calculations. But philosophy must ask itself why these symbols are more convenient than others and allow us to go further. Could we, by operating on them, rejoin experience, if the notions to which they correspond did not at least point out to us a direction in which to seek the representation of the real? Now, the direction they indicate is not doubtful; they show us, travelling through concrete extension, modifications, perturbations, changes of tension or of energy, and nothing else. It is chiefly in this that they tend to rejoin the purely psychological analysis of movement which we first gave, and which presented it to us, not as a simple change of relation between objects to which it would be added as an accident, but as a veritable and in some sort independent reality. Neither science nor consciousness would therefore be repelled by this last proposition: IV. - Real movement is rather the transport of a state than of a thing. In formulating these four propositions we have done no more, in reality, than progressively narrow the interval between two terms which are set in opposition to each other, qualities or sensations, and movements. At first sight, the distance appears impassable. Qualities are heterogeneous among themselves, movements homogeneous. Sensations, indivisible by essence, escape measurement; movements, always divisible, are distinguished by calculable differences of direction and velocity. We are fond of placing qualities, in the form of sensations, in consciousness, while movements are executed independently of us in space. These movements, compounding with one another, would never give anything but movements; by a mysterious process, our consciousness, unable to touch them, would translate them into sensations which would then be projected into space and come to cover over, one knows not how, the movements which they translate. Hence two different worlds, unable to communicate otherwise than by a miracle, on one side that of movements in space, on the other consciousness with its sensations. And, certainly, the difference remains irreducible, as we ourselves showed formerly, between quality, on the one hand, and pure quantity on the other. But the question is precisely whether real movements present only differences of quantity among themselves, or whether they might not be quality itself, vibrating, so to speak, inwardly and marking the beats of its own existence in a number, often incalculable, of moments. The movement which mechanics studies is only an abstraction or a symbol, a common measure, a common denominator allowing all real movements to be compared with one another; but these movements, considered in themselves, are indivisibles which occupy duration, presuppose a before and an after, and link the successive moments of time by a thread of variable quality which cannot be without some analogy to the continuity of our own consciousness. Can we not conceive, for example, that the irreducibility of two perceived colours is due chiefly to the narrow duration within which are contracted the trillions of vibrations which they execute in one of our instants? If we could stretch out this duration, that is to say, live it at a slower rhythm, should we not see, as this rhythm slackened, the colours pale and lengthen into successive impressions, still coloured no doubt, but ever nearer to merging with pure disturbances? Where the rhythm of the movement is slow enough to fit the habits of our consciousness, - as happens for the low notes of the scale, for example, - do we not feel the perceived quality decompose of itself into repeated and successive disturbances, linked together by an inner continuity? What usually hinders the comparison is the habit acquired of attaching movement to elements, - atoms or others, - which would interpose their solidity between the movement itself and the quality into which it contracts. As our daily experience shows us bodies which move, it seems to us that, to support the elementary movements to which qualities are reduced, there must be at least corpuscles. Movement is then no longer for our imagination more than an accident, a series of positions, a change of relations; and as it is a law of our representation that the stable displaces the unstable in it, the important and central element becomes for us the atom, whose movement would do no more than link its successive positions. But this conception has not only the drawback of reviving for the atom all the problems which matter raises; it has not only the fault of attributing an absolute value to that division of matter which appears chiefly to answer to the needs of life; it further renders unintelligible the process by which we grasp in our perception, at one and the same time, a state of our consciousness and a reality independent of us. This mixed character of our immediate perception, this appearance of contradiction realised, is the principal theoretical reason we have for believing in an external world which does not absolutely coincide with our perception; and as it is misunderstood in a doctrine which makes sensation altogether heterogeneous to the movements of which it would be only the conscious translation, this doctrine ought, it would seem, to confine itself to sensations, which it has made the sole datum, and not add to them movements which, without possible contact with them, are no more than their useless duplicate. Realism thus understood therefore destroys itself. In the end we have no choice: if our belief in a more or less homogeneous substrate of the sensible qualities is well founded, it can only be by an act which would make us grasp or divine, in the quality itself, something which goes beyond our sensation, as if this sensation were pregnant with details suspected and unperceived. Its objectivity, that is to say what it has more than it gives, will then consist precisely, as we foreshadowed, in the immense multiplicity of the movements which it executes, in some sort, within its chrysalis. It spreads out, motionless, on the surface; but it lives and vibrates in depth. To tell the truth, nobody represents otherwise the relation of quantity to quality. To believe in realities distinct from perceived realities is above all to recognise that the order of our perceptions depends on them, and not on us. There must therefore be, in the totality of the perceptions which occupy a given moment, the reason of what will happen in the following moment. And mechanism does no more than formulate this belief with greater precision when it affirms that the states of matter can be deduced from one another. This deduction is possible, it is true, only if beneath the apparent heterogeneity of the sensible qualities we discover homogeneous and calculable elements. But, on the other hand, if these elements are external to the qualities whose regular order they are to explain, they can no longer render the service asked of them, since the qualities are then superadded to them only by a kind of miracle and correspond to them only by virtue of a pre-established harmony. We are therefore compelled to put these movements in these qualities, in the form of inner disturbances, to regard these disturbances as less homogeneous and these qualities as less heterogeneous than they superficially appear, and to attribute the difference of aspect of the two terms to the necessity for this in some sort indefinite multiplicity of contracting within a duration too narrow to mark its moments. Let us insist on this last point, on which we have already touched elsewhere, but which we hold to be essential. The duration lived by our consciousness is a duration with a determinate rhythm, very different from that time of which the physicist speaks, which can store up, in a given interval, as great a number of phenomena as one pleases. In the space of a second, red light, - that which has the greatest wave-length and whose vibrations are consequently the least frequent, - accomplishes 400 trillions of successive vibrations. Do we wish to form an idea of this number? We must separate the vibrations from one another enough for our consciousness to be able to count them or at least to register their succession explicitly, and we shall inquire how many days, months, or years this succession would occupy. Now, the smallest interval of empty time of which we are conscious is equal, according to Exner, to 2 thousandths of a second; and it is still doubtful whether we can perceive several such short intervals in succession. Let us admit, however, that we are capable of it indefinitely. Let us imagine, in a word, a consciousness which should witness the march past of 400 trillions of vibrations, all instantaneous, and separated from one another only by the 2 thousandths of a second necessary to distinguish them. A very simple calculation shows that it would take more than 25,000 years to complete the operation. Thus this sensation of red light experienced by us during one second corresponds, in itself, to a succession of phenomena which, unrolled in our duration with the greatest possible economy of time, would occupy more than 250 centuries of our history. Is this conceivable? A distinction must be made here between our own duration and time in general. In our duration, that which our consciousness perceives, a given interval can contain only a limited number of conscious phenomena. Do we conceive that this content may increase, and when we speak of an indefinitely divisible time, is it really of this duration that we are thinking? So long as space is in question, the division can be pushed as far as one wishes; the nature of what is divided is in no way altered thereby. This is because space is external to us, by definition; because a part of space appears to us to subsist even when we cease to concern ourselves with it. So however much we leave it undivided, we know that it can wait, and that a fresh effort of imagination would decompose it in its turn. As, moreover, it never ceases to be space, it always implies juxtaposition and consequently possible division. Space is, besides, at bottom only the schema of indefinite divisibility. But it is quite otherwise with duration. The parts of our duration coincide with the successive moments of the act which divides it; as many instants as we fix in it, so many parts it has; and if our consciousness can distinguish in an interval only a determinate number of elementary acts, if it stops the division somewhere, there also divisibility stops. In vain does our imagination strive to go beyond, to divide the last parts in their turn, and to speed up in some sort the circulation of our inner phenomena: the very effort by which we should wish to push the division of our duration further would lengthen this duration by as much. And nevertheless we know that millions of phenomena succeed one another while we count scarcely a few of them. It is not physics alone which tells us so; the crude experience of the senses already lets us divine it; we sense in nature successions much more rapid than those of our inner states. How are we to conceive them, and what is this duration whose capacity surpasses all imagination? It is not ours, assuredly; but neither is it that impersonal and homogeneous duration, the same for everything and for everyone, which would flow on, indifferent and empty, outside of what endures. This so-called homogeneous time, as we have tried to demonstrate elsewhere, is an idol of language, a fiction whose origin is easily retraced. In reality, there is not a single rhythm of duration; one can imagine many different rhythms which, slower or more rapid, would measure the degree of tension or relaxation of consciousnesses, and, thereby, would fix their respective places in the series of beings. This representation of durations of unequal elasticity is perhaps painful to our mind, which has contracted the useful habit of substituting for true duration, lived by consciousness, a homogeneous and independent time; but first it is easy, as we have shown, to unmask the illusion which makes such a representation painful, and secondly this idea has in its favour, at bottom, the tacit assent of our consciousness. Does it not happen to us to perceive in ourselves, during our sleep, two contemporaneous and distinct persons of whom one sleeps a few minutes while the dream of the other occupies days and weeks? And would not the whole of history fit into a very short time for a consciousness more tense than ours, which should witness the development of humanity while contracting it, so to speak, into the great phases of its evolution? To perceive consists, then, in sum, in condensing enormous periods of an infinitely diluted existence into a few more differentiated moments of a more intense life, and thus in summing up a very long history. To perceive means to immobilise. That is to say that we grasp, in the act of perception, something which goes beyond perception itself, without the material universe nevertheless differing or being essentially distinguished from the representation we have of it. In one sense, my perception is indeed inward to me, since it contracts into a single moment of my duration what would be distributed, in itself, over an incalculable number of moments. But if you suppress my consciousness, the material universe subsists just as it was: only, as you have made abstraction of that particular rhythm of duration which was the condition of my action on things, these things return into themselves to mark their beats in as many moments as science distinguishes in them, and the sensible qualities, without vanishing, extend and dilute themselves in a duration incomparably more divided. Matter thus resolves itself into numberless disturbances, all linked in an uninterrupted continuity, all in solidarity with one another, and running in every direction like so many shivers. - Link together, in a word, the discontinuous objects of your daily experience; then resolve the motionless continuity of their qualities into disturbances on the spot; attach yourselves to these movements, freeing yourselves from the divisible space which underlies them so as to consider nothing more than their mobility, that undivided act which your consciousness grasps in the movements which you yourselves execute: you will obtain of matter a vision tiring perhaps to your imagination, but pure, and rid of what the exigencies of life make you add to it in external perception. - Restore now my consciousness, and, with it, the exigencies of life: from very far to very far, and each time leaping over enormous periods of the inner history of things, quasi-instantaneous views are going to be taken, picturesque views this time, whose more sharply contrasted colours condense an infinity of elementary repetitions and changes. Thus the thousand successive positions of a runner are contracted into a single symbolic attitude, which our eye perceives, which art reproduces, and which becomes, for everybody, the image of a man running. The glance which we cast around us, from moment to moment, thus grasps only the effects of a multitude of inner repetitions and evolutions, effects discontinuous by that very fact, and whose continuity we re-establish by the relative movements which we attribute to "objects" in space. Change is everywhere, but in depth; we localise it here and there, but on the surface; and we thus constitute bodies at once stable as to their qualities and mobile as to their positions, a simple change of place contracting within itself, in our eyes, the universal transformation. That there are, in a certain sense, multiple objects, that one man is distinguished from another man, a tree from a tree, a stone from a stone, is incontestable, since each of these beings, each of these things has characteristic properties and obeys a determinate law of evolution. But the separation between the thing and its surroundings cannot be absolutely clear-cut; we pass, by insensible gradations, from the one to the other: the close solidarity which binds together all the objects of the material universe, the perpetuity of their reciprocal actions and reactions, proves sufficiently that they have not the precise limits which we attribute to them. Our perception outlines, in some sort, the form of their residue; it ends them at the point where our possible action upon them stops and where they cease, consequently, to interest our needs. Such is the first and most apparent operation of the perceiving mind: it traces divisions in the continuity of extension, simply yielding to the suggestions of need and the necessities of practical life. But in order to divide the real in this way, we must first persuade ourselves that the real is arbitrarily divisible. We must consequently stretch beneath the continuity of sensible qualities, which is concrete extension, a net with meshes indefinitely deformable and indefinitely decreasing: this substrate, merely conceived, this wholly ideal schema of arbitrary and indefinite divisibility, is homogeneous space. – Now, at the same time as our actual and, so to speak, instantaneous perception effects this division of matter into independent objects, our memory solidifies into sensible qualities the continuous flow of things. It prolongs the past into the present, because our action will dispose of the future in the exact proportion in which our perception, swollen by memory, shall have contracted the past. To answer an action undergone by an immediate reaction which fits its rhythm and continues in the same duration, to be in the present, and in a present which ceaselessly begins again, this is the fundamental law of matter: in this consists necessity. If there are free actions, or at least partially undetermined ones, they can belong only to beings capable of fixing, from far to far, the becoming to which their own becoming is applied, of solidifying it into distinct moments, of thus condensing its matter and, by assimilating it, of digesting it into movements of reaction which will pass through the meshes of natural necessity. The higher or lower tension of their duration, which expresses, at bottom, their greater or lesser intensity of life, thus determines both the force of concentration of their perception and the degree of their freedom. The independence of their action upon surrounding matter asserts itself better and better as they free themselves more from the rhythm according to which this matter flows. So that the sensible qualities, as they figure in our perception doubled by memory, are indeed the successive moments obtained by the solidification of the real. But to distinguish these moments, and also to link them together by a thread common to our own existence and to that of things, we are indeed compelled to imagine an abstract schema of succession in general, a homogeneous and indifferent medium which is to the flow of matter, in the direction of length, what space is in the direction of breadth: in this consists homogeneous time. Homogeneous space and homogeneous time are therefore neither properties of things, nor essential conditions of our faculty of knowing them: they express, in an abstract form, the double work of solidification and division which we make the moving continuity of the real undergo in order to secure for ourselves points of support in it, to fix in it centres of operation, to introduce into it, in short, veritable changes; they are the schemata of our action upon matter. The first error, that which consists in making of this homogeneous time and space properties of things, leads to the insurmountable difficulties of metaphysical dogmatism, - mechanism or dynamism, - dynamism erecting into so many absolutes the successive sections which we make along the flowing universe and then striving in vain to link them together by a kind of qualitative deduction, mechanism attaching itself rather, in any one of the sections, to the divisions made in the direction of breadth, that is to say to the instantaneous differences of magnitude and position, and striving no less vainly to engender, with the variation of these differences, the succession of sensible qualities. Do we rally, on the contrary, to the other hypothesis? Do we wish, with Kant, that space and time should be forms of our sensibility? We end by declaring matter and mind equally unknowable. Now, if we compare the two opposed hypotheses, we discover in them a common ground: in making homogeneous time and homogeneous space either realities contemplated or forms of contemplation, they both attribute to space and time an interest rather speculative than vital. There would then be room, between metaphysical dogmatism on the one side and critical philosophy on the other, for a doctrine which would see in homogeneous space and time principles of division and solidification introduced into the real with a view to action, and not to knowledge, which would attribute to things a real duration and a real extension, and would see, finally, the origin of all the difficulties no longer in this duration and this extension which effectively belong to things and manifest themselves immediately to our mind, but in the homogeneous space and time which we stretch beneath them in order to divide the continuous, to fix becoming, and to furnish our activity with points of application. But the erroneous conceptions of sensible quality and of space are so deeply rooted in the mind that they cannot be attacked at too many points at once. Let us say, then, in order to uncover a new aspect of them, that they imply this double postulate, accepted equally by realism and by idealism: 1° between different kinds of qualities there is nothing in common; 2° there is nothing in common, either, between extension and pure quality. We maintain, on the contrary, that there is something in common between qualities of different orders, that they all participate in extension in varying degrees, and that these two truths cannot be disregarded without burdening the metaphysics of matter, the psychology of perception, and more generally the question of the relations of consciousness with matter, with a thousand difficulties. Without dwelling on these consequences, let us confine ourselves for the moment to showing, at the bottom of the various theories of matter, the two postulates that we contest, and let us trace back the illusion from which they proceed. The essence of English idealism is to hold extension to be a property of tactile perceptions. As it sees in sensible qualities nothing but sensations, and in sensations themselves nothing but states of the soul, it finds nothing in the various qualities that could found the parallelism of their phenomena: it is therefore forced to explain this parallelism by a habit, by which the present perceptions of sight, for example, suggest to us possible sensations of touch. If the impressions of two different senses resemble each other no more than the words of two languages do, it is in vain that we should seek to deduce the data of the one from the data of the other; they have no element in common. And consequently there is nothing in common either between extension, which is always tactile, and the data of the senses other than touch, which are extended in no way whatever. But atomistic realism, in its turn, which places movements in space and sensations in consciousness, can discover nothing in common between the modifications or phenomena of extension and the sensations that answer to them. These sensations would be given off from those modifications like a kind of phosphorescence, or else they would translate into the language of the soul the manifestations of matter; but in neither case would they reflect the image of their causes. No doubt they all go back to a common origin, which is movement in space; but precisely because they evolve outside space, they renounce, as sensations, the kinship that bound their causes together. Breaking with space, they break also among themselves, and thus participate neither in one another nor in extension. Idealism and realism therefore differ here only in that the former drives extension back as far as tactile perception, of which it becomes the exclusive property, whereas the latter thrusts extension still further away, outside all perception. But the two doctrines agree in affirming the discontinuity of the different orders of sensible qualities, as also the abrupt passage from what is purely extended to what is extended in no way whatever. Now, the principal difficulties that both encounter in the theory of perception derive from this common postulate. Do we wish, in fact, with Berkeley, that all perception of extension should relate to touch? We may, strictly, refuse extension to the data of hearing, smell and taste; but we shall at least have to explain the genesis of a visual space corresponding to tactile space. It is alleged, it is true, that sight ends by becoming symbolic of touch, and that there is nothing more, in the visual perception of spatial relations, than a suggestion of tactile perceptions. But we shall hardly be made to understand how the visual perception of relief, for example, a perception which makes upon us an impression sui generis, moreover indescribable, coincides with the mere recollection of a sensation of touch. The association of a recollection with a present perception may complicate this perception by enriching it with a familiar element, but cannot create a new kind of impression, a new quality of perception: now the visual perception of relief presents an absolutely original character. Will it be said that the illusion of relief is produced with a flat surface? Thereby it will be established that a surface on which the play of shadow and light of the object in relief is more or less successfully imitated suffices to recall relief to us; but still, for relief to be recalled, it must first have been genuinely perceived. We have said it already, but we cannot repeat it too often: our theories of perception are wholly vitiated by this idea that if a certain contrivance produces, at a given moment, the illusion of a certain perception, it could always have sufficed to produce that very perception; as if the rôle of memory were not precisely to make the complexity of the effect survive the simplification of the cause! Will it be said that the retina is itself a flat surface, and that if we perceive something extended by sight, it can in any case be only the retinal image? But is it not true, as we showed at the beginning of this book, that in the visual perception of an object the brain, the nerves, the retina and the object itself form a solidary whole, a continuous process of which the retinal image is only an episode: by what right do we isolate this image so as to sum up the whole perception in it? And then, as we have likewise shown,1 could a surface be perceived as a surface otherwise than in a space whose three dimensions would be restored? Berkeley, at least, went to the end of his thesis: he denied to sight all perception of extension. But the objections we raise then acquire all the more force, since it is not understood how what is original in our visual perceptions of line, surface and volume could be created by a simple association of recollections, perceptions so distinct that the mathematician is content with them, and ordinarily reasons upon an exclusively visual space. But let us not insist on these various points, nor on the contestable arguments drawn from the observation of the blind who have been operated upon: the theory, classical since Berkeley, of the acquired perceptions of sight does not seem likely to withstand the repeated assaults of contemporary psychology.2 Leaving aside the difficulties of a psychological order, we shall confine ourselves to drawing attention to another point, which for us is the essential one. Let us suppose for a moment that sight originally informs us of none of the relations of space. Visual form, visual relief, visual distance then become the symbols of tactile perceptions. But we shall have to be told why this symbolism succeeds. Here are objects that change shape and move. Sight observes determinate variations which touch then verifies. There is therefore, in the two series, visual and tactile, or in their causes, something that makes them correspond to one another and that ensures the constancy of their parallelism. What is the principle of this connection? For English idealism, it can only be some deus ex machina, and we are brought back to mystery. For vulgar realism, it is in a space distinct from sensations that the principle of the correspondence of sensations with one another would be found; but this doctrine puts the difficulty off and even aggravates it, for it will have to tell us how a system of homogeneous movements in space evokes diverse sensations that have no relation to them. A moment ago, the genesis of the visual perception of space by simple association of images seemed to us to imply a veritable creation ex nihilo; here, all the sensations are born out of nothing, or at least have no relation to the movement that occasions them. At bottom, this second theory differs much less than is supposed from the first. Amorphous space, the atoms that push and collide with one another, are nothing other than the tactile perceptions objectified, detached from the other perceptions by reason of the exceptional importance attributed to them, and set up as independent realities in order thereby to be distinguished from the other sensations, which become their symbols. They have moreover been emptied, in this operation, of a part of their content; after making all the senses converge upon touch, there is retained of touch itself only the abstract schema of tactile perception, with which to construct the external world. Need we be surprised that between this abstraction, on the one hand, and the sensations on the other, no possible communication is any longer to be found? But the truth is that space is no more outside us than in us, and that it does not belong to a privileged group of sensations. All sensations participate in extension; all of them thrust roots, more or less deep, into extension; and the difficulties of vulgar realism arise from this, that, the kinship of the sensations with one another having been extracted and posited apart in the form of an indefinite and empty space, we no longer see either how these sensations participate in extension or how they correspond with one another. The idea that all our sensations are extensive to some degree pervades contemporary psychology more and more. It is maintained, not without some semblance of reason, that there is no sensation without "extensity"1 or without "a feeling of volume".2 English idealism claimed to reserve to tactile perception the monopoly of extension, the other senses operating in space only to the extent that they recall to us the data of touch. A more attentive psychology reveals to us, on the contrary, and will no doubt reveal better and better, the necessity of holding all sensations to be primitively extensive, their extension growing pale and fading before the superior intensity and utility of tactile extension, and no doubt also of visual extension. Thus understood, space is indeed the symbol of fixity and of infinite divisibility. Concrete extension, that is, the diversity of sensible qualities, is not in it; it is we who put it into extension. It is not the support on which real movement rests; it is real movement, on the contrary, that deposits it beneath itself. But our imagination, preoccupied above all with the convenience of expression and the demands of material life, prefers to invert the natural order of the terms. Accustomed to seek its point of support in a world of ready-made, motionless images, whose apparent fixity reflects above all the invariability of our lower needs, it cannot help believing rest to be anterior to mobility, taking it for its point of reference, installing itself in it, and ceasing at last to see in movement anything but a variation of distance, space preceding movement. Then, in a homogeneous and indefinitely divisible space it will draw a trajectory and fix positions: applying movement thereafter against the trajectory, it will want it divisible like that line and, like it, devoid of quality. Need we be surprised if our understanding, henceforth exercising itself upon this idea, which represents precisely the inversion of the real, discovers in it only contradictions? Having assimilated movements to space, we find these movements homogeneous like space; and as we no longer wish to see between them anything but calculable differences of direction and speed, every relation between movement and quality is abolished. There then remains only to park movement in space, qualities in consciousness, and to establish between these two parallel series, by hypothesis incapable of ever meeting, a mysterious correspondence. Cast back into consciousness, sensible quality becomes powerless to reconquer extension. Relegated to space, and to abstract space, where there is never more than a single instant and where everything always begins anew, movement renounces that solidarity of present and past which is its very essence. And as these two aspects of perception, quality and movement, are enveloped in an equal obscurity, the phenomenon of perception, in which a consciousness shut up in itself and foreign to space would translate what takes place in space, becomes a mystery. – Let us set aside, on the contrary, every preconceived idea of interpretation or of measurement, let us place ourselves face to face with immediate reality: we no longer find an impassable distance, no more any essential difference, not even any genuine distinction between perception and the thing perceived, between quality and movement. We thus return, by a long detour, to the conclusions that we had drawn in the first chapter of this book. Our perception, we said, is originally in things rather than in the mind, outside us rather than in us. Perceptions of the various kinds mark so many true directions of reality. But this perception which coincides with its object, we added, exists by right rather than in fact: it would take place in the instantaneous. In concrete perception memory intervenes, and the subjectivity of sensible qualities is due precisely to the fact that our consciousness, which begins by being only memory, prolongs into one another, in order to contract them into a single intuition, a plurality of moments. Consciousness and matter, soul and body, thus entered into contact in perception. But this idea remained obscure on one side, because our perception, and consequently also our consciousness, then seemed to participate in the divisibility that is attributed to matter. If we naturally shrink, in the dualist hypothesis, from accepting the partial coincidence of the perceived object and the perceiving subject, it is because we are conscious of the undivided unity of our perception, whereas the object appears to us to be, by essence, indefinitely divisible. Hence the hypothesis of a consciousness with inextensive sensations, placed over against an extended multiplicity. But if the divisibility of matter is wholly relative to our action upon it, that is, to our faculty of modifying its aspect, if it belongs not to matter itself but to the space that we stretch beneath this matter in order to bring it within our grasp, then the difficulty vanishes. Extended matter, regarded as a whole, is like a consciousness in which everything is balanced, compensated and neutralised; it truly offers the indivisibility of our perception; so that, conversely, we may without scruple attribute to perception something of the extension of matter. These two terms, perception and matter, thus move toward each other in proportion as we strip ourselves further of what might be called the prejudices of action: sensation reconquers extension, concrete extension resumes its natural continuity and indivisibility. And homogeneous space, which reared itself between the two terms like an insurmountable barrier, has no other reality than that of a schema or a symbol. It concerns the proceedings of a being that acts upon matter, but not the work of a mind that speculates on its essence. Thereby is clarified, to a certain extent, the question toward which all our researches converge, that of the union of soul and body. The obscurity of this problem, in the dualist hypothesis, comes from the fact that matter is considered as essentially divisible and every state of the soul as strictly inextensive, so that one begins by cutting the communication between the two terms. And on probing this double postulate, one discovers in it, as regards matter, a confusion of concrete and indivisible extension with the divisible space that underlies it, as also, as regards mind, the illusory idea that there are no degrees, no possible transition, between the extended and the unextended. But if these two postulates conceal a common error, if there is a gradual passage from the idea to the image and from the image to the sensation, if, as it thus evolves toward actuality, that is, toward action, the state of the soul approaches nearer to extension, if finally this extension, once attained, remains undivided and thereby in no way clashes with the unity of the soul, then we understand that the mind can settle upon matter in the act of pure perception, unite itself with it consequently, and nevertheless distinguish itself from it radically. It distinguishes itself from it in that it is, even then, memory, that is, a synthesis of past and present with a view to the future, in that it contracts the moments of this matter in order to use them and to manifest itself by actions which are the reason for its union with the body. We were therefore right to say, at the beginning of this book, that the distinction of body and mind must be established not in terms of space but of time. The fault of vulgar dualism is to place itself at the standpoint of space, to put on one side matter with its modifications in space, on the other inextensive sensations in consciousness. Hence the impossibility of understanding how mind acts on body or body on mind. Hence the hypotheses which are, and can only be, disguised statements of the fact: the idea of a parallelism or that of a pre-established harmony. But hence also the impossibility of constituting either a psychology of memory or a metaphysics of matter. We have tried to establish that this psychology and this metaphysics are solidary, and that the difficulties are lessened in a dualism which, starting from pure perception, where subject and object coincide, pushes on the development of these two terms in their respective durations: matter, as its analysis is carried further, tending more and more to be nothing but a succession of infinitely rapid moments which are deduced from one another and thereby are equivalent; mind being already memory in perception, and asserting itself more and more as a prolongation of the past into the present, a progress, a genuine evolution. But does the relation of body to mind become clearer as a result? For a spatial distinction we substitute a temporal distinction: are the two terms any the more capable of uniting? It must be remarked that the first distinction admits of no degrees: matter is in space, mind is outside space; there is no possible transition between them. On the contrary, if the humblest rôle of mind is to bind together the successive moments of the duration of things, if it is in this operation that it makes contact with matter and by it also that it is at first distinguished from matter, we conceive an infinity of degrees between matter and the fully developed mind, the mind capable of action that is not only indeterminate but reasonable and reflective. Each of these successive degrees, which measures an increasing intensity of life, answers to a higher tension of duration and is expressed outwardly by a greater development of the sensori-motor system. Do we then consider this nervous system? Its increasing complexity will appear to leave a greater and greater latitude to the activity of the living being, the faculty of waiting before reacting, and of putting the excitation received in relation with an ever richer variety of motor mechanisms. But this is only the outside, and the more complex organisation of the nervous system, which seems to assure the living being a greater independence of matter, does no more than symbolise materially this very independence, that is, the inner force which enables the being to free itself from the rhythm of the flow of things, to retain the past better and better so as to influence the future more and more deeply, that is, in short, in the special sense that we give to this word, its memory. Thus, between brute matter and the mind most capable of reflection there are all possible intensities of memory, or, what comes to the same, all degrees of freedom. In the first hypothesis, that which expresses the distinction of mind and body in terms of space, body and mind are like two railway lines that would cut each other at a right angle; in the second, the rails join along a curve, so that one passes insensibly from one line to the other. But is there anything here other than an image? And does not the distinction remain sharp, the opposition irreducible, between matter properly so called and the humblest degree of freedom or of memory? Yes, no doubt, the distinction subsists, but the union becomes possible, since it would be given, in the radical form of partial coincidence, in pure perception. The difficulties of vulgar dualism do not come from the fact that the two terms are distinguished, but from the fact that we do not see how one of the two is grafted upon the other. Now, as we have shown, pure perception, which would be the lowest degree of mind, – mind without memory, – would truly form part of matter as we understand it. Let us go further: memory does not intervene as a function of which matter would have no presentiment and which it would not already imitate in its own way. If matter does not remember the past, it is because it repeats the past unceasingly, because, subject to necessity, it unrolls a series of moments each of which is equivalent to the preceding and can be deduced from it: thus, its past is truly given in its present. But a being that evolves more or less freely creates something new at each moment: it is therefore in vain that we should seek to read its past in its present if the past were not deposited in it in the state of recollection. Thus, to take up a metaphor which has already appeared several times in this book, it is necessary, for like reasons, that the past be played by matter, imagined by mind.

o: I. - L'idée que nous avons dégagée des faits et confirmée par le raisonnement est que notre corps est un instrument d'action, et d'action seulement. À aucun degré, en aucun sens, sous aucun aspect il ne sert à préparer, encore moins à expliquer une représentation. S'agit-il de la perception extérieure ? Il n'y a qu'une différence de degré, et non pas de nature, entre les facultés dites perceptives du cerveau et les fonctions réflexes de la moelle épinière. Tandis que la moelle transforme les ébranlements reçus en mouvement plus ou moins nécessairement exécuté, le cerveau les met en rapport avec des mécanismes moteurs plus ou moins librement choisis ; mais ce qui s'explique par le cerveau dans nos perceptions, ce sont nos actions commencées, ou préparées, ou suggérées, ce ne sont pas nos perceptions mêmes. - S'agit-il du souvenir ? Le corps conserve des habitudes motrices capables de jouer à nouveau le passé ; il peut reprendre des attitudes où le passé s'insérera ; ou bien encore, par la répétition de certains phénomènes cérébraux qui ont prolongé d'anciennes perceptions, il fournira au souvenir un point d'attache avec l'actuel, un moyen de reconquérir sur la réalité présente une influence perdue : mais en aucun cas le cerveau n'emmagasinera des souvenirs ou des images. Ainsi, ni dans la perception, ni dans la mémoire, ni, à plus forte raison, dans les opérations supérieures de l'esprit, le corps ne contribue directement à la représentation. En développant cette hypothèse sous ses multiples aspects, en poussant ainsi le dualisme à l'extrême, nous paraissions creuser entre le corps et l'esprit un abîme infranchissable. En réalité, nous indiquions le seul moyen possible de les rapprocher et de les unir. II. - Toutes les difficultés que ce problème soulève, en effet, soit dans le dualisme vulgaire, soit dans le matérialisme et dans l'idéalisme, viennent de ce que l'on considère, dans les phénomènes de perception et de mémoire, le physique et le moral comme des duplicata l'un de l'autre. Me placerai-je au point de vue matérialiste de la conscience-épiphénomène ? Je ne comprends pas du tout pourquoi certains phénomènes cérébraux s'accompagnent de conscience, c'est-à-dire à quoi sert ou comment se produit la répétition consciente de l'univers matériel qu'on a posé d'abord. - Passerai-je à l'idéalisme ? Je ne me donnerai alors que des perceptions, et mon corps sera l'une d'elles. Mais tandis que l'observation me montre que les images perçues se bouleversent de fond en comble pour des variations très légères de celle que j'appelle mon corps (puisqu'il me suffit de fermer les yeux pour que mon univers visuel s'évanouisse), la science m'assure que tous les phénomènes doivent se succéder et se conditionner selon un ordre déterminé, où les effets sont rigoureusement proportionnés aux causes. Je vais donc être obligé de chercher dans cette image que j'appelle mon corps, et qui me suit partout, des changements qui soient les équivalents, cette fois bien réglés et exactement mesurés les uns sur les autres, des images qui se succèdent autour de mon corps : les mouvements cérébraux, que je retrouve ainsi, vont redevenir le duplicat de mes perceptions. Il est vrai que ces mouvements seront des perceptions encore, des perceptions « possibles », de sorte que cette seconde hypothèse est plus intelligible que l'autre ; mais en revanche elle devra supposer à son tour une inexplicable correspondance entre ma perception réelle des choses et nia perception possible de certains mouvements cérébraux qui ne ressemblent à ces choses en aucune manière. Qu'on y regarde de près : on verra que l'écueil de tout idéalisme est là ; il est dans ce passage de l'ordre qui nous apparaît dans la perception à l'ordre qui nous réussit dans la science, - ou, s'il s'agit plus particulièrement de l'idéalisme kantien, dans le passage de la sensibilité à l'entendement. - Resterait alors le dualisme vulgaire. Je vais mettre d'un côté la matière, de l'autre l'esprit, et supposer que les mouvements cérébraux sont la cause ou l'occasion de ma représentation des objets. Mais s'ils en sont la cause, S'ils suffisent à la produire, je vais retomber, de degré en degré, sur l'hypothèse matérialiste de la conscience-épiphénomène. S'ils n'en sont que l'occasion, c'est qu'ils n'y ressemblent en aucune manière ; et dépouillant alors la matière de toutes les qualités que je lui ai conférées dans ma représentation, c'est à l'idéalisme que je vais revenir. Idéalisme et matérialisme sont donc les deux pôles entre lesquels ce genre de dualisme oscillera toujours ; et lorsque, pour maintenir la dualité des substances, il se décidera à les mettre l'une et l'autre sur le même rang, il sera amené à voir en elles deux traductions d'un même original, deux développements parallèles, réglés à l'avance, d'un seul et même principe, à nier ainsi leur influence réciproque, et, par une conséquence inévitable, à faire le sacrifice de la liberté. Maintenant, en creusant au-dessous de ces trois hypothèses, je leur découvre un fond commun : elles tiennent les opérations élémentaires de l'esprit, perception et mémoire, pour des opérations de connaissance pure. Ce qu'elles mettent à l'origine de la conscience, c'est tantôt le duplicat inutile d'une réalité extérieure, tantôt la matière inerte d'une construction intellectuelle toute désintéressée : mais toujours elles négligent le rapport de la perception à l'action et du souvenir à la conduite. Or, on peut concevoir sans doute, comme une limite idéale, une mémoire et une perception désintéressées ; mais, en fait, c'est vers l'action que perception et mémoire sont tournées, c'est cette action que le corps prépare. S'agit-il de la perception ? La complexité croissante du système nerveux met l'ébranlement reçu en rapport avec une variété de plus en plus considérable d'appareils moteurs et fait esquisser simultanément ainsi un nombre de plus en plus grand d'actions possibles. Considère-t-on la mémoire ? Elle a pour fonction première d'évoquer toutes les perceptions passées analogues à une perception présente, de nous rappeler ce qui a précédé et ce qui a suivi, de nous suggérer ainsi la décision la plus utile. Mais ce n'est pas tout. En nous faisant saisir dans une intuition unique des moments multiples de la durée, elle nous dégage du mouvement d'écoulement des choses, c'est-à-dire du rythme de la nécessité. Plus elle pourra contracter de ces moments en un seul, plus solide est la prise qu'elle nous donnera sur la matière; de sorte que la mémoire d'un être vivant parait bien mesurer avant tout la puissance de son action sur les choses, et n'en être que la répercussion intellectuelle. Partons donc de cette force d'agir comme du principe véritable ; supposons que le corps est un centre d'action, un centre d'action seulement, et voyons quelles conséquences vont découler de là pour la perception, pour la mémoire, et pour les rapports du corps avec l'esprit. III. - Pour la perception d'abord. Voici mon corps avec ses « centres perceptifs ». Ces centres sont ébranlés, et j'ai la représentation des choses. D'autre part, j'ai supposé que ces ébranlements ne pouvaient ni produire ni traduire ma perception. Elle est donc en dehors d'eux. Où est-elle ? Je ne saurais hésiter : en posant mon corps, j'ai posé une certaine image, mais, par là aussi, la totalité des autres images, puisqu'il n'y a pas d'objet matériel qui ne doive ses qualités, ses déterminations, son existence enfin à la place qu'il occupe dans l'ensemble de l'univers. Ma perception ne peut donc être que quelque chose de ces objets eux-mêmes ; elle est en eux plutôt qu'ils ne sont en elle. Mais qu'est-elle au juste de ces objets ? Je vois que ma perception paraît suivre tout le détail des ébranlements nerveux dits sensitifs, et d'autre part je sais que le rôle de ces ébranlements est uniquement de préparer des réactions de mon corps sur les corps environnants, d'esquisser mes actions virtuelles. C'est donc que percevoir consiste à détacher, de l'ensemble des objets, l'action possible de mon corps sur eux. La perception n'est alors qu'une sélection. Elle ne crée rien ; son rôle est au contraire d'éliminer de l'ensemble des images toutes celles sur lesquelles je n'aurais aucune prise, puis, de chacune des images retenues elles-mêmes, tout ce qui n'intéresse pas les besoins de l'image que j'appelle mon corps. Telle est du moins l'explication très simplifiée, la description schématique de ce que nous avons appelé la perception pure. Marquons tout de suite la position que nous prenions ainsi entre le réalisme et l'idéalisme. Que toute réalité ait une parenté, une analogie, un rapport enfin avec la conscience, c'est ce que nous concédions à l'idéalisme par cela même que nous appelions les choses des « images ». Aucune doctrine philosophique, pourvu qu'elle s'entende avec elle-même, ne peut d'ailleurs échapper à cette conclusion. Mais si l'on réunissait tous les états de conscience, passés, présents et possibles, de tous les êtres conscients, on n'aurait épuisé par là, selon nous, qu'une très petite partie de la réalité matérielle, parce que les images débordent la perception de toutes parts. Ce sont précisément ces images que la science et la métaphysique voudraient reconstituer, restaurant dans son intégralité une chaîne dont notre perception ne tient que quelques anneaux. Mais pour établir ainsi entre la perception et la réalité le rapport de la partie au tout, il fallait laisser à la perception son rôle véritable, qui est de préparer des actions. C'est ce que ne fait pas l'idéalisme. Pourquoi échoue-t-il, comme nous le disions tout à l'heure, à passer de l'ordre qui se manifeste dans la perception à l'ordre qui réussit dans la science, c'est-à-dire de la contingence avec laquelle nos sensations paraissent se succéder au déterminisme qui lie les phénomènes de la nature ? Précisément parce qu'il attribue à la conscience, dans la perception, un rôle spéculatif, de sorte qu'on ne voit plus du tout quel intérêt cette conscience aurait à laisser échapper entre deux sensations, par exemple, les intermédiaires par lesquels la seconde se déduit de la première. Ce sont ces intermédiaires et leur ordre rigoureux qui demeurent alors obscurs, soit qu'on érige ces intermédiaires en « sensations possibles », selon l'expression de Mill, soit qu'on attribue cet ordre, comme le fait Kant, aux substructions établies par l'entendement impersonnel. Mais supposons que ma perception consciente ait une destination toute pratique, qu'elle dessine simplement, dans l'ensemble des choses, ce qui intéresse mon action possible sur elles : je comprends que tout le reste m'échappe, et que tout le reste, cependant, soit de même nature que ce que je perçois. Ma connaissance de la matière n'est plus alors ni subjective, comme elle l'est pour l'idéalisme anglais, ni relative, comme le veut l'idéalisme kantien. Elle n'est pas subjective, parce qu'elle est dans les choses plutôt qu'en moi. Elle n'est pas relative, parce qu'il n'y a pas entre le « phénomène » et la « chose » le rapport de l'apparence à la réalité, mais simplement celui de la partie au tout. Par là nous semblions revenir au réalisme. Mais le réalisme, si on ne le corrige sur un point essentiel, est aussi inacceptable que l'idéalisme, et pour la même raison. L'idéalisme, disions-nous, ne peut passer de l'ordre qui se manifeste dans la perception à l'ordre qui réussit dans la science, c'est-à-dire à la réalité. Inversement, le réalisme échoue à tirer de la réalité la connaissance immédiate que nous avons d'elle. Se place-t-on en effet dans le réalisme vulgaire ? On a d'un côté une matière multiple, composée de parties plus ou moins indépendantes, diffuse dans l'espace, et de l'autre un esprit qui ne peut avoir aucun point de contact avec elle, à moins qu'il n'en soit, comme veulent les matérialistes, l'inintelligible épiphénomène. Considère-t-on de préférence le réalisme kantien ? Entre la chose en soi, c'est-à-dire le réel, et la diversité sensible avec laquelle nous construisons notre connaissance, on ne trouve aucun rapport concevable, aucune commune mesure. Maintenant, en approfondissant ces deux formes extrêmes du réalisme, on les voit converger vers un même point : l'une et l'autre dressent l'espace homogène comme une barrière entre l'intelligence et les choses. Le réalisme naïf fait de cet espace un milieu réel où les choses seraient en suspension ; le réalisme kantien y voit un milieu idéal où la multiplicité des sensations se coordonne; mais pour l'un et pour l'autre ce milieu est donné d'abord, comme la condition nécessaire de ce qui vient s'y placer. Et en approfondissant cette commune hypothèse à son tour, on trouve qu'elle consiste à attribuer à l'espace homogène un rôle désintéressé, soit qu'il rende à la réalité matérielle le service de la soutenir, soit qu'il ait la fonction, toute spéculative encore, de fournir aux sensations le moyen de se coordonner entre elles. De sorte que l'obscurité du réalisme, comme celle de l'idéalisme, vient de ce qu'il oriente notre perception consciente, et les conditions de notre perception consciente, vers la connaissance pure, non vers l'action. - Mais supposons maintenant que cet espace homogène ne soit pas logiquement antérieur, mais postérieur aux choses matérielles et à la connaissance pure que nous pouvons avoir d'elles; supposons que l'étendue précède l'espace ; supposons que l'espace homogène concerne notre action, et notre action seulement, étant comme un filet infiniment divisé que nous tendons au-dessous de la continuité matérielle pour nous en rendre maîtres, pour la décomposer dans la direction de nos activités et de nos besoins. Alors nous n'y gagnons pas seulement de rejoindre la science, qui nous montre chaque chose exerçant son influence sur toutes les autres, occupant par conséquent en un certain sens la totalité de l'étendue (bien que nous n'apercevions de cette chose que son centre et que nous en arrêtions les limites au point où notre corps cesserait d'avoir prise sur elle). Nous n'y gagnons pas seulement, en métaphysique, de résoudre ou d'atténuer les contradictions que soulève la divisibilité dans l'espace, contradictions qui naissent toujours, comme nous l'avons montré, de ce qu'on ne dissocie pas les deux points de vue de l'action et de la connaissance. Nous y gagnons surtout de faire tomber l'insurmontable barrière que le réalisme élevait entre les choses étendues et la perception que nous en avons. Tandis, en effet, qu'on posait d'un côté une réalité extérieure multiple et divisée, de l'autre des sensations étrangères à l'étendue et sans contact possible avec elle, nous nous apercevons que l'étendue concrète n'est pas divisée réellement, pas plus que la perception immédiate n'est véritablement inextensive. Partis du réalisme, nous revenons au même point où l'idéalisme nous avait conduits ; nous replaçons la perception dans les choses. Et nous voyons réalisme et idéalisme tout près de coïncider ensemble, à mesure que nous écartons le postulat, accepté sans discussion par l'un et par l'autre, qui leur servait de limite commune. En résumé, si nous supposons une continuité étendue, et, dans cette continuité même, le centre d'action réelle qui est figuré par notre corps, cette activité paraîtra éclairer de sa lumière toutes les parties de la matière sur lesquelles à chaque instant elle aurait prise. Les mêmes besoins, la même puissance d'agir qui ont découpé notre corps dans la matière vont délimiter des corps distincts dans le milieu qui nous environne. Tout se passera comme si nous laissions filtrer l'action réelle des choses extérieures pour en arrêter et en retenir l'action virtuelle : cette action virtuelle des choses sur notre corps et de notre corps sur les choses est notre perception même. Mais comme les ébranlements que notre corps reçoit des corps environnants déterminent sans cesse, dans sa substance, des réactions naissantes, et que ces mouvements intérieurs de la substance cérébrale donnent ainsi à tout moment l'esquisse de notre action possible sur les choses, l'état cérébral correspond exactement à la perception. Il n'en est ni la cause, ni l'effet, ni, en aucun sens, le duplicat : il la continue simplement, la perception étant notre action virtuelle et l'état cérébral notre action commencée. IV. - Mais cette théorie de la « perception pure » devait être atténuée et complétée tout à la fois sur deux points. Cette perception pure, en effet, qui serait comme un fragment détaché tel quel de la réalité, appartiendrait à un être qui ne mêlerait pas à la perception des autres corps celle de son corps, c'est-à-dire ses affections, ni à son intuition du moment actuel celle des autres moments, c'est-à-dire ses souvenirs. En d'autres termes, nous avons d'abord, pour la commodité de l'étude, traité le corps vivant comme un point mathématique dans l'espace et la perception consciente comme un instant mathématique dans le temps. Il fallait restituer au corps son étendue et à la perception sa durée. Par là nous réintégrions dans la conscience ses deux éléments subjectifs, l'affectivité et la mémoire. Qu'est-ce qu'une affection ? Notre perception, disions-nous, dessine l'action possible de notre corps sur les autres corps. Mais notre corps, étant étendu, est capable d'agir sur lui-même aussi bien que sur les autres. Dans notre perception entrera donc quelque chose de notre corps. Toutefois, lorsqu'il s'agit des corps environnants, ils sont, par hypothèse, séparés du nôtre par un espace plus ou moins considérable, qui mesure l'éloignement de leurs promesses ou de leurs menaces dans le temps : c'est pourquoi notre perception de ces corps ne dessine que des actions possibles. Au contraire, plus la distance décroît entre ces corps et le nôtre, plus l'action possible tend à se transformer en action réelle, l'action devenant d'autant plus urgente que la distance est moins considérable. Et quand cette distance devient nulle, c'est-à-dire quand le corps à percevoir est notre propre corps, c'est une action réelle, et non plus virtuelle, que la perception dessine. Telle est précisément la nature de la douleur, effort actuel de la partie lésée pour remettre les choses en place, effort local, isolé, et par là même condamné à l'insuccès dans un organisme qui n'est plus apte qu'aux effets d'ensemble. La douleur est donc à l'endroit où elle se produit, comme l'objet est à la place où il est perçu. Entre l'affection sentie et l'image perçue, il y a cette différence que l'affection est dans notre corps, l'image hors de notre corps. Et c'est pourquoi la surface de notre corps, limite commune de ce corps et des autres corps, nous est donnée à la fois sous forme de sensations et sous forme d'image. Dans cette intériorité de la sensation affective consiste sa subjectivité, dans cette extériorité des images en général leur objectivité. Mais nous retrouvons ici l'erreur sans cesse renaissante que nous avons poursuivie à travers tout le cours de notre travail. On veut que sensation et perception existent pour elles-mêmes ; on leur attribue un rôle tout spéculatif ; et comme on a négligé ces actions réelles et virtuelles avec lesquelles elles font corps et qui serviraient à les distinguer, on ne peut plus trouver entre elles qu'une différence de degré. Alors, profitant de ce que la sensation affective n'est que vaguement localisée (à cause de la confusion de l'effort qu'elle enveloppe), on la déclare tout de suite inextensive ; et on fait de ces affections diminuées ou sensations inextensives les matériaux avec lesquels nous construirions des images dans l'espace. Par là on se condamne à n'expliquer ni d'où viennent les éléments de conscience ou sensations, qu'on pose comme autant d'absolus, ni comment, inextensives, ces sensations rejoignent l'espace pour s'y coordonner, ni pourquoi elles y adoptent un ordre plutôt qu'un autre, ni enfin par quel moyen elles réussissent à y constituer une expérience stable, commune à tous les hommes. C'est au contraire de cette expérience, théâtre nécessaire de notre activité, qu'il faut partir. C'est donc la perception pure, c'est-à-dire l'image, qu'on doit se donner d'abord. Et les sensations, bien loin d'être les matériaux avec lesquels l'image se fabrique, apparaîtront au contraire alors comme l'impureté qui s'y mêle, étant ce que nous projetons de notre corps dans tous les autres. V. - Mais tant que nous en restons à la sensation et à la perception pure, on peut à peine dire que nous ayons affaire à l'esprit. Sans doute nous établissons contre la théorie de la conscience-épiphénomène qu'aucun état cérébral n'est l'équivalent d'une perception. Sans doute la sélection des perceptions parmi les images en général est l'effet d'un discernement qui annonce déjà l'esprit. Sans doute enfin l'univers matériel lui-même, défini comme la totalité des images, est une espèce de conscience, une conscience où tout se compense et se neutralise, une conscience dont toutes les parties éventuelles, s'équilibrant les unes les autres par des réactions toujours égales aux actions, s'empêchent réciproquement de faire saillie. Mais pour toucher la réalité de l'esprit, il faut se placer au point où une conscience individuelle, prolongeant et conservant le passé dans un présent qui s'en enrichit, se soustrait ainsi à la loi même de la nécessité, qui veut que le passé se succède sans cesse à lui-même dans un présent qui le répète simplement sous une autre forme, et que tout s'écoule toujours. En passant de la perception pure à la mémoire, nous quittions définitivement la matière pour l'esprit. VI. - La théorie de la mémoire, qui forme le centre de notre travail, devait être à la fois la conséquence théorique et la vérification expérimentale de notre théorie de la perception pure.
