Que les états cérébraux qui accompagnent la perception n'en soient ni la cause ni le duplicat, que la perception entretienne avec son concomitant physiologique le rapport de l'action virtuelle à l'action commencée, c'est ce que nous ne pouvions établir par des faits, puisque tout se passera dans notre hypothèse comme si la perception résultait de l'état cérébral. Dans la perception pure, en effet, l'objet perçu est un objet présent, un corps qui modifie le nôtre. L'image en est donc actuellement donnée, et dès lors les faits nous permettent indifféremment de dire (quittes à nous entendre très inégalement avec nous-mêmes) que les modifications cérébrales esquissent les réactions naissantes de notre corps ou qu'elles créent le duplicat conscient de l'image présente. Mais il en est tout autrement pour la mémoire, car le souvenir est la représentation d'un objet absent. Ici les deux hypothèses donneront des conséquences opposées. Si, dans le cas d'un objet présent, un état de notre corps suffisait déjà à créer la représentation de l'objet, à plus forte raison cet état suffira-t-il encore dans le cas du même objet absent. Il faudra donc, dans cette théorie, que le souvenir naisse de la répétition atténuée du phénomène cérébral qui occasionnait la perception première, et consiste simplement dans une perception affaiblie. D'où cette double thèse La mémoire n'est qu'une fonction du cerveau, et il n'y a qu'une différence d'intensité entre la perception et le souvenir. - Au contraire, si l'état cérébral n'engendrait aucunement notre perception de l'objet présent mais la continuait simplement, il pourra encore prolonger et encore faire aboutir le souvenir que nous en évoquons, mais non pas le faire naître. Et comme, d'autre part, notre perception de l'objet présent était quelque chose de cet objet lui-même, notre représentation de l'objet absent sera un phénomène de tout autre ordre que la perception, puisqu'il n'y a entre la présence et l'absence aucun degré, aucun milieu. D'où cette double thèse, inverse de la précédente : La mémoire est autre chose qu'une fonction du cerveau, et il n'y a pas une différence de degré, mais de nature, entre la perception et le souvenir. - L'opposition des deux théories prend alors une forme aiguë, et l'expérience peut cette fois les départager. Nous ne reviendrons pas ici sur le détail de la vérification que nous avons tentée. Rappelons-en simplement les points essentiels. Tous les arguments de fait qu'on peut invoquer en faveur d'une accumulation probable des souvenirs dans la substance corticale se tirent des maladies localisées de la mémoire. Mais si les souvenirs étaient réellement déposés dans le cerveau, aux oublis nets correspondraient les lésions du cerveau caractérisées. Or, dans les amnésies où toute une période de notre existence passée, par exemple, est brusquement et radicalement arrachée de la mémoire, on n'observe pas de lésion cérébrale précise ; et au contraire dans les troubles de la mémoire où la localisation cérébrale est nette et certaine, c'est-à-dire dans les aphasies diverses et dans les maladies de la reconnaissance visuelle ou auditive, ce ne sont pas tels ou tels souvenirs déterminés qui Sont comme arrachés du lieu où ils siégeraient, c'est la faculté de rappel qui est plus ou moins diminuée dans sa vitalité, comme si le sujet avait plus ou moins de peine à amener ses souvenirs au contact de la situation présente. C'est donc le mécanisme de ce contact qu'il faudrait étudier, afin de voir si le rôle du cerveau ne serait pas d'en assurer le fonctionnement, bien plutôt que d'emprisonner les souvenirs eux-mêmes dans ses cellules. Nous étions amenés ainsi à suivre dans toutes ses évolutions le mouvement progressif par lequel le passé et le présent arrivent au contact l'un de l'autre, c'est-à-dire la reconnaissance. Et nous avons trouvé, en effet, que la reconnaissance d'un objet présent pouvait se faire de deux manières absolument différentes, mais que, dans aucun des deux cas, le cerveau ne se comportait comme un réservoir d'images. Tantôt, en effet, par une reconnaissance toute passive, plutôt jouée que pensée, le corps fait correspondre à une perception renouvelée une démarche devenue automatique : tout s'explique alors par les appareils moteurs que l'habitude a montés dans le corps, et des lésions de la mémoire pourront résulter de la destruction de ces mécanismes. Tantôt, au contraire, la reconnaissance se fait activement, par des images-souvenirs qui se portent au-devant de la perception présente ; mais alors il faut que ces souvenirs, au moment de se poser sur la perception, trouvent moyen d'actionner dans le cerveau les mêmes appareils que la perception met ordinairement en jeu pour agir : sinon, condamnés d'avance à l'impuissance, ils n'auront aucune tendance à s'actualiser. Et c'est pourquoi, dans tous les cas où une lésion du cerveau atteint une certaine catégorie de souvenirs, les souvenirs atteints ne se ressemblent pas, par exemple, en ce qu'ils sont de la même époque, ou en ce qu'ils ont une parenté logique entre eux, mais simplement en ce qu'ils sont tous auditifs, ou tous visuels, ou tous moteurs. Ce qui paraît lésé, ce sont donc les diverses régions sensorielles et motrices ou, plus souvent encore, les annexes qui permettent de les actionner de l'intérieur même de l'écorce, bien plutôt que les souvenirs eux-mêmes. Nous sommes allés plus loin, et, par une étude attentive de la reconnaissance des mots ainsi que des phénomènes de l'aphasie sensorielle, nous avons essayé d'établir que la reconnaissance ne se faisait pas du tout par un réveil mécanique de souvenirs assoupis dans le cerveau. Elle implique, au contraire, une tension plus ou moins haute de la conscience, qui va chercher dans la mémoire pure les souvenirs purs, pour les matérialiser progressivement au contact de la perception présente. Mais qu'est-ce que cette mémoire pure, et que sont ces souvenirs purs ? En répondant à cette question, nous complétions la démonstration de notre thèse. Nous venions d'en établir le premier point, à savoir que la mémoire est autre chose qu'une fonction du cerveau. Il nous restait à montrer, par l'analyse du « souvenir pur », qu'il n'y a pas entre le souvenir et la perception une simple différence de degré, mais une différence radicale de nature. VII. - Signalons tout de suite la portée métaphysique, et non plus simplement psychologique, de ce dernier problème. C'est sans doute une thèse de pure psychologie que celle-ci : le souvenir est une perception affaiblie. Mais qu'on ne s'y trompe pas : si le souvenir n'est qu'une perception plus faible, inversement la perception sera quelque chose comme un souvenir plus intense. Or, le germe de l'idéalisme anglais est là. Cet idéalisme consiste à ne voir qu'une différence de degré, et non pas de nature, entre la réalité de l'objet perçu et l'idéalité de l'objet conçu. Et l'idée que nous construisons la matière avec nos états intérieurs, que la perception n'est qu'une hallucination vraie, vient de là également. C'est cette idée que nous n'avons cessé de combattre quand nous avons traité de la matière. Ou bien donc notre conception de la matière est fausse, ou le souvenir se distingue radicalement de la perception. Nous avons ainsi transposé un problème métaphysique au point de le faire coïncider avec un problème de psychologie, que l'observation pure et simple peut trancher. Comment le tranche-t-elle ? Si le souvenir d'une perception n'était que cette perception affaiblie, il nous arriverait, par exemple, de prendre la perception d'un son léger pour le souvenir d'un bruit intense. Or, pareille confusion ne se produit jamais. Mais on peut aller plus loin, et prouver, par l'observation encore, que jamais la conscience d'un souvenir ne commence par être un état actuel plus faible que nous chercherions à rejeter dans le passé après avoir pris conscience de sa faiblesse : comment d'ailleurs, si nous n'avions pas déjà la représentation d'un passé précédemment vécu, pourrions-nous y reléguer les états psychologiques les moins intenses, alors qu'il serait si simple de les juxtaposer aux états forts comme une expérience présente plus confuse à une expérience présente plus claire ? La vérité est que la mémoire ne consiste pas du tout dans une régression du présent au passé, mais au contraire dans un progrès du passé au présent. C'est dans le passé que nous nous plaçons d'emblée. Nous partons d'un « état virtuel », que nous conduisons peu à peu, à travers une série de plans de conscience différents, jusqu'au terme où il se matérialise dans une perception actuelle, c'est-à-dire jusqu'au point où il devient un état présent et agissant, c'est. à-dire enfin jusqu'à ce plan extrême de notre conscience où se dessine notre corps. Dans cet état virtuel consiste le souvenir pur. D'où vient qu'on méconnaît ici le témoignage de la conscience ? D'où vient qu'on fait du souvenir une perception plus faible, dont on ne peut dire ni pourquoi nous la rejetons dans le passé, ni comment nous en retrouvons la date, ni de quel droit elle réapparaît à un moment plutôt qu'à un autre ? Toujours de ce qu'on oublie la destination pratique de nos états psychologiques actuels. On fait de la perception une opération désintéressée de l'esprit, une contemplation seulement. Alors, comme le souvenir pur ne peut évidemment être que quelque chose de ce genre (puisqu'il ne correspond pas à une réalité présente et pressante), souvenir et perception deviennent des états de même nature, entre lesquels on ne peut plus trouver qu'une différence d'intensité. Mais la vérité est que notre présent ne doit pas se définir ce qui est plus intense : il est ce qui agit sur nous et ce qui nous fait agir, il est sensoriel et il est moteur ; - notre présent est avant tout l'état de notre corps. Notre passé est au contraire ce qui n'agit plus, mais pourrait agir, ce qui agira en s'insérant dans une sensation présente dont il empruntera la vitalité. Il est vrai qu'au moment où le souvenir s'actualise ainsi en agissant, il cesse d'être souvenir, il redevient perception. On comprend alors pourquoi le souvenir ne pouvait pas résulter d'un état cérébral. L'état cérébral continue le souvenir ; il lui donne prise sur le présent par la matérialité qu'il lui confère ; mais le souvenir pur est une manifestation spirituelle. Avec la mémoire nous sommes bien véritablement dans le domaine de l'esprit. VIII. - Nous n'avions pas à explorer ce domaine. Placés au confluent de l'esprit et de la matière, désireux avant tout de les voir couler l'un dans l'autre, nous ne devions retenir de la spontanéité de l'intelligence que son point de jonction avec un mécanisme corporel. C'est ainsi que nous avons pu assister au phénomène de l'association des idées, et à la naissance des idées générales les plus simples. Quelle est l'erreur capitale de l'associationnisme ? C'est d'avoir mis tous les souvenirs sur le même plan, d'avoir méconnu la distance plus ou moins considérable qui les sépare de l'état corporel présent, c'est-à-dire de l'action. Aussi n'a-t-il pu expliquer ni comment le souvenir adhère à la perception qui l'évoque, ni pourquoi l'association se fait par ressemblance ou contiguïté plutôt que de toute autre manière, ni enfin par quel caprice ce souvenir déterminé est élu parmi les mille souvenirs que la ressemblance ou la contiguïté rattacherait aussi bien à la perception actuelle. C'est dire que l'associationnisme a brouillé et confondu tous les plans de conscience différents, s'obstinant à ne voir dans un souvenir moins complet qu'un souvenir moins complexe, alors que c'est en réalité un souvenir moins rêvé, c'est-à-dire plus proche de l'action et par là même plus banal, plus capable de se modeler, - comme un vêtement de confection, - sur la nouveauté de la situation présente. Les adversaires de l'associationnisme l'ont d'ailleurs suivi sur ce terrain. Ils lui reprochent d'expliquer par des associations les opérations supérieures de l'esprit, mais non pas de méconnaître la vraie nature de l'association elle-même. Là est pourtant le vice originel de l'associationnisme. Entre le plan de l'action, - le plan où notre corps a contracté son passé en habitudes motrices, - et le plan de la mémoire pure, où notre esprit conserve dans tous ses détails le tableau de notre vie écoulée, nous avons cru apercevoir au contraire mille et mille plans de conscience différents, mille répétitions intégrales et pourtant diverses de la totalité de notre expérience vécue. Compléter un souvenir par des détails plus personnels ne consiste pas du tout à juxtaposer mécaniquement des souvenirs à ce souvenir, mais à se transporter sur un plan de conscience plus étendu, à s'éloigner de l'action dans la direction du rêve. Localiser un souvenir ne consiste pas davantage à l'insérer mécaniquement entre d'autres souvenirs, mais à décrire, par une expansion croissante de la mémoire dans son intégralité, un cercle assez large pour que ce détail du passé y figure. Ces plans ne sont pas donnés, d'ailleurs, comme des choses toutes faites, superposées les unes aux autres. Ils existent plutôt virtuellement, de cette existence qui est propre aux choses de l'esprit. L'intelligence, se mouvant à tout moment le long de l'intervalle qui les sépare, les retrouve ou plutôt les crée à nouveau sans cesse : sa vie consiste dans ce mouvement même. Alors nous comprenons pourquoi les lois de l'association sont la ressemblance et la contiguïté plutôt que d'autres lois, et pourquoi la mémoire choisit, parmi les souvenirs semblables ou contigus, certaines images plutôt que d'autres images, et enfin comment se forment, par le travail combiné du corps et de l'esprit, les premières notions générales. L'intérêt d'un être vivant est de saisir dans une situation présente ce qui ressemble à une situation antérieure, puis d'en rapprocher ce qui a précédé et surtout ce qui a suivi, afin de profiter de son expérience passée. De toutes les associations qu'on pourrait imaginer, les associations par ressemblance et par contiguïté sont donc d'abord les seules qui aient une utilité vitale. Mais pour comprendre le mécanisme de ces associations et surtout la sélection en apparence capricieuse qu'elles opèrent entre les souvenirs, il faut se placer tour à tour sur ces deux plans extrêmes que nous avons appelés le plan de l'action et le plan du rêve. Dans le premier ne figurent que des habitudes motrices, dont on peut dire que ce sont des associations joué" ou vécues plutôt que représentées : ici, ressemblance et contiguïté sont fondues ensemble, car des situations extérieures analogues, en se répétant, ont fini par lier certains mouvements de notre corps entre eux, et dès lors la même réaction automatique dans laquelle nous déroulerons ces mouvements contigus extraira aussi de la situation qui les occasionne sa ressemblance avec les situations antérieures. Mais à mesure qu'on passe des mouvements aux images, et des images plus pauvres aux images plus riches, ressemblance et contiguïté se dissocient : elles finissent par s'opposer sur cet autre plan extrême où aucune action n'adhère plus aux images. Le choix d'une ressemblance parmi beaucoup de ressemblances, d'une contiguïté parmi d'autres contiguïtés, ne s'opère donc pas au hasard : il dépend du degré sans cesse variable de tension de la mémoire, qui, selon qu'elle incline davantage à s'insérer dans l'action présente ou à s'en détacher, se transpose tout entière dans un ton ou dans un autre. Et c'est aussi ce double mouvement de la mémoire entre ses deux limites extrêmes qui dessine, comme nous l'avons montré, les premières notions générales, l'habitude motrice remontant vers les images semblables pour en extraire les similitudes, les images semblables redescendant vers l'habitude motrice pour se confondre, par exemple, dans la prononciation automatique du mot qui les unit. La généralité naissante de l'idée consiste donc déjà dans une certaine activité de l'esprit, dans un mouvement entre l'action et la représentation. Et c'est pourquoi il sera toujours facile à une certaine philosophie, disions-nous, de localiser l'idée générale à une des deux extrémités, de la faire cristalliser en mots ou évaporer en souvenirs, alors qu'elle consiste en réalité dans la marche de l'esprit qui va d'une extrémité à l'autre. IX. - En nous représentant ainsi l'activité mentale élémentaire, en faisant cette fois de notre corps, avec tout ce qui l'environne, le dernier plan de notre mémoire, l'image extrême, la pointe mouvante que notre passé pousse à tout moment dans notre avenir, nous confirmions et nous éclaircissions ce que nous avions dit du rôle du corps, en même temps que nous préparions les voies à un rapprochement entre le corps et l'esprit. Après avoir étudié tour à tour, en effet, la perception pure et la mémoire pure, il nous restait à les rapprocher l'une de l'autre. Si le souvenir pur est déjà l'esprit, et si la perception pure serait encore quelque chose de la matière, nous devions, en nous plaçant au point de jonction entre la perception pure et le souvenir pur, projeter quelque lumière sur l'action réciproque de l'esprit et de la matière. En fait, la perception « pure », c'est-à-dire instantanée, n'est qu'un idéal, une limite. Toute perception occupe une certaine épaisseur de durée, prolonge le passé dans le présent, et participe par là de la mémoire. En prenant alors la perception sous sa forme concrète, comme une synthèse du souvenir pur et de la perception pure, c'est-à-dire de l'esprit et de la matière, nous resserrions dans ses plus étroites limites le problème de l'union de l'âme au corps. Tel est l'effort que nous avons tenté dans la dernière partie surtout de notre travail. L'opposition des deux principes, dans le dualisme en général, se résout en la triple opposition de l'inétendu à l'étendu, de la qualité à la quantité, et de la liberté à la nécessité. Si notre conception du rôle du corps, si nos analyses de la perception pure et du souvenir pur doivent éclaircir par quelque côté la corrélation du corps à l'esprit, ce ne peut être qu'à la condition de lever ou d'atténuer ces trois oppositions. Examinons-les donc tour à tour, en présentant ici sous une forme plus métaphysique les conclusions que nous avons voulu tenir de la seule psychologie. 1º Si l'on imagine d'un côté une étendue réellement divisée en corpuscules, par exemple, de l'autre une conscience avec des sensations par elles-mêmes inextensives qui viendraient se projeter dans l'espace, on ne trouvera évidemment rien de commun entre cette matière et cette conscience, entre le corps et l'esprit. Mais cette opposition de la perception et de la matière est l'œuvre artificielle d'un entendement qui décompose et recompose selon ses habitudes ou ses lois : elle n'est pas donnée à l'intuition immédiate. Ce qui est donné, ce ne sont pas des sensations inextensives : comment iraient-elles rejoindre l'espace, y choisir un lieu, s'y coordonner enfin pour construire une expérience universelle ? Ce qui est réel, ce n'est pas davantage une étendue divisée en parties indépendantes : comment d'ailleurs, n'ayant ainsi aucun rapport possible avec notre conscience, déroulerait-elle une série de changements dont l'ordre et les rapports correspondraient exactement à l'ordre et aux rapporte de nos représentations ? Ce qui est donné, ce qui est réel, c'est quelque chose d'intermédiaire entre l'étendue divisée et l'inétendu pur; c'est ce que nous avons appelé l'extensif. L'extension est la qualité la plus apparente de la perception. C'est en la consolidant et en la subdivisant au moyen d'un espace abstrait, tendu par nous au-dessous d'elle pour les besoins de l'action, que nous constituons l'étendue multiple et indéfiniment divisible. C'est en la subtilisant au contraire, c'est en la faisant tour à tour dissoudre en sensations affectives et évaporer en contrefaçons des idées pures, que nous obtenons ces sensations inextensives avec lesquelles nous cherchons vainement ensuite à reconstituer des images. Et les deux directions opposées dans lesquelles nous poursuivons ce double travail s'ouvrent à nous tout naturellement, car il résulte des nécessités mêmes de l'action que l'étendue se découpe pour nous en objets absolument indépendants (d'où une indication pour subdiviser l'étendue), et qu'on passe par degrés insensibles de l'affection à la perception (d'où une tendance à supposer la perception de plus en plus inextensive). Mais notre entendement, dont le rôle est justement d'établir des distinctions logiques et par conséquent des oppositions tranchées, s'élance dans les deux voies tour à tour, et dans chacune d'elles va jusqu'au bout. Il érige ainsi, à l'une des extrémités, une étendue indéfiniment divisible, à l'autre des sensations absolument inextensives. Et il crée ainsi l'opposition dont il se donne ensuite le spectacle. 2º Beaucoup moins artificielle est l'opposition de la qualité à la quantité, c'est-à-dire de la conscience au mouvement : mais cette seconde opposition n'est radicale que si l'on commence par accepter la première. Supposez en effet que les qualités des choses se réduisent à des sensations inextensives affectant une conscience, en sorte que ces qualités représentent seulement, comme autant de symboles, des changements homogènes et calculables s'accomplissant dans l'espace, vous devrez imaginer entre ces sensations et ces changements une incompréhensible correspondance. Renoncez au contraire à établir a priori entre eux cette contrariété factice : vous allez voir tomber une à une toutes les barrières qui semblaient les séparer. D'abord, il n'est pas vrai que la conscience assiste, enroulée sur elle-même, à un défilé intérieur de perceptions inextensives. C'est donc dans les choses perçues elles-mêmes que vous allez replacer la perception pure, et vous écarterez ainsi un premier obstacle. Vous en rencontrez, il est vrai, un second : les changements homogènes et calculables sur lesquels la science opère semblent appartenir à des éléments multiples et indépendants, tels que les atomes, dont ils ne seraient que l'accident; cette multiplicité va s'interposer entre la perception et son objet. Mais si la division de l'étendue est purement relative à notre action possible sur elle, l'idée de corpuscules indépendants est a fortiori schématique et provisoire; la science elle-même, d'ailleurs, nous autorise à l'écarter. Voilà une seconde barrière tombée. Un dernier intervalle reste à franchir : celui qu'il y a de l'hétérogénéité des qualités à l'homogénéité apparente des mouvements dans l'étendue. Mais justement parce que nous avons éliminé les éléments, atomes ou autres, que ces mouvements auraient pour siège, il ne peut plus être question ici du mouvement qui est l'accident d'un mobile, du mouvement abstrait que la mécanique étudie et qui n'est, au fond, que la commune mesure des mouvements concrets. Comment ce mouvement abstrait, qui devient immobilité quand on change de point de repère, pourrait-il fonder des changements réels, c'est-à-dire sentis ? Comment, composé d'une série de positions instantanées, remplirait-il une durée dont les parties se prolongent et se continuent les unes dans les autres ? Une seule hypothèse reste donc possible, c'est que le mouvement concret, capable, comme la conscience, de prolonger son passé dans son présent, capable, en se répétant, d'engendrer les qualités sensibles, soit déjà quelque chose de la conscience, déjà quelque chose de la sensation. Il serait cette même sensation diluée, répartie sur un nombre infiniment plus grand de moments, cette même sensation vibrant, comme nous disions, à l'intérieur de sa chrysalide. Alors un dernier point resterait à élucider : comment s'opère la contraction, non plus sans doute de mouvements homogènes en qualités distinctes, mais de changements moins hétérogènes en changements plus hétérogènes ? Mais à cette question répond notre analyse de la perception concrète : cette perception, synthèse vivante de la perception pure et de la mémoire pure, résume nécessairement dans son apparente simplicité une multiplicité énorme de moments. Entre les qualités sensibles envisagées dans notre représentation, et ces mêmes qualités traitées comme des changements calculables, il n'y a donc qu'une différence de rythme de durée, une différence de tension intérieure. Ainsi, par l'idée de tension nous avons cherché à lever l'opposition de la qualité à la quantité, comme par l'idée d'extension celle de l'inétendu à l'étendu. Extension et tension admettent des degrés multiples, mais toujours déterminés. La fonction de l'entendement est de détacher de ces deux genres, extension et tension, leur contenant vide, c'est-à-dire l'espace homogène et la quantité pure, de substituer par là à des réalités souples, qui comportent des degrés, des abstractions rigides, nées des besoins de l'action, qu'on ne peut que prendre ou laisser, et de poser ainsi à la pensée réfléchie des dilemmes dont aucune alternative n'est acceptée par les choses. 3º Mais si l'on envisage ainsi les rapports de l'étendu à l'inétendu, de la qualité à la quantité, on aura moins de peine à comprendre la troisième et dernière opposition, celle de la liberté à la nécessité. La nécessité absolue serait représentée par une équivalence parfaite des moments successifs de la durée les uns aux autres. En est-il ainsi de la durée de l'univers matériel ? Chacun de ses moments pourrait-il se déduire mathématiquement du précédent ? Nous avons supposé dans tout ce travail, pour la commodité de l'étude, qu'il en était bien ainsi ; et telle est en effet la distance entre le rythme de notre durée et celui de l'écoulement des choses que la contingence du cours de la nature, si profondément étudiée par une philosophie récente, doit équivaloir pratiquement pour nous à la nécessité. Conservons donc notre hypothèse, qu'il y aurait pourtant lieu d'atténuer. Même alors, la liberté ne sera pas dans la nature comme un empire dans un empire. Nous disions que cette nature pouvait être considérée comme une conscience neutralisée et par conséquent latente, une conscience dont les manifestations éventuelles se tiendraient réciproquement en échec et s'annuleraient au moment précis où elles veulent paraître. Les premières lueurs qu'y vient jeter une conscience individuelle ne l'éclairent donc pas d'une lumière inattendue : cette conscience n'a fait qu'écarter un obstacle, extraire du tout réel une partie virtuelle, choisir et dégager enfin ce qui l'intéressait; et si, par cette sélection intelligente, elle témoigne bien qu'elle tient de l'esprit sa forme, c'est de la nature qu'elle tire sa matière. En même temps d'ailleurs que nous assistons à l'éclosion de cette conscience, nous voyons se dessiner des corps vivants, capables, sous leur forme la plus simple, de mouvements spontanés et imprévus. Le progrès de la matière vivante consiste dans une différenciation des fonctions qui amène la formation d'abord, puis la complication graduelle d'un système nerveux capable de canaliser des excitations et d'organiser des actions : plus les centres supérieurs se développent, plus nombreuses deviendront les voies motrices entre lesquelles une même excitation proposera à l'action un choix. Une latitude de plus en plus grande laissée au mouvement dans l'espace, voilà bien en effet ce qu'on voit. Ce qu'on ne voit pas, c'est la tension croissante et concomitante de la conscience dans le temps. Non seulement, par sa mémoire des expériences déjà anciennes, cette conscience retient de mieux en mieux le passé pour l'organiser avec le présent dans une décision plus riche et plus neuve, mais vivant d'une vie plus intense, contractant, par sa mémoire de l'expérience immédiate, un nombre croissant de moments extérieurs dans sa durée présente, elle devient plus capable de créer des actes dont l'indétermination interne, devant se répartir sur une multiplicité aussi grande qu'on voudra des moments de la matière, passera d'autant plus facilement à travers les mailles de la nécessité. Ainsi, qu'on l'envisage dans le temps ou dans l'espace, la liberté paraît toujours pousser dans la nécessité des racines profondes et s'organiser intimement avec elle. L'esprit emprunte à la matière les perceptions d'où il tire sa nourriture, et les lui rend sous forme de mouvement, où il a imprimé sa liberté.
e: I. – The idea that we have drawn from the facts and confirmed by reasoning is that our body is an instrument of action, and of action only. In no degree, in no sense, under no aspect does it serve to prepare, still less to explain, a representation. Is it a question of external perception? There is only a difference of degree, and not of kind, between the so-called perceptive faculties of the brain and the reflex functions of the spinal cord. Whereas the cord transforms the disturbances received into movement more or less necessarily executed, the brain puts them in relation with motor mechanisms more or less freely chosen; but what is explained by the brain in our perceptions is our actions begun, or prepared, or suggested, not our perceptions themselves. – Is it a question of recollection? The body preserves motor habits capable of playing the past anew; it can resume attitudes into which the past will be inserted; or again, by the repetition of certain cerebral phenomena that have prolonged former perceptions, it will furnish recollection with a point of attachment with the actual, a means of reconquering over present reality an influence it had lost: but in no case will the brain store up recollections or images. Thus neither in perception, nor in memory, nor, still less, in the higher operations of the mind, does the body contribute directly to representation. In developing this hypothesis under its manifold aspects, in thus pushing dualism to the extreme, we seemed to be digging between body and mind an impassable abyss. In reality we were indicating the only possible means of bringing them together and uniting them. II. – All the difficulties that this problem raises, whether in vulgar dualism, in materialism or in idealism, come from the fact that, in the phenomena of perception and memory, the physical and the moral are considered as duplicates of one another. Shall I take up the materialist standpoint of consciousness as epiphenomenon? I do not understand at all why certain cerebral phenomena are accompanied by consciousness, that is, what purpose is served by, or how there comes about, the conscious repetition of the material universe which was posited at the outset. – Shall I go over to idealism? Then I shall give myself nothing but perceptions, and my body will be one of them. But while observation shows me that the perceived images are turned upside down from top to bottom by very slight variations of the one I call my body (since it is enough for me to close my eyes for my visual universe to vanish), science assures me that all phenomena must succeed and condition one another in a determinate order, in which the effects are rigorously proportioned to the causes. I shall therefore be obliged to look, in this image that I call my body, and which follows me everywhere, for changes that are the equivalents – this time well regulated and exactly measured against one another – of the images that succeed one another around my body: the cerebral movements, which I thus find again, will once more become the duplicate of my perceptions. It is true that these movements will be perceptions still, "possible" perceptions, so that this second hypothesis is more intelligible than the other; but in return it will in its turn have to suppose an inexplicable correspondence between my real perception of things and my possible perception of certain cerebral movements that in no way resemble those things. Let us look closely: we shall see that the stumbling-block of every idealism lies there; it lies in this passage from the order that appears to us in perception to the order that succeeds with us in science – or, if it is more particularly a question of Kantian idealism, in the passage from sensibility to understanding. – There would remain, then, vulgar dualism. I shall place matter on one side and mind on the other, and suppose that the cerebral movements are the cause or the occasion of my representation of objects. But if they are its cause, if they suffice to produce it, I shall fall back, step by step, on the materialist hypothesis of consciousness as epiphenomenon. If they are only its occasion, it is because they in no way resemble it; and stripping matter of all the qualities that I conferred on it in my representation, it is to idealism that I shall return. Idealism and materialism are therefore the two poles between which this kind of dualism will always oscillate; and when, in order to maintain the duality of substances, it decides to put the two on the same footing, it will be led to see in them two translations of one and the same original, two parallel developments, regulated in advance, of one and the same principle, and so to deny their reciprocal influence and, by an inevitable consequence, to sacrifice freedom. Now, digging beneath these three hypotheses, I discover in them a common ground: they hold the elementary operations of the mind, perception and memory, to be operations of pure knowledge. What they place at the origin of consciousness is sometimes the useless duplicate of an external reality, sometimes the inert matter of a wholly disinterested intellectual construction; but they always neglect the relation of perception to action and of recollection to conduct. Now, we can no doubt conceive, as an ideal limit, a disinterested memory and a disinterested perception; but, in fact, it is towards action that perception and memory are turned, and it is this action that the body prepares. Is it a question of perception? The growing complexity of the nervous system puts the disturbance received into relation with an ever more considerable variety of motor apparatus, and thus causes a greater and greater number of possible actions to be sketched simultaneously. Do we consider memory? Its first function is to evoke all the past perceptions analogous to a present perception, to recall to us what preceded and what followed, and thus to suggest to us the most useful decision. But that is not all. By making us grasp, in a single intuition, multiple moments of duration, it frees us from the flowing movement of things, that is, from the rhythm of necessity. The more of these moments it can contract into one, the firmer the hold it will give us on matter; so that the memory of a living being appears to measure, above all, the power of its action on things, and to be only its intellectual repercussion. Let us start, then, from this power of acting as from the true principle; let us suppose that the body is a centre of action, a centre of action only, and let us see what consequences will flow from this for perception, for memory, and for the relations of body with mind. III. – For perception first. Here is my body with its "perceptive centres." These centres are disturbed, and I have the representation of things. On the other hand, I supposed that these disturbances could neither produce nor translate my perception. It is therefore outside them. Where is it? I cannot hesitate: in positing my body, I posited a certain image, but by that very fact also the totality of the other images, since there is no material object that does not owe its qualities, its determinations, its existence in short to the place it occupies in the whole of the universe. My perception, then, can only be something of these objects themselves; it is in them rather than they in it. But what exactly is it of these objects? I see that my perception appears to follow the whole detail of the nervous disturbances called sensory, and on the other hand I know that the rôle of these disturbances is solely to prepare reactions of my body upon the surrounding bodies, to sketch my virtual actions. It follows that to perceive consists in detaching, from the whole of the objects, the possible action of my body upon them. Perception is then only a selection. It creates nothing; its rôle is, on the contrary, to eliminate from the whole of the images all those on which I should have no hold, and then, from each of the retained images themselves, everything that does not interest the needs of the image I call my body. Such is at least the very simplified explanation, the schematic description, of what we have called pure perception. Let us mark at once the position we thereby took between realism and idealism. That all reality has a kinship, an analogy, a relation in short with consciousness, is what we conceded to idealism by the very fact of calling things "images." No philosophical doctrine, moreover, provided it is consistent with itself, can escape this conclusion. But if we were to gather together all the states of consciousness, past, present and possible, of all conscious beings, we should have exhausted by that, in our view, only a very small part of material reality, because images overflow perception on all sides. It is precisely these images that science and metaphysics would like to reconstitute, restoring in its integrality a chain of which our perception holds only a few links. But in order thus to establish between perception and reality the relation of part to whole, it was necessary to leave to perception its true rôle, which is to prepare actions. This idealism does not do. Why does it fail, as we were saying just now, to pass from the order that manifests itself in perception to the order that succeeds in science, that is, from the contingency with which our sensations appear to succeed one another to the determinism that binds the phenomena of nature? Precisely because it attributes to consciousness, in perception, a speculative rôle, so that one no longer sees at all what interest this consciousness could have in letting escape, between two sensations, for example, the intermediaries by which the second is deduced from the first. It is these intermediaries and their rigorous order that then remain obscure, whether one raises these intermediaries to the rank of "possible sensations," in Mill's expression, or whether one attributes this order, as Kant does, to the substructions established by the impersonal understanding. But let us suppose that my conscious perception has a wholly practical destination, that it simply outlines, in the whole of things, what interests my possible action upon them: I understand that all the rest escapes me, and that all the rest, nevertheless, is of the same nature as what I perceive. My knowledge of matter is then neither subjective, as it is for English idealism, nor relative, as Kantian idealism would have it. It is not subjective, because it is in things rather than in me. It is not relative, because there is not between the "phenomenon" and the "thing" the relation of appearance to reality, but simply that of part to whole. By this we seemed to return to realism. But realism, unless it is corrected on one essential point, is as unacceptable as idealism, and for the same reason. Idealism, we said, cannot pass from the order that manifests itself in perception to the order that succeeds in science, that is, to reality. Conversely, realism fails to derive from reality the immediate knowledge we have of it. Do we take our stand in vulgar realism? We have on one side a multiple matter, composed of parts more or less independent, diffused in space, and on the other a mind that can have no point of contact with it, unless it be, as the materialists would have it, its unintelligible epiphenomenon. Do we prefer to consider Kantian realism? Between the thing in itself, that is, the real, and the sensible diversity with which we construct our knowledge, we find no conceivable relation, no common measure. Now, on probing these two extreme forms of realism, we see them converge on one and the same point: both set up homogeneous space as a barrier between the intelligence and things. Naive realism makes of this space a real medium in which things would be suspended; Kantian realism sees in it an ideal medium in which the multiplicity of sensations is coordinated; but for the one and the other this medium is given first, as the necessary condition of what comes to be placed in it. And on probing this common hypothesis in its turn, we find that it consists in attributing to homogeneous space a disinterested rôle, whether it renders to material reality the service of supporting it, or whether it has the function, still wholly speculative, of furnishing sensations with the means of coordinating themselves with one another. So that the obscurity of realism, like that of idealism, comes from the fact that it directs our conscious perception, and the conditions of our conscious perception, towards pure knowledge, not towards action. – But let us now suppose that this homogeneous space is not logically prior but posterior to material things and to the pure knowledge we can have of them; let us suppose that extension precedes space; let us suppose that homogeneous space concerns our action, and our action only, being like an infinitely divided net that we stretch beneath material continuity in order to make ourselves masters of it, to decompose it in the direction of our activities and our needs. Then we gain not only that we rejoin science, which shows us each thing exerting its influence on all the others, and therefore occupying in a certain sense the totality of extension (although we perceive of this thing only its centre, and arrest its limits at the point where our body would cease to have a hold on it). We gain not only, in metaphysics, that we resolve or attenuate the contradictions raised by divisibility in space, contradictions which always arise, as we have shown, from our failing to dissociate the two points of view of action and of knowledge. We gain above all that we bring down the insurmountable barrier that realism raised between extended things and the perception we have of them. For whereas one posited on one side a multiple and divided external reality, and on the other sensations foreign to extension and without possible contact with it, we perceive that concrete extension is not really divided, any more than immediate perception is truly inextensive. Having set out from realism, we come back to the very point to which idealism had led us; we replace perception in things. And we see realism and idealism very near to coinciding, as we set aside the postulate, accepted without discussion by both, which served them as a common limit. To sum up, if we suppose an extended continuity, and, within this very continuity, the centre of real action which is figured by our body, this activity will appear to illumine with its light all the parts of matter on which at each instant it would have a hold. The same needs, the same power of acting, which cut out our body from matter, will delimit distinct bodies in the surroundings that environ us. Everything will happen as if we let the real action of external things filter through, in order to arrest and retain its virtual action: this virtual action of things upon our body and of our body upon things is our perception itself. But since the disturbances that our body receives from surrounding bodies ceaselessly determine, in its substance, nascent reactions, and since these interior movements of the cerebral substance thus give at every moment the sketch of our possible action upon things, the cerebral state corresponds exactly to perception. It is neither its cause, nor its effect, nor, in any sense, its duplicate: it simply continues it, perception being our virtual action and the cerebral state our action begun. IV. – But this theory of "pure perception" had to be at once attenuated and completed on two points. This pure perception, in fact, which would be like a fragment detached just as it is from reality, would belong to a being who did not mingle with the perception of other bodies that of his own body, that is, his affections, nor with his intuition of the present moment that of other moments, that is, his recollections. In other words, we first treated, for the convenience of study, the living body as a mathematical point in space and conscious perception as a mathematical instant in time. It was necessary to restore to the body its extension and to perception its duration. By this we reinstated in consciousness its two subjective elements, affectivity and memory. What is an affection? Our perception, we said, outlines the possible action of our body upon other bodies. But our body, being extended, is capable of acting upon itself as well as upon others. Something of our body will therefore enter into our perception. However, when it is a question of surrounding bodies, they are, by hypothesis, separated from ours by a space more or less considerable, which measures the remoteness in time of their promises or their threats: that is why our perception of these bodies outlines only possible actions. On the contrary, the more the distance between these bodies and ours decreases, the more the possible action tends to be transformed into real action, the action becoming the more urgent the less considerable the distance. And when this distance becomes nil, that is, when the body to be perceived is our own body, it is a real action, and no longer a virtual one, that perception outlines. Such is precisely the nature of pain, the actual effort of the injured part to set things right again, a local, isolated effort, and by that very fact condemned to failure in an organism which is fit now only for effects of the whole. Pain is therefore at the place where it is produced, as the object is at the place where it is perceived. Between the affection felt and the image perceived there is this difference, that the affection is within our body, the image outside our body. And this is why the surface of our body, the common limit of this body and of other bodies, is given to us at once in the form of sensations and in the form of image. In this interiority of affective sensation consists its subjectivity, in this exteriority of images in general their objectivity. But here we find again the ever-recurring error that we have pursued throughout the whole course of our work. It is held that sensation and perception exist for themselves; a wholly speculative rôle is attributed to them; and since one has neglected those real and virtual actions with which they form one body and which would serve to distinguish them, one can find between them no more than a difference of degree. Then, taking advantage of the fact that affective sensation is only vaguely localised (because of the confusion of the effort it envelops), it is at once declared inextensive; and of these diminished affections or inextensive sensations are made the materials with which we are supposed to construct images in space. By this one condemns oneself to explaining neither whence come the elements of consciousness or sensations, which one posits as so many absolutes, nor how, being inextensive, these sensations join space in order to be coordinated there, nor why they adopt there one order rather than another, nor finally by what means they succeed in constituting there a stable experience, common to all men. It is on the contrary from this experience, the necessary theatre of our activity, that we must start. It is therefore pure perception, that is, the image, that we must give ourselves first. And sensations, far from being the materials with which the image is fabricated, will then appear on the contrary as the impurity that mingles with it, being what we project of our body into all the others. V. – But so long as we remain with sensation and pure perception, we can hardly say that we have to do with mind. No doubt we establish, against the theory of consciousness as epiphenomenon, that no cerebral state is the equivalent of a perception. No doubt the selection of perceptions from among images in general is the effect of a discernment which already announces mind. No doubt, finally, the material universe itself, defined as the totality of images, is a kind of consciousness, a consciousness in which everything compensates and neutralises itself, a consciousness all of whose eventual parts, balancing one another by reactions always equal to the actions, reciprocally prevent one another from standing out. But in order to touch the reality of mind, we must place ourselves at the point where an individual consciousness, prolonging and preserving the past in a present which is enriched by it, thus withdraws from the very law of necessity, which requires that the past should ceaselessly succeed itself in a present that simply repeats it under another form, and that everything should always flow away. In passing from pure perception to memory, we definitively left matter for mind. VI. – The theory of memory, which forms the centre of our work, was to be at once the theoretical consequence and the experimental verification of our theory of pure perception. That the cerebral states which accompany perception are neither its cause nor its duplicate, that perception maintains with its physiological concomitant the relation of virtual action to action begun, is what we could not establish by facts, since everything will happen in our hypothesis as if perception resulted from the cerebral state. In pure perception, indeed, the perceived object is a present object, a body which modifies our own. The image of it is therefore actually given, and the facts accordingly allow us indifferently to say (at the risk of being very unequally consistent with ourselves) that the cerebral modifications sketch the nascent reactions of our body or that they create the conscious duplicate of the present image. But it is quite otherwise with memory, for the recollection is the representation of an absent object. Here the two hypotheses will give opposite consequences. If, in the case of a present object, a state of our body already sufficed to create the representation of the object, then a fortiori will this state still suffice in the case of the same object absent. It will therefore be necessary, in this theory, that the recollection should arise from the attenuated repetition of the cerebral phenomenon which occasioned the first perception, and consist simply in a weakened perception. Whence this twofold thesis: Memory is only a function of the brain, and there is only a difference of intensity between perception and recollection. – On the contrary, if the cerebral state in no way engendered our perception of the present object but simply continued it, it will still be able to prolong and to bring to completion the recollection that we evoke of it, but not to give it birth. And as, on the other hand, our perception of the present object was something of that object itself, our representation of the absent object will be a phenomenon of quite another order than perception, since between presence and absence there is no degree, no middle term. Whence this twofold thesis, the inverse of the preceding: Memory is something other than a function of the brain, and there is not a difference of degree, but of kind, between perception and recollection. – The opposition of the two theories then takes a sharp form, and experience can this time decide between them. We shall not return here to the detail of the verification we attempted. Let us simply recall its essential points. All the arguments of fact that can be invoked in favour of a probable accumulation of recollections in the cortical substance are drawn from the localised diseases of memory. But if recollections were really deposited in the brain, definite lesions of the brain would correspond to clear-cut losses of memory. Now, in the amnesias in which a whole period of our past existence, for example, is suddenly and radically torn from memory, no precise cerebral lesion is observed; and on the contrary, in the disturbances of memory in which the cerebral localisation is clear and certain, that is, in the various aphasias and in the diseases of visual or auditory recognition, it is not such and such determinate recollections that are torn, as it were, from the place where they would be seated, it is the faculty of recall that is more or less diminished in its vitality, as if the subject had more or less difficulty in bringing his recollections into contact with the present situation. It is therefore the mechanism of this contact that would have to be studied, in order to see whether the rôle of the brain might not be to ensure its working, rather than to imprison the recollections themselves in its cells. We were thus led to follow in all its evolutions the progressive movement by which past and present come into contact with one another, that is, recognition. And we found, in fact, that the recognition of a present object could be effected in two absolutely different ways, but that in neither case did the brain behave as a reservoir of images. Sometimes, in fact, by a wholly passive recognition, acted rather than thought, the body makes a movement that has become automatic correspond to a renewed perception: everything is then explained by the motor apparatus that habit has set up in the body, and lesions of memory may result from the destruction of these mechanisms. Sometimes, on the contrary, recognition is effected actively, by memory-images that move forward to meet the present perception; but then it is necessary that these recollections, at the moment of settling upon the perception, should find the means of actuating in the brain the same apparatus that perception ordinarily brings into play in order to act: otherwise, condemned in advance to impotence, they will have no tendency to actualise themselves. And that is why, in all the cases in which a lesion of the brain attacks a certain category of recollections, the recollections attacked do not resemble one another, for example, in belonging to the same epoch, or in having a logical kinship with one another, but simply in being all auditory, or all visual, or all motor. What appears to be injured, therefore, is the various sensory and motor regions or, more often still, the appendages which make it possible to actuate them from within the cortex itself, rather than the recollections themselves. We went further, and, by a careful study of the recognition of words as well as of the phenomena of sensory aphasia, we tried to establish that recognition was not effected at all by a mechanical awakening of recollections lying dormant in the brain. It implies, on the contrary, a tension of consciousness more or less high, which goes to seek in pure memory the pure recollections, in order to materialise them progressively in contact with the present perception. But what is this pure memory, and what are these pure recollections? In answering this question we were completing the demonstration of our thesis. We had just established its first point, namely that memory is something other than a function of the brain. It remained for us to show, by the analysis of "pure recollection", that there is not between recollection and perception a mere difference of degree, but a radical difference of nature. VII. – Let us point out at once the metaphysical, and no longer merely psychological, bearing of this last problem. It is doubtless a thesis of pure psychology that recollection is a weakened perception. But let there be no mistake: if recollection is only a weaker perception, then conversely perception will be something like a more intense recollection. Now, the germ of English idealism lies there. This idealism consists in seeing only a difference of degree, and not of nature, between the reality of the perceived object and the ideality of the conceived object. And the idea that we construct matter out of our inner states, that perception is only a true hallucination, comes from there likewise. It is this idea that we have never ceased to combat when we treated of matter. Either, then, our conception of matter is false, or recollection is radically distinct from perception. We have thus transposed a metaphysical problem to the point of making it coincide with a problem of psychology, which simple observation can decide. How does it decide it? If the recollection of a perception were only that perception weakened, it would happen to us, for example, to take the perception of a faint sound for the recollection of an intense noise. Now, such a confusion never occurs. But we can go further, and prove, again by observation, that the consciousness of a recollection never begins by being a weaker actual state which we would seek to throw back into the past after having become aware of its weakness: how indeed, if we did not already have the representation of a previously lived past, could we relegate to it the least intense psychological states, when it would be so simple to juxtapose them to the strong states, as a more confused present experience to a clearer present experience? The truth is that memory does not at all consist in a regression from the present to the past, but on the contrary in a progress from the past to the present. It is in the past that we place ourselves at once. We start from a "virtual state", which we lead little by little, through a series of different planes of consciousness, to the point where it is materialised in an actual perception, that is to say to the point where it becomes a present and acting state, that is to say, finally, to that extreme plane of our consciousness where our body is outlined. In this virtual state pure recollection consists. Whence comes it that the testimony of consciousness is here disregarded? Whence comes it that recollection is made into a weaker perception, of which we can say neither why we throw it back into the past, nor how we recover its date, nor by what right it reappears at one moment rather than another? Always from the fact that the practical destination of our actual psychological states is forgotten. Perception is made into a disinterested operation of the mind, a mere contemplation. Then, since pure recollection can evidently be only something of this kind (as it does not correspond to a present and pressing reality), recollection and perception become states of the same nature, between which only a difference of intensity can any longer be found. But the truth is that our present is not to be defined as that which is more intense: it is what acts upon us and what makes us act, it is sensory and it is motor; – our present is above all the state of our body. Our past, on the contrary, is what no longer acts, but might act, what will act by inserting itself into a present sensation from which it will borrow its vitality. It is true that at the moment when the recollection is thus actualised by acting, it ceases to be recollection, it becomes perception again. We then understand why recollection could not result from a cerebral state. The cerebral state continues the recollection; it gives it a hold on the present through the materiality which it confers upon it; but pure recollection is a spiritual manifestation. With memory we are truly and really in the domain of mind. VIII. – We had no need to explore this domain. Placed at the confluence of mind and matter, desirous above all of seeing them flow into one another, we had to retain of the spontaneity of the intelligence only its point of junction with a bodily mechanism. It is thus that we were able to witness the phenomenon of the association of ideas, and the birth of the simplest general ideas. What is the capital error of associationism? It is to have put all recollections on the same plane, to have disregarded the more or less considerable distance which separates them from the present bodily state, that is to say from action. Hence it has been able to explain neither how the recollection adheres to the perception which evokes it, nor why the association takes place by resemblance or contiguity rather than in any other way, nor finally by what caprice this particular recollection is chosen from among the thousand recollections which resemblance or contiguity would equally well attach to the actual perception. This is to say that associationism has blurred and confounded all the different planes of consciousness, obstinately seeing in a less complete recollection only a less complex recollection, whereas it is in reality a less dreamed recollection, that is to say one nearer to action and for that very reason more commonplace, more capable of moulding itself – like a ready-made garment – on the novelty of the present situation. The adversaries of associationism have, moreover, followed it on to this ground. They reproach it with explaining the higher operations of the mind by associations, but not with misjudging the true nature of association itself. Yet there lies the original vice of associationism. Between the plane of action – the plane where our body has contracted its past into motor habits – and the plane of pure memory, where our mind preserves in all its details the picture of our vanished life, we have, on the contrary, thought we perceived thousands upon thousands of different planes of consciousness, thousands upon thousands of integral and yet diverse repetitions of the totality of our lived experience. To complete a recollection by more personal details does not at all consist in mechanically juxtaposing recollections to this recollection, but in transporting oneself to a more extended plane of consciousness, in moving away from action in the direction of dream. To localise a recollection consists no more in mechanically inserting it between other recollections, but in describing, by a growing expansion of memory in its integrality, a circle wide enough for this detail of the past to appear in it. These planes are not given, moreover, as ready-made things, superposed upon one another. They exist rather virtually, with that existence which is peculiar to the things of the mind. The intelligence, moving at every moment along the interval which separates them, finds them again, or rather continually creates them anew: its life consists in this very movement. Then we understand why the laws of association are resemblance and contiguity rather than other laws, and why memory chooses, among similar or contiguous recollections, certain images rather than other images, and finally how the first general notions are formed, by the combined work of body and mind. The interest of a living being is to seize in a present situation what resembles an earlier situation, and then to bring together with it what preceded and above all what followed, in order to profit by its past experience. Of all the associations that might be imagined, associations by resemblance and by contiguity are therefore at the outset the only ones that have a vital utility. But in order to understand the mechanism of these associations, and above all the seemingly capricious selection which they effect among recollections, we must place ourselves in turn on those two extreme planes which we have called the plane of action and the plane of dream. In the first there figure only motor habits, of which it may be said that they are associations acted or lived rather than represented: here, resemblance and contiguity are fused together, for analogous external situations, by repeating themselves, have ended by linking certain movements of our body with one another, and hence the same automatic reaction in which we shall unroll these contiguous movements will also extract from the situation which occasions them its resemblance to earlier situations. But as one passes from movements to images, and from poorer images to richer images, resemblance and contiguity become dissociated: they end by being opposed on that other extreme plane where no action adheres any longer to the images. The choice of one resemblance among many resemblances, of one contiguity among other contiguities, is therefore not made at random: it depends on the ceaselessly varying degree of tension of memory, which, according as it inclines more to insert itself into the present action or to detach itself from it, transposes itself as a whole into one key or another. And it is also this double movement of memory between its two extreme limits that outlines, as we have shown, the first general notions, motor habit rising towards similar images to extract their similarities, similar images descending again towards motor habit to be merged, for example, in the automatic pronunciation of the word that unites them. The nascent generality of the idea thus already consists in a certain activity of the mind, in a movement between action and representation. And that is why it will always be easy for a certain philosophy, we said, to localise the general idea at one of the two extremities, to make it crystallise into words or evaporate into recollections, whereas it consists in reality in the march of the mind which goes from one extremity to the other. IX. – In thus representing to ourselves elementary mental activity, in making this time of our body, with all that surrounds it, the last plane of our memory, the extreme image, the moving point which our past pushes at every moment into our future, we were confirming and clarifying what we had said of the rôle of the body, at the same time that we were preparing the way for a rapprochement between body and mind. After having studied in turn pure perception and pure memory, it remained for us in effect to bring them nearer to one another. If pure recollection is already mind, and if pure perception would still be something of matter, we ought, by placing ourselves at the point of junction between pure perception and pure recollection, to throw some light on the reciprocal action of mind and matter. In fact, "pure" perception, that is to say instantaneous perception, is only an ideal, a limit. Every perception occupies a certain thickness of duration, prolongs the past into the present, and thereby partakes of memory. Taking perception then under its concrete form, as a synthesis of pure recollection and pure perception, that is to say of mind and matter, we were narrowing within its tightest limits the problem of the union of soul and body. Such is the effort which we attempted chiefly in the last part of our work. The opposition of the two principles, in dualism in general, resolves itself into the threefold opposition of the unextended to the extended, of quality to quantity, and of freedom to necessity. If our conception of the rôle of the body, if our analyses of pure perception and pure recollection are to clarify in some respect the correlation of body to mind, it can only be on condition of removing or attenuating these three oppositions. Let us examine them then in turn, presenting here under a more metaphysical form the conclusions which we sought to draw from psychology alone. 1° If we imagine on the one side an extension really divided into corpuscles, for example, on the other a consciousness with sensations in themselves inextensive which would come to be projected into space, we shall evidently find nothing in common between this matter and this consciousness, between body and mind. But this opposition of perception and matter is the artificial work of an understanding which decomposes and recomposes according to its habits or its laws: it is not given to immediate intuition. What is given is not inextensive sensations: how would they go and join space, choose a place in it, coordinate themselves in it at last so as to construct a universal experience? What is real is no more an extension divided into independent parts: how indeed, having thus no possible relation with our consciousness, would it unroll a series of changes whose order and relations would correspond exactly to the order and relations of our representations? What is given, what is real, is something intermediate between divided extension and the pure unextended; it is what we have called the extensive. Extension is the most apparent quality of perception. It is by consolidating it and subdividing it by means of an abstract space, stretched by us beneath it for the needs of action, that we constitute multiple and indefinitely divisible extension. It is by subtilising it, on the contrary, by making it in turn dissolve into affective sensations and evaporate into counterfeits of pure ideas, that we obtain those inextensive sensations with which we then vainly seek to reconstitute images. And the two opposite directions in which we pursue this double work open themselves to us quite naturally, for it results from the very necessities of action that extension is cut up for us into absolutely independent objects (whence an indication for subdividing extension), and that we pass by insensible degrees from affection to perception (whence a tendency to suppose perception more and more inextensive). But our understanding, whose rôle is precisely to establish logical distinctions and consequently sharp oppositions, darts into the two paths in turn, and in each of them goes to the end. It thus erects, at one extremity, an indefinitely divisible extension, at the other absolutely inextensive sensations. And it thus creates the opposition of which it afterwards gives itself the spectacle. 2° Much less artificial is the opposition of quality to quantity, that is to say of consciousness to movement: but this second opposition is radical only if we begin by accepting the first. Suppose, in effect, that the qualities of things are reduced to inextensive sensations affecting a consciousness, so that these qualities represent only, as so many symbols, homogeneous and calculable changes taking place in space, you will have to imagine between these sensations and these changes an incomprehensible correspondence. Renounce, on the contrary, establishing between them a priori this factitious contrariety: you will see all the barriers which seemed to separate them fall one by one. First, it is not true that consciousness witnesses, rolled up upon itself, an inner procession of inextensive perceptions. It is therefore in the perceived things themselves that you will replace pure perception, and you will thus set aside a first obstacle. You meet, it is true, a second: the homogeneous and calculable changes on which science operates seem to belong to multiple and independent elements, such as atoms, of which they would be only the accident; this multiplicity will interpose itself between perception and its object. But if the division of extension is purely relative to our possible action upon it, the idea of independent corpuscles is a fortiori schematic and provisional; science itself, moreover, authorises us to set it aside. Here is a second barrier fallen. One last interval remains to be crossed: that which lies between the heterogeneity of qualities and the apparent homogeneity of movements in extension. But precisely because we have eliminated the elements, atoms or others, in which these movements would have their seat, there can no longer be question here of the movement which is the accident of a mobile, of abstract movement, which mechanics studies and which is at bottom only the common measure of concrete movements. How could this abstract movement, which becomes immobility when we change the point of reference, found real changes, that is to say felt changes? How, composed of a series of instantaneous positions, would it fill a duration whose parts prolong and continue one another? One hypothesis alone therefore remains possible, namely that concrete movement, capable, like consciousness, of prolonging its past into its present, capable, by repeating itself, of engendering sensible qualities, is already something of consciousness, already something of sensation. It would be this same sensation diluted, distributed over an infinitely greater number of moments, this same sensation vibrating, as we said, within its chrysalis. Then one last point would remain to be elucidated: how is effected the contraction, no longer indeed of homogeneous movements into distinct qualities, but of less heterogeneous changes into more heterogeneous changes? But to this question our analysis of concrete perception replies: this perception, living synthesis of pure perception and pure memory, necessarily sums up in its apparent simplicity an enormous multiplicity of moments. Between the sensible qualities envisaged in our representation, and these same qualities treated as calculable changes, there is therefore only a difference of rhythm of duration, a difference of inner tension. Thus, by the idea of tension we have sought to remove the opposition of quality to quantity, as by the idea of extension that of the unextended to the extended. Extension and tension admit of multiple degrees, but always determinate ones. The function of the understanding is to detach from these two kinds, extension and tension, their empty container, that is to say homogeneous space and pure quantity, to substitute thereby for supple realities, which admit of degrees, rigid abstractions, born of the needs of action, which can only be taken or left, and so to pose to reflective thought dilemmas of which no alternative is accepted by things. 3° But if we thus envisage the relations of the extended to the unextended, of quality to quantity, we shall have less difficulty in understanding the third and last opposition, that of freedom to necessity. Absolute necessity would be represented by a perfect equivalence of the successive moments of duration to one another. Is it so with the duration of the material universe? Could each of its moments be deduced mathematically from the preceding one? We have supposed throughout this work, for convenience of study, that it was indeed so; and such is in fact the distance between the rhythm of our duration and that of the flow of things that the contingency of the course of nature, so profoundly studied by a recent philosophy, must be practically equivalent for us to necessity. Let us therefore keep our hypothesis, which there would nevertheless be reason to attenuate. Even then, freedom will not be in nature as an empire within an empire. We said that this nature might be regarded as a neutralised and consequently latent consciousness, a consciousness whose eventual manifestations would hold one another reciprocally in check and cancel out at the very moment when they wish to appear. The first gleams which an individual consciousness comes to cast upon it do not therefore light it with an unexpected light: this consciousness has only removed an obstacle, extracted from the real whole a virtual part, chosen and disengaged, in short, what interested it; and if, by this intelligent selection, it bears witness that it holds its form from mind, it is from nature that it draws its matter. At the same time, moreover, that we witness the dawning of this consciousness, we see living bodies outlined, capable, in their simplest form, of spontaneous and unforeseen movements. The progress of living matter consists in a differentiation of functions which brings about first the formation, then the gradual complication, of a nervous system capable of channelling excitations and organising actions: the more the higher centres develop, the more numerous will become the motor paths among which one and the same excitation proposes a choice to action. A latitude ever greater left to movement in space, that indeed is what one sees. What one does not see is the increasing and concomitant tension of consciousness in time. Not only, by its memory of already distant experiences, does this consciousness retain the past better and better in order to organise it with the present in a richer and newer decision, but, living a more intense life, contracting, by its memory of immediate experience, a growing number of external moments into its present duration, it becomes more capable of creating acts whose internal indetermination, having to be distributed over a multiplicity of moments of matter as great as one pleases, will pass all the more easily through the meshes of necessity. Thus, whether it be envisaged in time or in space, freedom seems always to thrust deep roots into necessity and to be organised intimately with it. The mind borrows from matter the perceptions from which it draws its nourishment, and gives them back to it in the form of movement, on which it has stamped its freedom.
